Flax (Linum usitatissimum) is an annual plant grown for its fiber and oil-rich seeds (linseed).

Magickal Properties

  • Gender: Masculine
  • Planet: Mercury
  • Element: Fire
  • Deity: Hulda
  • Powers: Money, Protection, Beauty, Psychic Powers, Healing

Folk Names

Linseed

Ritual Uses

Offered in rites to Hulda (Holle), who taught mortals the arts of spinning and weaving. Flax was once among the plants most closely tied to women's primal power, and legend credits Hulda with first bringing flax to people. The spinning of flax runs through many fairy tales. Linen was made from this plant in ancient Egypt. Flax is a protection against sorcery; kept in the home it protects against disturbing outside influences and promotes peace.

Magickal Uses

For money: Keep seeds in pocket, wallet, or purse. Keep a jar on the altar with coins and flax seed added daily. Flax in the shoe wards off poverty.

For protection and sleep: Blue flowers worn against sorcery. Flax plus mustard by the bed with a pan of water on the other side guards sleep.

For household warding: Red pepper with flax in a box prevents evil from entering.

For beauty and health: Children dancing in growing flax at age seven promotes beauty. Sprinkle altar with seed in healing. Tie a hank around loins for lumbago.

For divination: Drink a cup of flaxseed tea before beginning divination to enhance the process.

For dizziness: Run naked three times through a flax field after sunset to cure dizziness (traditional lore).

Meaning When Gifted

When flax is gifted it carries the meaning of domestic life.

Foxglove (Digitalis purpurea) is a tall biennial with pendulous, thimble‑shaped flowers; powerfully protective but dangerously poisonous.

Magickal Properties

Gender: Feminine (source: Cold)

Planet: Venus

Element: Water (source: Earth/Air)

Powers: Protection, Health, Creativity, Imagination

Entities: Astarte/Hathor, Freyja

Magickal Uses

Fairy lore: The markings on foxglove blossoms are said to be where elves have placed their fingers. The plant is sacred to fairies, and cultivating it in the garden invites their presence and protection.

Garden ward: Grown in the garden, foxglove welcomes the fairies and draws their protection, warding off unwelcome intruders and inviting the wisdom of other plants in through the fairy kingdom.

Love work: Under the dominion of Venus, foxglove lends itself to love spells and rituals, especially those concerned with empowerment and self-love.

Omen of true love: To spot a foxglove in the day is taken to mean you will see your true love before nightfall.

Cut flower caution: Bringing foxglove indoors as a cut flower is considered unlucky. It is a poison plant fiercely guarded by unseen forces from the Other World, so work it with care.

Old Welsh charm: Leaves were used to make a black dye to paint crossed lines on cottage stone floors to bar evil from entering.

The Hidden Language of the Bells

A Digitalis purpurea in full bloom is the source of its own fairy lore. Each pendulous bell carries an array of purple mottling, pinks, whites, and near-blacks arranged in patterns that look almost written, as though the fairies had penned secret messages inside the flower for those clear-sighted enough to read them.

Witch's Gloves and Thimbles

Few plants carry a longer string of common names, and the names themselves spell out the powers. Witch's Gloves and Goblin's Gloves describe witches and fairies slipping the little bells onto each finger when cavorting in the woods. Witch's Thimble and Lady's Thimble describe the same flowers worn while sewing magickal garments. Whatever the wearer, the flower is medicine and magick worn at the fingertip.

The Foxes and the Fairy Bells

The names foxglove and foxbell point to an older bond between fairies, foxes, and the plant. Fairies, the stories say, gave foxes the secret of the bells: slip the blossoms onto the paws to move silently into the chicken coop, and ring them softly to send a sound only other foxes can hear, warning the pack when a hunter is afoot. The story is strongest in Norse and Finnish telling. In Finland the fox is a sacred animal, and the aurora borealis is called foxfire, the sun reflecting off the tails of magickal foxes running across the sky. When a foxglove bends in still air, it is bowing to a passing fairy or other-worldly being.

The Legend of Knockgrafton

In Ireland the plant is fairy cap and also lusmore. A poor hunchback in the legend wears a sprig of the fairy cap in his hat at all times and is known by the name Lusmore. He encounters the fairies one night, joins their song in a manner that completes rather than interrupts it, and is rewarded with the lifting of his hump. A neighbour woman comes to learn his secret for her own son Jack. Jack is greedy, impatient, and cantankerous. He breaks into the fairy song rather than singing with it. The fairies do not lift his hump. They drag over Lusmore's discarded one and lay it onto Jack's back, doubling his burden, and he soon dies of it. The story is a warning to keep fairy time and fairy rhythm.

From Folk Cure to Cardiac Medicine

In 1785 William Withering recorded the foxglove as the active herb hidden inside a Shropshire wise-woman's family receipt for dropsy, a remedy of twenty or more herbs long kept secret and known for producing violent vomiting and purging while quietly drawing fluid from the body. Bruised, the herb yielded a juice he made into an ointment for the King's Evil. He went on to prescribe digitalis for asthma, shortness of breath, edema, dropsy, inflammation, ovarian cysts, gout, jaundice, weak pulse, consumption, swelling of the brain, enlarged liver, bladder stones, heart palpitations, paralysis, and a host of other ailments, many tied to heavy drinking or childbirth, with mixed results across leaves and root. The cardiac glycosides he was working with, digitoxin and digoxin, are still used today to treat heart failure and arrhythmia.

The Vegetable Drugs Committee

When drugs and nearly everything else fell short in Britain during the Second World War, a Vegetable Drugs Committee was formed to grow and gather foxglove from the public. Home gardeners, women's institutions, Boy Scouts, and Girl Scouts worked alongside doctors and botanists, raising and harvesting the plants that were then processed into digitoxin.

☠️
DEADLY POISON: Though known for healing properties (digitalis is used in heart medication), foxglove can cause serious problems, even death. Do not take internally. Lethal to cats. All parts of the plant are toxic.

Meaning When Gifted

When foxglove is gifted it carries the meaning of stateliness and youth.

Frankincense (Boswellia spp., especially Boswellia sacra) is a fragrant resin obtained from trees of the Boswellia genus, used since ancient times in religious and magical ceremonies. The Boswellia sacra tree is notably hardy, growing readily in difficult conditions, including directly out of solid rock. The resin is harvested by slashing the bark and allowing the sap to seep out and harden into rounded lumps known as tears.

Magickal Properties

  • Gender: Masculine
  • Planet: Sun
  • Element: Fire
  • Deities: Ra, Baal
  • Powers: Protection, Exorcism, Spirituality

Folk Names

Olibanum

Lore & History

Frankincense was one of the incenses burned by the ancient Hebrews in various sacrificial rites. The sweet-smelling smoke symbolized the divine name and was emblematic of prayer and humanity's connection to the divine. In the New Testament, frankincense was one of the gifts brought by the Magi to the infant Jesus alongside myrrh and gold, which some interpret as an allusion to his eventual role as a sacrificial figure. It has remained a core component of Catholic ritual to this day.

Agrippa wrote that frankincense is ruled by the sun and included it in his recipe for a fumigation to be used in solar workings.

Science lends support to the plant's solar, uplifting reputation: a 2008 study by researchers from Johns Hopkins University and the Hebrew University in Jerusalem found that incensole acetate, a chemical constituent of frankincense, lowered anxiety in mice. The implication is that frankincense may function as an effective natural antidepressant.

Ritual Uses

Burned at sunrise by the ancient Egyptians to honor Ra. Still used in church incenses.

Magickal Uses

For elevation and cleansing: Burn to raise vibrations, purify spaces, and drive out negativity.

For protection and exorcism: Add to blends for warding and banishing.

For visions and meditation: Burn to induce visions and aid deep meditation.

For luck and growth: Add to sachets to draw luck and spiritual growth.

For sacredness: Frankincense is used to consecrate sacred spaces and objects, and to honor the sacred in ritual.

Protective incense blend: Mix with cumin and burn as a powerful protective incense useful for general workings.

Egyptian Incense recipe: Frankincense, benzoin, and aloe wood.

Church Incense recipe: 10 oz frankincense, 4 oz powdered benzoin, 1 oz storax.

Substitution: Rosemary may be used if frankincense is unavailable.

Ancestor Veneration

Frankincense makes a powerful regular offering to the ancestors, particularly for those with Mediterranean heritage. It can also be burned specifically in times of hardship, or when seeking the ancestors' help in battling anxiety or depression, given its mood-lifting chemical properties.

To emphasize its solar qualities, burn frankincense immediately after sunrise on a Sunday.

Botanical Description

Frankincense (also known as olibanum or gum thus) is a handsome small tree or shrub with abundant pinnate leaves and white or pale pink flowers. It yields a natural oleo gum resin collected by making incisions into the bark; at first a milky-white liquid appears, which then solidifies into tear-shaped amber to orange-brown lumps between the size of a pea and a walnut.

Origin & Distribution

Native to the Red Sea region; grows wild throughout north-east Africa. The gum is mainly produced in Somalia, Ethiopia, China, and south Arabia, then distilled in Europe and, to a lesser extent, India.

Related Species

Other Boswellia species also yield olibanum gum, such as the Indian variety B. serrata. Constituents vary according to type and locality. The species Boswellia carteri is also commonly cited as a primary source of frankincense alongside B. sacra.

Folk Tradition

Used since antiquity as an incense in India, China, and the west by the Catholic Church. In ancient Egypt it was used in rejuvenating face masks, cosmetics, and perfumes. It has been used medicinally in the east and west for a wide range of conditions including syphilis, rheumatism, respiratory and urinary tract infections, skin diseases, as well as digestive and nervous complaints.

A Tree of Resilience

The Boswellia is a remarkably tough tree, taking root where there seems to be no soil at all and even drawing itself up out of bare stone by means of a sucker-like hold, and for this it has become an emblem of resilience. Its resin is gathered by slashing the bark so that the sap bleeds and hardens into the rounded lumps known as tears. The rising smoke is held to carry the thoughts and prayers of the faithful up to the heavens, and the fragrance itself was taken as a sign of life, mixed with oils to anoint newborn children. Paired with the myrrh used to embalm the dead, frankincense stands at the beginning of life as myrrh stands at its end, each a token of spiritual transformation.

Botanical Information

German Chamomile (Matricaria chamomilla or M. recutita) belongs to the Asteraceae family. This strongly aromatic annual reaches up to 60 cm tall, with a hairless erect branching stem, delicate feathery leaves, and simple daisy-like white flowers on single stems. Native to Europe and northern and western Asia, it is now naturalized across North America and Australia. Despite its common name, it is no longer cultivated in Germany; the bulk of commercial production is centred in Hungary and the rest of Eastern Europe.

Other Species

There are many varieties of chamomile, such as pineapple weed (Chamaemelium suaveolens) and Roman chamomile (Chamaemelum nobile), both of which are used to produce an essential oil. See Roman Chamomile and Roman Chamomile Essential Oil. Moroccan Chamomile (Ormenis multicaulis) is also marketed under the chamomile name, but it is only distantly related botanically and chemically and olfactorily distinct from both German and Roman chamomile; it is not a substitute for either. See also Moroccan Chamomile Essential Oil. In appearance German chamomile is very similar to corn chamomile (Anthemis arvensis) but can be distinguished from it because the latter is scentless. German chamomile shares many of the same qualities as Roman chamomile, except that its anti-inflammatory properties are greater due to the higher percentage of azulene.

Folk Tradition

A long-standing medicinal tradition, especially in Europe, for all states of tension and the visceral symptoms that can arise therefrom, such as nervous dyspepsia and nervous bowel, tension headaches, and sleeplessness; especially useful for all children's conditions, calming without depressing. An excellent skin care remedy.

German Chamomile Essential Oil

For the inky-blue, anti-inflammatory steam-distilled oil drawn from the flower heads, see German Chamomile Essential Oil.

Dual Nature and Associations

Chamomile holds two valid magickal associations depending on how you work with the plant. The bright, sunny appearance of its flowers and apple-like scent create solar associations linked to Apollo. However, the plant's watery, cooling nature and healing properties also connect it strongly to lunar energy. Both associations are supported by research and tradition.

Symbolism & Mythology

The chamomile flower draws its name from a Greek word meaning apple, a nod to the distinct apple scent the plant gives off, especially when its foliage is crushed. The Egyptians held it sacred to the Sun God Ra, and the Teutons in turn dedicated it to their own Sun God, Balder. Its protective reputation runs deep as well: a wreath of chamomile hung in the home is said to guard the house against thunder and lightning.

Financial Magick

Chamomile flowers have long been associated with financial prosperity. Gamblers traditionally washed their hands in chamomile infusions to attract money. The plant is added to love oils to draw a mate who is generous with their finances.

Cooling and Empowering Properties

In herbal medicine, chamomile is recognized as a cooling herb. It subdues hot flashes, excitability, and hysteria. Beyond its cooling nature, chamomile is profoundly empowering. It strengthens the emotionally weak and soothes heated tempers, anxiety, and heightened emotional states.

Magickal Uses

For prosperity: Use chamomile in prosperity charms and money-drawing sachets.

For meditation and sleep: Add to incenses intended to bring on restful states for meditation and sleep. Chamomile tea can induce sleep when taken before bed.

As a strewing herb: A common medieval strewing herb prized for its wonderful apple-like aroma. Can be added to magickal floor washes.

Ancient Egyptian use: Revered by the ancient Egyptians, who used it for many purposes including in massage oil and ritual offerings.

Burn chamomile flowers over incense charcoal for quick purification. Drink chamomile tea while grounding and centering to prepare for magickal work. Wash hands and feet in strong chamomile tea (no sugar) before job interviews, sales meetings, or loan proposals to attract good luck. Keep a sachet of chamomile (preferably purple) at your workspace to deflect bickering. Add Rowan to the sachet to be rewarded for maintaining peace. Fill a muslin tea bag with chamomile flowers and place inside your pillowcase to banish nightmares. Drinking chamomile tea before bed also prevents nightmares. Carry a chamomile sachet in your pocket to draw money for needed physical goods. Drink chamomile tea before difficult conversations to soothe anxiety while maintaining both boldness and tenderness.

History

Chamomile traces its origins to western Europe, India, and Asia. Its earliest documented use was as a remedy for fevers in ancient Egyptian medicine, and the Egyptians incorporated it into ritual offerings to their gods. It earned a reputation as something of a cure-all across Europe.

Characteristics

A low-growing perennial rarely exceeding ten inches in height. Beyond its well-known calming qualities, it is a bitter herb that supports the digestion of fats and settles the stomach. The chamomile family includes German, Hungarian, Roman, and English varieties.

Seasonal Associations

Season: Summer

Sabbats: Litha and Lughnasadh

Magickal Principle: Culmination and manifesting

Beauty & Skincare

Chamomile soothes reactive or sensitive skin and is used in hair rinses to brighten and condition light-colored hair. A chamomile infusion applied as a facial rinse can reduce redness and promote an even complexion.

Infant Protection

Bunches of chamomile hung above a baby's crib are used as a protective charm, shielding the child from harmful influences and malevolent spirits.

Magickal Teas

Chamomile tea serves as a magickal brew to promote calmness, deepen meditation, attract prosperity, and support purification. Drink 1 to 2 cups only during the spell event itself.

Moon Magick

Key themes for lunar workings: Money, peace, love, purification, communication.

Meaning When Gifted

When chamomile is gifted it carries the meaning of energy in action.

Recipe Grimoire

Creating Your Own Recipes

Once you've worked with established formulas for a while, you may feel the urge to create something entirely your own. This is natural. Just as experienced cooks develop original dishes, the magickal herbalist often wants to craft unique blends tailored to personal needs and energies.

You don't have to create your own recipes. There are enough formulas in traditional sources to keep you busy for years. But if you want to try, this guide walks through the process step by step.

Why Create Original Blends?

Mixtures you design yourself are intimately connected to your personal beliefs and energies. They may prove more powerful simply because they come from you. Traditional recipes certainly work, but there's something uniquely satisfying about crafting your own blends and witnessing their results.

Trust your intuition when selecting ingredients and proportions. And most importantly, have fun with the process.

Step One: Define the Goal

Every mixture begins with a clear magickal intention. Ask yourself what you need this blend to accomplish:

  • Bring money into your life
  • Ease depression or anxiety
  • Attract new love
  • Draw health or vitality
  • Provide protection
  • Create peace and calm
  • Increase personal power

You might be addressing an immediate need, or you might be preparing something for future use. Either way, start with a defined purpose.

Step Two: Choose the Form

Once you know your goal, decide what kind of product to make: incense, oil, bath salt, bath herbs, tincture, sachet, ointment, or something else.

Ask yourself these questions:

Which form suits this goal best?

Some forms work better for certain intentions. A protection incense won't help you at the office or during your commute. A protective oil or amulet would be more practical.

Which procedures do I know well?

Stick to processes you have experience with. Familiarity with a technique almost guarantees better results.

Which forms produce the best results for me?

If you find combustible incense (cones, blocks, sticks) less effective than loose incense on charcoal, go with noncombustible blends. If oil-anointed candles consistently work well for you, create an oil.

Remember: While these products contain their own energies, their effectiveness largely depends on their ability to shift you into a state of ritual consciousness.

Which forms do I enjoy using?

If you hate carrying sachets, don't make one. If slipping into an herb-scented bath gets your energy flowing, create bath salts or bath herbs.

Step Three: Select Your Ingredients

Now choose which herbs, oils, or other materials to include.

Start with correspondences. Check the Correspondence Grimoire for materials aligned with your magickal goal. For a protection blend, you'd look up protective herbs, oils, and resins.

Check your supplies. Compare your list against what you actually have on hand. If you're missing key ingredients, either obtain them or find suitable substitutes.

Expand through planetary and elemental connections. If you need more options, consult the planetary and elemental associations for your goal. Protection, for example, relates to the Sun, Mars, and the element of Fire. Any herb or oil ruled by these forces could potentially work in a protection formula.

Keeping an Inventory

Maintaining lists of your supplies saves enormous time. Keep a notebook near your herb cabinet with:

  1. Herbs and botanicals you currently have
  2. Oils in your collection
  3. Processing supplies (cheesecloth, bottles, eyedroppers, cloth, cord, thread, potassium nitrate, alcohol, etc.)
  4. Wish list of items you need to obtain

Update these lists whenever you use up or acquire something. This prevents the frustrating experience of rummaging through dozens of jars trying to figure out what you have.

Even well-organized herb cabinets become cluttered over time. A simple inventory system saves you from checking every bottle.

Step Four: Narrow Your List

Once you have a preliminary list of herbs from Step Three, compare it against your stock list. Cross out any you don't currently have.

Next, determine which herbs are most favorable to the type of product you've decided to make. Some ingredients are immediately inappropriate for certain forms.

For incense: Though garlic is a fine protective herb, it's best not to use it in incense formulas. The smell would be unpleasant and counterproductive. Cross inappropriate herbs off your list.

Test by burning: If necessary, light a charcoal block, place it in an incense burner, and burn a small amount of each remaining herb. Remove any that don't appeal to you. Trust your senses. If an herb smells wrong for your purpose, it probably is.

After this refinement process, you might end up with a shorter, more focused list. For a protection incense, you might have:

  • Rosemary
  • Basil
  • Orange peel
  • Cedar
  • Frankincense
  • Cinnamon
  • Pine
  • Juniper

In a sense, the recipe has formulated itself. After determining the relative amounts of each ingredient, you could mix these herbs, empower them, and burn as a protective incense.

Step Five: Create Combinations

You don't have to use every herb on your refined list. Create recipes using only a few. Some possible protective incense combinations:

Option 1Option 2Option 3Option 4
FrankincenseFrankincenseFrankincenseFrankincense

Many other combinations are possible. Notice that frankincense appears in each combination.

💡
Always Include a Resin

In general, use at least one gum resin in every incense recipe. Resins include frankincense, myrrh, benzoin, gum arabic, mastic, copal, and dragon's blood. Even if a resin doesn't appear on your correspondence lists, include one for best results.

Step Six: Record and Compound

Once you've decided on a formula, write it down immediately. Copy it on a three-by-five-inch index card or in your herbal notebook. Even if you think you'll change it later, record it! Give the blend a name as well.

Now compound the mixture:

  1. Grind herbs if necessary in your mortar and pestle
  2. Mix the ingredients together
  3. Align their energies as you blend
  4. Empower the mixture for its intended purpose
  5. Use immediately or store in a labeled bottle

You've just created a new recipe.

Creating Deity-Specific Formulas

Formulas dedicated to specific deities are created somewhat differently.

Research mythology. Check into mythology to discover which plants (if any) were used in a deity's worship. These are ritually appropriate.

Use corresponding herbs. Alternatively, use herbs and plants that relate to the deity's basic influences. For a Pele incense honoring the Hawaiian goddess of volcanoes, fiery herbs would be ideal. Though fiery Hawaiian plants would be perfect, they aren't easily obtainable elsewhere. Substitute with accessible fiery herbs that carry similar energy.

Match the deity's domain:

  • Love deities: Venus-ruled, Water-element herbs
  • War deities: Mars-ruled, Fire-element herbs
  • Wisdom deities: Mercury-ruled, Air-element herbs
  • Earth/harvest deities: Earth-element, fertility herbs
  • Sea deities: Water-element, lunar herbs

Final Thoughts

With these simple steps you can create magickal products for an endless variety of uses:

  • Rely on your inner wisdom. Your intuition knows what works for you.
  • Research. Study correspondences, mythology, and traditional uses.
  • Experiment. Try different combinations and proportions.
  • Record everything. Keep detailed notes on what works and what doesn't.

And most of all, enjoy the powers of herbs.

Bath Sachet & Salts Guide

Herbal bath sachets transform an ordinary bath into a ritual experience. When herbs steep in warm water, they release their colors, scents, and magickal energies into the liquid. The bather essentially brews in a giant pot of herbal tea, absorbing the plants' power through the skin.

Bath sachets are among the simplest forms of herbal magick, yet they remain powerful tools for psychic development, love drawing, healing acceleration, and personal protection.

Making Bath Sachets

Ingredients

Use any of the bath sachet recipes in the Recipe Grimoire, or design your own blend based on your magickal intention.

Preparation

  1. Gather your ingredients and place them in a mixing bowl
  2. Blend the herbs with your fingers while visualizing your magickal goal
  3. Pour your personal energy into the mixture as you work
  4. Place about a handful of the blend in the center of a cheesecloth square (a washcloth works as an alternative)
  5. Gather the corners and tie securely

Storage

Prepare multiple sachets at once for convenience. Store in an airtight jar until needed. Properly stored, dry herb blends keep for several months.

Using Bath Sachets

Standard Bath Method

Fill a clean tub with warm water. Drop the sachet into the water and allow it to steep until the bath is colored and fragrant.

Shower Method

If you prefer showers or lack a bathtub, prepare a sachet in a washcloth. After your regular shower, scrub your body with the herb-filled cloth before toweling dry.

Infusion Method

For a stronger preparation:

  1. Boil two cups of water
  2. Pour over one or two sachets in a heat-proof container
  3. Cover and steep for ten to thirteen minutes
  4. Remove sachets and squeeze out remaining liquid
  5. Add the infusion to your bathwater

Direct Addition (Not Recommended)

Some practitioners add loose herbs directly to the bathwater without a sachet. This method often results in plant material clinging to your skin and clogging drains. The cleanup usually takes longer than any benefit gained.

Ritual Practice

As you enter the water, feel the herbal energies mingling with your own. Maintain your visualization throughout the bath. The herbs assist your magick, but you must actively participate by directing their energy toward your goal.

Duration: Repeat the bath for as many consecutive days as feels right. There are no fixed rules. Continue until you sense the working is complete.

Optional Enhancements:

  • Burn incense aligned with your magickal intention
  • Light candles in corresponding colors
  • Play soft music or maintain silence for deeper focus

Bath Salts

Bath salts offer an easy-to-prepare alternative to herbal sachets. Unlike many commercial products laden with harsh chemicals that can irritate skin, homemade ritual bath salts are gentle and fully customizable.

Creating Bath Salts

Base Recipe

Combine these ingredients in a large bowl:

  • 3 parts Epsom salts (magnesium sulfate)
  • 2 parts Baking soda (sodium bicarbonate)
  • 1 part Table salt (or Borax)

Mix thoroughly. This neutral base can be divided into portions for multiple recipes or prepared as one large batch of a single type.

Adding Color

Use plain food coloring to align your salts with color correspondences:

  1. Add drops one at a time onto the salt base
  2. For mixed hues (like purple), blend colors in a spoon first to avoid streaking
  3. Stir until color distributes evenly throughout
  4. More drops create deeper color; fewer drops yield lighter tints
  5. Recipes marked "Color: White" should remain untinted

Adding Fragrance

Incorporate essential oils drop by drop:

  1. Add one oil at a time, mixing between additions
  2. Continue until the scent feels balanced to your nose
  3. Stir until all salt particles are lightly moistened
  4. This process may take up to half an hour
  5. Visualize the oils' energies merging with each other and the salt
  6. Hold your magickal intention in mind throughout

General guideline: No more than ten total drops of essential oil per half-cup of bath salts. The finished product should be strongly scented, a more potent aroma means you'll use less per bath.

Using Bath Salts

Add two tablespoons to one-half cup of ritual bath salts to a full tub. Mix with your hands, feeling the energies dissolve into the water.

While soaking, open yourself to receive the salt's power, or alternatively, consciously release unwanted energies into the water.

Important Notes

  • Use genuine essential oils only: synthetic fragrances lack magickal potency
  • Clean your tub before and after ritual baths, using a commercial cleanser or baking soda on a damp cloth
  • Ritual baths in dirty tubs won't produce desired results
  • Recipe proportions are relative (parts, not exact measurements), trust your nose to determine final quantities

Recipe Grimoire

Incense Guide

Incense has been part of magickal practice for over 5,000 years. Ancient practitioners burned it to carry prayers skyward, create sacred space, and commune with divine forces.

Why Burn Incense?

Ritual Consciousness

Burning incense helps shift awareness into the focused state needed for magickal work. The rising smoke, the fragrance, and the act of preparation all signal to the mind that sacred work is beginning.

Purification

Smoke cleanses a space of stagnant or unwanted energies before ritual. This clearing establishes the right atmosphere for effective magick.

Directing Energy

Blends formulated for specific purposes help attract and channel particular energies. A healing incense draws healing forces; a prosperity blend attracts abundance.

Offerings

Some incenses honor deities or spirits. Juniper burned for Inanna in ancient Sumer is one of the oldest recorded examples.

How Incense Works

Every substance carries its own energetic signature. When incense burns, these energies release from physical form into the environment. The smoke carries the vibrations outward, where they blend with the practitioner's focused intent and move toward manifestation.

Select incense based on its correspondences. For healing work, burn herbs associated with health and restoration.

Scent and Magick

Scent matters less than you might expect in magickal incense. The general rule:

  • Pleasant scents suit positive workings
  • Harsh scents suit banishing and exorcism

Many effective magickal incenses smell strange, bitter, or intensely resinous. Ritual blends prioritize energetic alignment over pleasant fragrance. If you want something that simply smells nice, make a separate household blend for that purpose.

⚠️
Reserve Magickal Incense for Magickal Work

Burning empowered incense casually wastes its energy. Keep magickal blends for ritual use.

Essential Incense Materials

Stock these 14 ingredients for a solid incense-making foundation:

Resins and GumsWoods and BarksHerbs and Flowers
FrankincenseSandalwoodRose petals
MyrrhCedarBay
BenzoinJuniperThyme
CopalPineBasil
CinnamonRosemary
📝
Test Your Materials

Many herbs smell completely different when burned. Drop small amounts onto hot charcoal and note the results. Record the scent, your impressions, and any intuitive responses. This builds practical knowledge no book can provide.

Two Forms of Incense

Noncombustible (Loose/Granular)

Sprinkled onto hot charcoal to release fragrance. Contains no burning agents.

Most magickal incense is noncombustible because:

  • Simpler to make
  • Allows control over smoke quantity
  • Produces the billowing smoke some rituals require

Combustible (Cones, Sticks, Blocks)

Contains potassium nitrate (saltpeter) so it burns independently. More convenient but more complex to create.

Choosing a Form

Noncombustible Works Best ForCombustible Works Best For
Heavy smoke effectsQuick, simple rituals
Divination and evocationPortability
Controlling burn amountConsistent burn rate
BeginnersConvenience

Making Noncombustible Incense

Gather all ingredients before starting. Substitutions are fine if needed.

Step 1: Grind Everything

Reduce all ingredients to fine powder using mortar and pestle or electric grinder. Resins can be stubborn. Work patiently and they will cooperate.

Step 2: Blend Resins First

In a wooden or ceramic bowl, combine resins and gums by hand. Focus on your intention throughout. Visualize energy flowing from your hands into the mixture. This personal charge distinguishes handmade incense from commercial products.

Step 3: Add Remaining Dry Ingredients

Mix in powdered leaves, barks, flowers, and roots while maintaining focus on the blend's purpose.

Step 4: Add Liquids

Include any oils, wine, honey, or other liquids the recipe calls for. Use sparingly. If substituting oil for a missing herb, use only true essential oils. Synthetic fragrances produce acrid smoke.

Step 5: Add Boosters (Optional)

Some recipes call for powdered gemstones. Crush the stone with a hammer, then grind to powder. Add only a tiny pinch. Amber works as a general power amplifier.

Step 6: Empower and Store

Charge the completed blend with your intention. Store in labeled, airtight jars. Include the name and date.

Making Combustible Incense

Combustible incense requires more effort and specific ingredients. The process can be messy. Results vary with practice.

💭
On Saltpeter

Some practitioners avoid combustible incense because potassium nitrate has Mars associations. However, charcoal blocks also contain saltpeter. Consider your own practice and preferences.

Making Tragacanth Glue

This binding agent holds molded incense together. Available at herb shops and some pharmacies.

  1. Add one teaspoon ground gum tragacanth to one glass warm water
  2. Whisk until particles disperse
  3. Skim off foam
  4. Let sit until it becomes thick paste

One ounce of tragacanth absorbs up to a gallon of water over a week. Adjust thickness by adding water. Keep covered with damp cloth.

Gum arabic substitutes well if tragacanth is unavailable.

Cone Incense Base #1 (Traditional)

IngredientAmount
Ground charcoal (not self-igniting)6 parts
Ground benzoin1 part
Ground sandalwood2 parts
Ground orris root1 part
Essential oil6 drops
Empowered incense blend2-4 parts
  1. Combine first four ingredients
  2. Add essential oil and mix by hand
  3. Add empowered incense blend
  4. Weigh total mixture
  5. Add potassium nitrate at exactly 10% of total weight
  6. Mix thoroughly

Cone Incense Base #2 (Without Charcoal)

Charcoal requires frequent hand-washing and adds an off-note to the scent. This version uses wood instead:

IngredientAmount
Powdered sandalwood, cedar, pine, or juniper6 parts
Powdered benzoin, frankincense, or myrrh2 parts
Ground orris root1 part
Essential oil6 drops
Empowered incense blend3-5 parts

Match the wood to your incense recipe when possible. Sandalwood works as a neutral default.

Follow the same process: combine dry ingredients, add oil, add incense blend, weigh, add 10% saltpeter.

Shaping

Cones: Add tragacanth glue gradually until mixture reaches stiff dough consistency. Shape into cones on waxed paper. Dry 2-7 days.

Blocks: Roll dough ⅓ inch thick. Cut into 1-inch squares. Dry completely.

Sticks: Thin the mixture with extra glue. Dip bamboo skewers, wooden splints, or broom straws repeatedly, drying between coats. Or roll thin dough around sticks. Stand upright to dry.

Critical Rules for Combustible Incense

🚫
Saltpeter must be exactly 10% of total weight.

More burns too fast. Less may not burn at all.

Wood to Resin Ratio: Maintain at least 2:1 powdered wood to gum resins. Higher resin content prevents proper burning. Resins should never exceed one-third of the final mixture.

Sourcing Potassium Nitrate

  • Pharmacies (ask the pharmacist directly)
  • Chemical supply companies
  • Garden centers (sold as fertilizer)

Incense Papers

An alternative combustible form using tinctures and paper instead of molded dough.

Making the Papers

  1. Cut white blotter paper into strips (6 inches by 1 inch)
  2. Dissolve 1½ teaspoons potassium nitrate in ½ cup warm water
  3. Soak strips until saturated
  4. Hang to dry

Adding Scent

Tinctures work better than essential oils for papers. Gum and resin tinctures produce the best results.

  1. Empower your tincture
  2. Coat one side of each strip with tincture
  3. Dry completely
  4. Store in airtight containers

Use one tincture per paper rather than mixing.

Using Papers

Light one end, let it catch fully, blow out the flame, and place in censer. Papers can also substitute for charcoal: burn an unscented paper and sprinkle loose incense over it.

Ensure air circulates beneath the paper for consistent burning. Prop it in sand or salt, or rest it on a heat-safe object.

The Censer

Any heat-safe container works. Elaborate thuribles and simple bowls of sand function equally well. Choose based on personal preference and practicality. Sand or salt in a bowl protects surfaces from heat and provides a base for propping stick incense.

Burning Combustible Incense

Light the tip, wait for it to glow, blow out the flame, and place in censer. Visualize your goal as it burns.

Burning Noncombustible Incense

  1. Light a charcoal block and place in censer
  2. Wait for sparking to stop and the block to glow evenly
  3. Sprinkle a small amount of incense onto the block

Add more as smoke diminishes. Large amounts extinguish the charcoal. Resin-heavy blends burn longer than herb-heavy ones. Leave ash in place unless the scent turns unpleasant.

Charcoal Blocks

Self-igniting blocks contain saltpeter and spark dramatically when lit. Available at religious supply and occult shops in various sizes.

Light by holding with tongs or tweezers, or light directly in the censer. If a block resists lighting, it may have absorbed moisture. Keep trying until it glows evenly red.

Magickal Oils Guide

Magickal oils have been used in ritual practice for thousands of years. Ancient practitioners created scented oils by heating fragrant plant materials in oil or fat, transferring the botanical essence into the base. Today, a wide array of both genuine and synthetic oils are available for magickal work.

Why Not Make Your Own Essential Oils?

Extracting true essential oils at home is impractical for most practitioners:

  • Equipment costs are significant. Condensers, fractionating columns, and other specialized apparatus are expensive and must be adapted for distillation.
  • Large quantities of plant material are required. Extracting a small amount of oil may require hundreds of pounds of fresh petals, leaves, or roots. The plant material must also be the correct species, as certain varieties produce superior oils.
  • The process demands precision. Temperature fluctuations or missed steps compromise quality. Homemade attempts often yield disappointing results that do not capture the true scent of the plant.

For most botanical oils, purchasing high-quality products is more practical than attempting home extraction.

Buying Oils

Types of Commercial Oils

  • Genuine essential oils are extracted directly from the plant material they are named after. Lavender essential oil, for example, comes from lavender.
  • Bouquets or compounds recreate a specific scent by blending multiple true essential oils together.
  • Synthetic oils are laboratory-created fragrances. Many companies sell these without labeling them as synthetic.

Choosing Quality

Genuine essential oils are preferred for magickal work because they contain the full energetic signature of the plant. While more expensive, they are also more concentrated, so smaller amounts are needed.

Synthetics can function in magick but tend to be less potent than true botanical oils. Be cautious of "essential oil" labels on products that are actually synthetic. Purchasing from reputable suppliers specializing in aromatherapy or essential oils is the best way to ensure authenticity.

For scents unavailable as true essential oils (such as tuberose, sweet pea, or lotus), bouquet recipes can be blended from genuine oils to approximate the fragrance.

Blending Oils

Basic Method

  1. Gather the essential oils and any bouquets called for in the recipe
  2. Add 1/8 cup of carrier oil to a clean, sterilized glass jar

Carrier Oil Options

OilNotes
JojobaPreferred choice. Technically a liquid wax, so it never goes rancid and stores well long-term
Sweet AlmondCommon, gentle carrier
GrapeseedLight and absorbs quickly
Apricot KernelGentle, good for skin
SunflowerReadily available
SafflowerLight texture
CoconutSolid at room temperature, melts on contact with skin
HazelnutRich, slightly heavier
  1. Using an eye dropper or the dispensers included with essential oil bottles, add the essential oils in the proportions specified by the recipe
  2. Swirl the oils together gently in a clockwise motion. Do not stir.
  3. Store in airtight, opaque or dark glass bottles away from heat, light, and moisture

Example: Fast Money Oil

IngredientAmount
Patchouli7 drops
Cedarwood5 drops
Vetivert4 drops
Ginger2 drops

Add jojoba to a sterilized jar while visualizing the magickal goal. Add each essential oil one at a time, swirling and focusing on intention after each addition. The fragrance builds and deepens as the oils blend. After empowering the completed oil, it is ready for use.

Using Magickal Oils

Candle Dressing

The most common application. Rub oil onto candles before burning them in ritual. The oil's energy combines with the candle color and flame, amplified by the practitioner's visualization.

Anointing the Body

Apply oil to pulse points to absorb its energies. Love oils might be rubbed on wrists, neck, and over the heart. Courage oils can be applied before facing challenges.

Ritual Baths

Add several drops to bathwater. Immersing in the scented water brings the oil's energies within while inhaling the fragrance.

Talismans and Amulets

Anoint charms, sachets, or other magickal objects with appropriate oils to charge them with specific intentions.

Crystals and Stones

Rub oils onto quartz and other stones to enhance their energies for spellwork. The stones can then be worn, carried, or arranged in ritual patterns.

Diluting Essential Oils

True essential oils should be diluted before skin application. Essential oils are volatile, meaning they are easily absorbed through the skin and will damage tissue if applied undiluted. They should only ever be used topically as an active ingredient in a dilution with a carrier oil such as jojoba, coconut, olive, or grapeseed. As a general guideline:

5 to 7 drops per 1/8 cup carrier oil

This dilution prevents skin irritation while preserving the fragrance. Some essential oils are severe skin irritants and require extra caution or should be avoided for topical use entirely. Individual oil entries note such concerns.

Ointment Guide

The notorious "flying ointments" of historical witchcraft (psychoactive herb mixtures suspended in fat and applied to the skin for astral travel) represent just one category of magickal salves. Practitioners have long used ointments for countless practical magickal purposes that mirror the uses of oils.

Converting any magickal oil formula into an ointment is straightforward: blend it into melted beeswax, lard, or vegetable shortening. Store finished ointments in glass or ceramic containers with secure lids, kept cool and away from light.

☠️
Warning: Some historical ointment recipes contain lethal herbs. These formulas appear here only as documentation of magickal history. Never attempt toxic preparations.

Creating Ointments

An ointment requires two components: magickal herbs or oils and a fatty base. Traditional recipes called for hog's lard due to availability, though modern practitioners achieve superior results with vegetable shortening or beeswax. The base should liquefy when heated but solidify at room temperature.

Shortening Method

  1. Melt 4 parts vegetable shortening over gentle heat, avoiding scorching.
  2. Stir in 1 part powdered dried herbs using a wooden spoon.
  3. Maintain low heat, stirring periodically, until the herb fragrance permeates the air.
  4. Filter through cheesecloth into a glass jar.
  5. Preserve with 1/2 teaspoon benzoin tincture per pint.
  6. Refrigerate for storage.

These preparations remain viable for weeks to months. Discard at first sign of mold.

Beeswax Method

This technique yields a lighter, less greasy consistency. Works best with essential oils rather than whole herbs since straining proves difficult.

  1. Shave unbleached beeswax into small pieces using a sturdy knife.
  2. Measure roughly 1/4 cup shaved wax into a double boiler arrangement.
  3. Add approximately 1/4 cup carrier oil (olive, hazelnut, or sesame work well).
  4. Stir until fully incorporated.
  5. Cool briefly until slightly thickened. This prevents essential oil evaporation.
  6. Blend in your essential oil mixture.
  7. Transfer to containers and label.

Compresses

A compress is made by soaking a clean cloth into an infusion or decoction and then applying it to the body to receive the healing benefits of the herbal preparation. Compresses can be either hot or cold and are commonly used to address pain and swelling.

To infuse a compress with magick, focus on the transference of energy and treat the cloth as a ritual object. You can charge it by placing it on your altar and exposing it to sunlight or moonlight depending on the type of effect you desire. Since a compress is reusable, think of it as one of your magickal tools dedicated to the sacred task of healing.

Liniments

A liniment is an herbal extract added to vinegar or alcohol for topical application. Liniments are used for healing purposes and are particularly effective for treating strained and stiff muscles, bruises, and sprains.

Poultices

Poultices are made by macerating fresh herbs in a mortar and pestle, gathering them into a cloth, and dipping them into hot or boiling water. Poultices are well suited for treating insect bites, skin inflammations, cuts, and scrapes.

The mortar and pestle is itself a magickal tool, representing the sacred union of the goddess and the god. Preparing a poultice can be performed as part of a ritual or spell. Consider using a mortar and pestle dedicated solely to healing work. If you also craft incense or use one for other types of spells and charms, it is worth investing in a separate set devoted entirely to healing and tonic herbs.

Charging Ointments

After cooling, consecrate the finished ointment with your specific magickal intention. This step activates the preparation for ritual work.

Application

Ointments are applied to the body to manifest magickal effects. Combine application with focused visualization, trusting the preparation to accomplish its purpose.

Recipe Grimoire

Potion Guide

Brews, also called potions, range from everyday herbal teas to mystical infusions. They descend from ancient magickal, ritual, and medicinal traditions, and remain just as effective today. In practical herb magick, a brew is simply an herbal infusion. Your kitchen stove works perfectly well, no forest clearing or open fire required.

Brews serve many purposes: some are consumed, others added to baths, and still others prepared to release fragrant steam that fills a space with herbal vibrations.

Choosing Your Water

Water quality matters in brewing.

Best choices:

  • Spring water
  • Distilled water
  • Rain water (collected away from polluted areas)
  • Well water from clean sources

Avoid:

  • Sea water (too mineral-heavy)
  • Mineral water (same issue)
  • Tap water (use only as a last resort due to chlorine, fluoride, and potential contaminants)

If you plan to drink your brew, distilled or spring water is always the safer choice.

Heat Sources

Any standard heat source will work:

  • Stovetop (gas or electric)
  • Fireplace
  • Outdoor fire

Note: While technically possible, microwave heating isn't recommended, it removes some of the ritual connection from the process.

Vessels and Containers

Avoid direct contact between herbs and metal during brewing. This is a longstanding principle in herbalism, with few exceptions (traditional cauldron work or double-boiler preparations).

Recommended materials:

  • Glass (especially for solar infusions)
  • Ceramic
  • Earthenware

For solar infusions, place water and herbs in a clear glass jar and set it in direct sunlight, preferably outdoors, for most of the day.

Basic Brewing Method

Unless a specific recipe states otherwise, follow this standard process:

  1. Prepare the herbs: Gather, grind, and mix your ingredients. If the brew will be consumed, use a separate mortar and pestle reserved for culinary purposes.
  2. Empower the mixture: Focus your magickal intention into the herbs as you work.
  3. Heat the water: Bring approximately two cups of water to a boil.
  4. Combine: Place about one handful of prepared herbs into a heat-proof, non-metallic container (a teapot works well).
  5. Steep: Pour boiling water over the herbs and cover with a tight-fitting, non-metallic lid. Allow to steep for approximately 13 minutes.
  6. Strain: Filter through cheesecloth or a bamboo strainer.
  7. Use promptly: Apply as directed in your specific recipe.

Storage

Brews are best used immediately after preparation. If storage is necessary, refrigerate for no more than three to four days. After this time, return the liquid to the earth and prepare a fresh batch.

Oxymels

An oxymel is an elixir made by combining herbs with vinegar and honey. The honey acts as a sweetener that can make bitter herbs more palatable. For example, Mullein is often used in oxymels to support respiratory health.

Not every herbal remedy is suitable for an oxymel. Carminative herbs used to aid digestion, particularly of fats, must remain bitter in order to stimulate bile production. Sweetening a carminative herb would negate its digestive effects.

Simples

Simples are herbal remedies that contain only one ingredient. They are easy to prepare and are generally drawn from the tonic herbs for the purpose of nourishing the body. A simple is a good starting point for anyone new to herbal preparations, as it allows you to learn how each individual plant behaves before combining them in more complex formulas.

Tonics

Tonics are liquid herbal preparations ingested for health purposes such as strengthening and healing. They can be made from roots, leaves, berries, flowers, or bark and are created by either infusing or decocting. A preservative such as brandy or another type of alcohol may be added.

The key distinction between a tonic and a tea is time and quantity. A tonic steeps for much longer, typically twenty to thirty minutes compared to five for a tea, and a significantly greater amount of plant material is used. Where a tea might call for a few teaspoons, a tonic may use a cup or more of herbs.

A Note on "Love Potions"

No brew can force someone to fall in love with you or emotionally enslave another person. Such potions don't exist. However, certain herbal preparations have traditionally been used to:

  • Relax inhibitions and ease tension
  • Mellow emotional states
  • Smooth difficulties in established relationships

A few such recipes appear in this grimoire, but understand them for what they are, gentle aids, not magickal compulsions.

Recipe Grimoire

Food Magick

Every week of the year, on most continents around this planet, millions of people participate in a profoundly magickal ritual whereby two very basic everyday foodstuffs have a spell cast over them by means of a sacred incantation. The person officiating over this ceremony makes symbolic gestures with their hands and arms. This spellbinding usually takes place in a language very few fully comprehend, a language full of secrets, and as a result these mundane objects are transformed into something as mystical, sacred, and awe-inspiring as anything you could ever imagine.

In addition, this ritual generally takes place in a building whose architecture and design has been informed by knowledge of the directions, shapes, and patterns that link the Heavens with the Earth in an arrangement of the sacred symbols which some say were dictated to man by the very angels themselves.

When the Holy Communion of the Roman Catholic Church takes place, the simple ingredients of bread and wine are transformed, many believe, into the actual body and blood of the Christ. This is not just a symbolic representation, some say, but a very real and profound belief that underpins the foundations of the religion. By eating this holy, sacred food, imbued with magickal intent, the recipient voluntarily absorbs the spirit of the Messiah.

The ritual and perceived reality of this act are inseparable, but bread and wine are not the only sacred foods we absorb as part of our everyday lives. We need food to live, so it comes as no surprise that we have accorded many ingredients with magickal powers. Indeed, some of the things we eat every day carry both constituent elements and meanings which go far beyond mere nutrition.

Ambrosia

For the Greeks, Ambrosia was the food of the Gods. Given that it conferred immortality, the Deities on Mount Olympus guarded it jealously. As well as ensuring eternal life, Ambrosia could be used as an ointment that could heal any wound.

However, for a mortal, eating Ambrosia was a big mistake. Take the story of Tantalus, for example. He was invited to eat with the Gods, and so, presuming that he was accepted as one of them, he ate Ambrosia. In the tradition of all good dinner party guests, he decided to return the favor and invited the Gods round to his place. Deciding somewhat sycophantically that they should feast upon all the good things that they had given him, he served up the flesh of his own children, and was banished to Hades.

Chocolate

Long before the discovery of the Americas, the natives of Brazil, Mexico, the West Indies, and South America used the seeds of the chocolatl tree to make a stimulating drink. These bean-like seeds were cacahuatl, or cocoa. Primarily symbolic of love, chocolate is a sensual food with aphrodisiac properties that are due, in part, to association. However, its melting point is the same temperature as blood, a very satisfying sensation.

The botanical name of the plant gives a clue as to its sacred status. Theobroma cacao means "food of the Gods," from the Greek "Theo," meaning God and "Broma," meaning food.

The beans were so highly valued that the Mayans used them as currency. Possibly the world's first chocoholic, their ruler Montezuma was completely addicted to the beans. He drank them infused in cold water with no seasoning. He served this sacred drink in goblets of beaten gold, and at the coronation of Montezuma II in 1502 a concoction of chocolate and psilocybin mushrooms was served to the guests.

Cortes cultivated the plant primarily because of its reputation as an aphrodisiac; this secret was divulged by one of the nineteen young women given to him by Montezuma as a tribute. Perhaps the 2000 chocolatl trees that he consequently planted were testimony to the efficacy of the beans.

By 1550, chocolate factories were operating in Lisbon, Genoa, Marseilles, and other European cities. The recipes became more and more refined. Catherine de Medici slowed down the progress of chocolate for a while because it was so good that she wanted it all to herself. However, although the Church tried to ban many of the foodstuffs discovered in the New World, especially those considered as stimulants, their advice was largely ignored. Neither Catherine nor all the forces of the Church could stop the world becoming chocolate coated.

Today, the form of chocolate has changed so much that Montezuma would probably find it unrecognizable, both in taste and form. However, it is still unrivalled as a token and symbol of love.

Honey

Legislation decrees that all packaged food carry a "best before" date, but this seems to be particularly unnecessary in the case of honey, since jars of the stuff found in the tombs of Egyptian kings from several thousand years ago have proved to be perfectly edible even now. It could well be because honey is so long lasting, and because it is used as a preservative, that it is a symbol of immortality and is used in funerary rites. The bees that make the honey have their place in the realms of magickal creatures accorded with supernatural powers. The Promised Land is said to "flow with milk and honey" as being the very best that the Gods can offer.

The sweetness of honey is believed to confer gifts of learning and poetry. We'll never know if the story that Pythagoras existed on honey alone is true, but the fact that the rumor exists is in accord with his God-like status. As well as being edible and fermentable, honey has healing and antiseptic qualities, and a dollop of honey smeared onto a wound will soon draw out any impurities and speed the healing process.

Honey is said to be an aphrodisiac and to encourage fertility and virility, wealth and abundance, and is a symbol of the Sun, partly because of the flowers from which it is made but also because of its color.

Manna

When the Children of Israel were struggling to survive in the wilderness, manna appeared, miraculously, overnight, and so they could eat. Precisely what manna was, or is, is debatable. Some believe it might be a kind of fungus, others believe that it might be sap or resin exuded from the tamarisk tree. The symbolic meaning of manna is of something provided freely by the Universe or by God and is the ultimate reminder that we have everything we need. Manna is also associated with the Bread of Life or the Eucharist.

Mead

Like honey, mead also carries the gift of immortality. The Celts believed it was the favored drink of the Gods in the Otherworld. Mead is a sacred drink in Africa, too, where it is believed that drinking the stuff will make you more knowledgeable.

Mead is very simple to make: it is simply honey mixed with water and allowed to ferment. This process of fermentation is akin to a magickal process in itself, which is akin to transmutation in alchemy.

Milk

Given that milk is the first food, it is not surprising that it is associated with many stories of the Creation, and is a symbol of divinity. Amrita, or Soma, the absolute nectar of life for Hindus and the equivalent of Ambrosia, was created as a cosmic sea of milk was churned. The curds that were created by this epic stirring formed the Earth, the Universe, and the stars. Along with honey, there is an abundance of milk in the Promised Land, and Indian myths tell of a magickal milk tree in Heaven. Because of its color and its association with the feminine, milk is a symbol of the Moon.

The main food source for milk for us human beings (once we are weaned) is the cow. The cow is sacred in India because during times of famine it made far more sense to keep the animal alive for its milk rather than slaughter and eat it purely for its meat, so all parts of the cow are accorded sacred status and are ruled over by one or other of the Gods or Goddesses.

In the hidden symbolic language of alchemy, the Philosopher's Stone is sometimes called the Virgin's Milk.

Nectar

Nectar is often referred to as Ambrosia, but has secrets of its own to tell. Flowers create it, and its scent attracts the bees, which then transform the nectar into honey. Seemingly insignificant, nectar is nevertheless a very magickal ingredient, created from flowers, sunshine, and bees working together in a collective consciousness known as the "hive mind" in an environment which itself is constructed from one of the key shapes in sacred geometry, the hexagon.

Soma

Like the Greek Olympians, Indian deities have a sacred food that confers immortality. This food is Soma, also called Amrita. In contrast to the dangers faced by mortals who dared to eat Ambrosia, the Indian gods were said to be more generous with Soma. A mortal who consumed it was granted immortality and access to Heaven.

In the Ramayana, Soma is tied to the story of Rama. An angel brought magickal food to Rama’s father, and by eating this Soma, he was able to father children who were human incarnations of the god Vishnu.

Wine

The symbolic meanings of wine are most often attached to red wine, rather than white or rosé. Because red wine resembles blood, it is linked to blood and can be used in rites where blood would otherwise be required. When ceremonial wine is shared from a chalice, it is also understood, like bread, as a unifying principle.

Wine is described as male, with bread as its female counterpart. In the Eucharist, consecrated wine becomes the blood of Christ, holding the meanings of sacrifice and immortal life, and its power to transform is central to its mystique. In the story of the Marriage at Cana, water becoming wine shows the transformation of the mundane into the magickal, and the Earthly into the Heavenly.

The process of fermentation also helps explain wine’s association with Bacchus or Dionysus, and intoxication can symbolize divine possession. The phrase “In Vino Veritas” links wine to truth, noting that intoxication may loosen speech for better or worse.

Powders Guide

Powders are ground herbs sprinkled to release their energies. Think of them as incense that is never burned, or a sachet that is never worn. Many ritual uses of powders are unique to this form.

Making Powders

Grind herbs as finely as possible using a mortar and pestle. While grinding, visualize your magickal goal. The physical process of mortaring creates an opportunity to connect deeply with the plant materials and program them with intent.

Once powdered, mix the herbs together and empower the blend before use.

Using Magickal Powders

Scattering

The simplest method. Sprinkle powders when and where their energies are needed.

Circle Casting

Sprinkle powder in a circle around yourself, beginning and ending in the East, moving clockwise. Sit within this circle to absorb the powder's energies.

Crystal Work

Sprinkle appropriate powder around crystals on the altar to amplify their power.

Candle Magick

Scatter powders around candles before lighting to boost their energies.

Altar Preparation

Sprinkle ritually appropriate powder over the altar before spellwork.

Symbolic Shapes

Sprinkle powder on the altar in specific shapes as focal points for visualization:

  • Protection powder in pentagrams
  • Love powder in hearts
  • Psychic powder in circles

The shape need not remain intact for long to be effective.

Powders for Capsules

Beyond scattering, powdered herbs can also be used as filler for capsules, making them easy to ingest in measured doses. This is a common method for taking healing herbs for a specific ailment. For example, powdered Valerian root is widely used as a sleep aid.

Caution

Some powders, particularly those containing dragon's blood, will stain carpets, bedsheets, clothing, and other materials. Be mindful when sprinkling.

Ritual Soaps Guide

Picture yourself in a warm bath, surrounded by herb-scented water as you prepare for ritual. Incense drifts through the air while you hold your magickal intention in mind. Steam rises, carrying the essence of flowers, seeds, roots, and leaves. Then you reach for the soap and its artificial, cloying perfume shatters your concentration.

Sound familiar? While soaping is not required during magickal baths, a properly crafted ritual soap can enhance any working. Even washing your hands before ritual serves as a small act of purification that helps shift your mind into a ceremonial state.

Commercial soaps are loaded with harsh chemicals that irritate skin and carry overpowering synthetic fragrances. Occult shops occasionally stock ritual soaps of varying quality, but making your own is simple, enjoyable, and ensures you control exactly what touches your skin.

Getting Started

You will not need a cauldron bubbling over an open fire or risk burns from lye. The simplest approach uses pure, natural castile soap as a base. Castile soap (named after Castile, Spain) is typically made from coconut or olive oil and can be found at most drugstores and markets. Coconut-based varieties tend to work best.

Note: Castile soap can be drying. If this is a concern, add one to two teaspoons of apricot, almond, or coconut oil to your water before mixing, reducing the water amount slightly to compensate.

Two types of ritual soaps are covered here: solid spheres and liquid soaps.

Making Soap Spheres

Ingredients

  • 4 oz bar of castile soap
  • Slightly less than 1/3 cup water
  • 20 to 50 drops of empowered essential oils (mixed according to your intention)

Method

  1. Cut the soap into very small cubes, no larger than 1/4 inch. Smaller is better.
  2. Place the cubes in a heat-proof, non-metallic container.
  3. Heat the water until nearly boiling, then pour it over the soap. Let sit until cool enough to handle.
  4. Mix with your hands. The chips should be moist but not floating. If floating, add more soap. Let sit about nine minutes until mushy. If the cubes remain hard, gently reheat the bowl in a pan of water.
  5. Add your oils. While waiting, mix and empower your essential oils with your magickal goal. Once the water has cooled (warm water evaporates oils), add 20 to 50 drops and mix thoroughly. The scent should be strong enough to override the soap's natural antiseptic smell.
  6. Form into spheres. Divide the mixture into three or four portions and shape into balls.
  7. Wrap each sphere in a nine-inch square of cotton cheesecloth. Pull the fabric tight, gather the ends at the top, twist, and tie securely with strong string.
  8. Hang to dry in a warm place for three days or until completely hard (they will not give to finger pressure).
  9. Unwrap and use in ritual baths, or rewrap in clean cheesecloth, label, and store or gift to friends.

Making Liquid Soap (Oil Method)

Despite modern advertising treating liquid soap as a new invention, the concept is ancient. Indigenous peoples worldwide created cleansing solutions by agitating suds-producing plants in water. This method uses castile as the base.

Ingredients

  • 1 cup grated castile soap (packed tightly)
  • 3 cups water
  • 50 to 60 drops of empowered essential oils

Method

  1. Grate the soap into a large bowl and pack it into a measuring cup until you have exactly one cup.
  2. Heat three cups of water until almost boiling.
  3. Add the soap chips to the hot water, remove from heat, and whisk with a wooden utensil until completely melted.
  4. Let cool, then add 50 to 60 drops of your mixed, empowered oils. Stop when the soap is strongly scented.
  5. Transfer to a jar using a funnel, cap tightly, and shake vigorously to mix.
  6. Label and store until needed.

Making Liquid Soap (Brew Method)

You can substitute herb brews for essential oils in liquid soaps.

Method

  1. Add five to six tablespoons of mixed, dried, ground, and empowered herbs to three cups of hot water.
  2. Remove from heat, steep for 10 to 13 minutes, then strain.
  3. Gently reheat the herbal water, add one cup of grated castile soap, and whisk until dissolved.
  4. Let cool and bottle.

Note: Herb brews change dramatically when mixed with castile soap, sometimes creating unexpected scents. If the result is not appealing, add a few drops of an essential oil that matches one of the herbs to strengthen the fragrance.

Using Ritual Soaps

For liquid soaps, wet your hands and apply a few drops. The soap foams easily and leaves skin clean and scented.

For soap spheres, use them during ritual baths as you would any bar soap.

Always visualize your magickal goal as you wash. The soap is a tool; your focused intention is what powers the working.

Optional Enhancements

Some recipes call for rose water or orange flower water in place of plain water. If using these, ensure they are scented with genuine essential oils rather than synthetic fragrances.

Storage

Store unused soaps in your altar (if it has enclosed shelves or cupboards) or in your herb cabinet. Keep them labeled and accessible for ritual use.

Signature Cocktail Guide

Mixing Drinks and Friends

When grateful gatherings become selective soirées, knowing what to have on hand, how to prepare it, and how to pair it can make a party perfect. Whether you're having a casual planning session for a large group event, or throwing a huge bash to celebrate your big promotion, getting guests in the mood will guarantee they'll be talking about it for a long time.

How to Design the Perfect Signature Drink

When enjoying the presence of friends or magickal practitioners, the ability to craft a delightful cocktail is a rare treat. Anyone can follow a recipe and make the same old, tired margarita. Instead of falling back on an old, reliable cocktail, why not create something they have never seen before, and really knock their socks off?

What's the occasion?

Having the type of gathering in mind will help develop the correct feeling for your drink before you put out the wrong glassware or stumble over garnishes. Your cocktail should reflect:

  • Who you are
  • The mood of the event (if not the theme)
  • The attendees
Gathering TypeDrink Style
Staid gathering (colleagues, formal)Original takes on classic cocktails
Raucous gathering (close friends)More adventurous drinks
Intimate gathering (confidantes)Something showing your personality
Funeral or wakeNothing overly cheery or childish

An irreverent cocktail selection can encourage chatter and enliven conversation, while a new take on a classic will let people know that you have sophisticated tastes but still enjoy trying new things.

How much do you know about cocktails?

An honest assessment of your abilities is a must for this exercise.

🌱
For beginners: Try something less tricky to make but that still says you made an effort. A cocktail based on a Shrubs (Fruit Vinegar Drinks) is a great option. Something like a watermelon and prosecco vinegar shrub would pair well with a botanical gin. Vinegar-based shrubs are cooling on the body, so they will relax people in the heat and allow them to enjoy the flavors of the season.

By making your own syrup to flavor cocktails, you keep the price down and inspire people to think you're a bartending legend they knew nothing about.

What time of year is it?

Making sure your cocktail is seasonally appropriate is important. You don't want to jar guests out of their party mood.

  • Don't serve a hot tea cocktail in summer
  • Don't serve a frozen drink in a blizzard

Consider Mocktail Counterparts

As a good host, consider if your cocktail could have a mocktail counterpart for attendees who aren't drinking.

🍻
Asking "leaded or unleaded" or some variation allows guests to pick how they would like to moderate their alcohol intake without making a big deal out of it. No one owes anyone else an explanation as to why they don't drink.

Letting people know there will be mocktails and alcohol alternatives will help people who otherwise might have skipped feel welcomed.

Building Your Drink

Think in Categories, Not Singular Ingredients

This will put you on your way to making a delicious drink with your own flair.

Before you go mixing bottles of expensive liquor trying to find just the right balance, make lemonade. You will have to find just the right balance of water, sugar, and lemon. It'll teach you to have a gentle hand with sours like lemon, while feeling out the right balance of all three.
Sarah Mitchell, Lab Bar London

Basic Ratios

Shrub Cocktail:

  • 1 part syrup
  • 1 part alcohol
  • 4 parts sparkling water
  • Stir gently

Balanced Cocktail (1:1:2):

  • 1 part sweetness
  • 1 part tartness
  • 2 parts alcohol

The alcohol portion can be made of two different spirits, but try to keep them along the same lines so they don't clash on the palate. Adding triple sec to a margarita gives it jazz because orange is still within the realm of citrus. A rusty nail is a classic because Drambuie is still a whiskey at heart.

Oleosaccharum Punch:

  • ½ part oleosaccharum
  • 1 part alcohol
  • 4 parts sparkling water
  • Garnish
  • Stir gently
📏
Scaling: Recipes given in parts allow for scaling. Turn parts into ounces for one glass, or into cups for a pitcher.

Practice, Practice, Practice!

Once you have an idea of what you would like to create, allow yourself room for errors and time to perfect the drink. Have a friend come over the day before and try out variations on the theme.

For sober-friendly versions: Shrub-based drinks are already sober friendly. Just add an additional part of sparkling water where the alcohol would be.

Be Willing to Accept Feedback

Not every drink will entice every person, but if you're getting a lot of feedback, look at what you're accomplishing and how.

Creating Seasonal Cocktails for Sabbats

A method for designing drinks that honor the eight sabbats of the witch's year:

  1. Grab a notepad and pen and sit where you won't be disturbed.
  2. Label eight sections for the sabbats: Samhain, Yule, Imbolc, Ostara, Beltane, Litha, Lughnasadh, Mabon. (Adjust for other holy tides you celebrate.)
  3. Under each holy tide, list:
    • Flavors associated with the festival
    • Colors associated with the festival
    • Feelings associated with the festival
  4. Use context clues from feelings and colors for how the drink should be prepared. If the feeling is cozy, you might choose a warm cocktail like a toddy.
📝
By working out your thoughts on paper before you start to play alchemist, you will save time and money. It also gives you a chance to plan ahead if you are going to incorporate cordials, ingredients, or syrups that need to be prepared ahead of time.

  • Oleosaccharum

Sachet Guide

Magickal sachets, sometimes called herbal charms, amulets, or talismans, are small bundles of herbs and other materials wrapped in cloth. Some sachets repel unwanted energies or protect against illness, while others attract specific situations or powers into your life.

This section includes astrological sachets for those wishing to amplify the positive qualities of their Sun sign. Wear them daily as a personal power boost or place them on your altar to represent yourself in workings.

Sachets have a long history and cloth is only one of many traditional containers. Throughout time, people have carried herbs in horns, seashells, leather pouches, fur wrappings, and lockets. Magickal rings were sometimes designed as tiny sachets by placing an herb beneath the gemstone, allowing both materials to work together toward a goal. Herbs were also sewn directly into clothing for protection.

Creating Sachets

A handful of empowered herbs (or less) is usually sufficient. Household sachets tend to be larger than those meant to be carried on your person.

Method

  1. Mix your herbs according to the recipe and empower them with your magickal intention. As you work, know that the herbs are pulsing with specific, programmed energies directed toward your goal.
  2. Select your cloth. Choose a natural fiber such as felt, wool, or cotton in a color that corresponds to your intention. Synthetic materials like polyester can disrupt the herbs' frequencies.
  3. Cut the cloth into a square between four and nine inches across.
  4. Assemble the sachet. Place the empowered herbs in the center of the cloth, gather the corners together, and tie firmly with natural cord such as wool yarn or cotton twine.

Helpful Supplies

Keep a variety of cloth and yarn colors on hand. Felt is especially useful since it comes in many shades and does not fray when cut.

Using Sachets

Personal charms: Hold in your hand and squeeze gently to release the fragrance. Carry with you at all times.

Home or vehicle sachets: Squeeze to activate, then place in the most appropriate location.

Maintenance

Replace sachets every three months or so. Disassemble the old ones and bury the contents to return them to the earth.
