Recipe Grimoire

Tea Magick Guide

Herbal Tea Brewing

Dried herbs should be kept in airtight containers. Most herbs require using one teaspoon dried herbs or two tablespoons fresh herbs to one cup of water. When drinking tea for pleasure rather than medicine, adjust the herbs to suit your taste.

Infusion: Pour boiling water over the herbs and steep for ten to thirty minutes. Keep the container tightly covered. This is the standard method for most leaf and flower herbs.

Decoction: The preferred method for roots, barks, and hard nuts or seeds. Simmer the herbs in boiling water for fifteen to thirty minutes with the pot kept tightly covered.

Flavor Reference

🌶️ Spicy

  • Nutmeg — Spicy; don't use too much
  • Cloves — Hot, spicy, aromatic; add only a few buds
  • Cinnamon — Warming, fragrant, pleasant
  • Ginger — Energizing, warming; avoid too much or the tea will taste hot

🍋 Lemon

  • Lemon peel — Bitter if brewed too long
  • Lemon balm — Good when fresh; rather bland when dried
  • Lemongrass — Fragrant, delicious, and high in vitamin A
  • Orange peel — Very tangy and fragrant; bitter if brewed too long

🌿 Mint

  • Spearmint — Classic mint; blends flavors well
  • Peppermint — Strong, calming flavor
  • Wintergreen — Woodsy mint

🍓 Tart

  • Rose hips — Refreshingly tart
  • Hibiscus — Very tart and rich in vitamin C

🍬 Sweet

  • Licorice — Sweet flavored
  • Anise seed — Licorice flavored
  • Fennel — Sweet licorice flavored
  • Vanilla bean — Chop for a rich vanilla flavor

🌸 Flowers

  • Chamomile — Fragrant and bittersweet; bitter if brewed too long
  • Roses — Mildly relaxing, delicious flavor
  • Lavender — Violet color and pungent flavor

🌲 Woodsy

  • Star anise — Wonderful with a slightly licorice flavor
  • Birch bark — Woodsy, refreshing "root beer"-like taste
  • Sarsaparilla — Richly fragrant with vanilla-like odor and flavor

The Magickal Uses of Tea

Tea is a plant that grows in China, India, and the American South. The teas we commonly associate with our ritual cuppa all come from the same plant, Camellia sinensis. It was reputedly discovered by the Chinese emperor Shen-nong in 2737 BCE when a leaf fell into his boiling water, entrancing him with its flavor and energy.

Not everything called tea really is. Herbs and botanicals that aren't Camellia sinensis made in hot water are called tisanes. A tisane can be honeybush with cinnamon, or a cup of chamomile with honey after a long day.

Tea and Witchcraft

Incorporating tea into your magickal practice has a long history and blends two well-known disciplines: plant magick and divination. Tea is a plant of transformation with so many varieties and preparations that perform unique magickal tasks.

Though all tea comes from the same plant, the growing environment plays a large part in the outcome, as do the methods of drying and variety. The tea plant is so delicate that leaves pick up the aromas of their environment. Hawaiian tea tastes vastly different from Chinese tea because Hawaiian tea farms are often near pineapple crops, allowing leaves to mature and retain a hint of their pineapple neighbors.

Types of Tea

White Tea

Brewing: 1½ tsp dried leaves, 175°F water, steep 4-5 minutes. Water too hot or steeping too long results in bitter brew.

Season: Spring

Magickal Correspondences: Purification, aura cleansing, prosperity, fecundity, psychic protection, abundance, clarity, beginnings, beauty, childhood, blessings, connection with beneficial spirits

White tea is comprised of young leaves picked before maturity. Its delicate flavor connects it to spring's new buds and explosion of color, fertility, and life. It makes an excellent offering to various gods as it blesses and fosters connection with others, including beneficial spirits.

Green Tea

Brewing: 1 tsp dried leaves, 175°F water, steep 1-2 minutes only.

Season: Summer

Magickal Correspondences: Abundance, health, long life, banishing negative energies, love (aphrodisiac), cleansing spaces

Green tea arises from dried mature leaves. Many think green tea is too bitter or grassy, but that's usually due to improper preparation. It has a soft, vegetative flavor that pairs well with fruits, especially citrus.

Green tea's antioxidants and moderate caffeine connect it to health and longevity. The caffeine lends itself to banishing negative energies. Brew it to asperge and cleanse a home or workplace. Green tea is also an aphrodisiac used in love spells where the mild caffeination can improve circulation to vital areas.

⚠️
Note: When mild caffeination is mentioned for green tea, it is not matcha being discussed. Matcha is green tea with the entire leaf powdered and consumed, meaning all caffeine is consumed. Matcha has 3-4 times the caffeine of brewed green tea.

Oolong Tea

Brewing: 1 tsp tea, 195°F water, steep 3-4 minutes.

Season: Fall

Magickal Correspondences: Peace, inner examination, divination, centering emotions, affection, love, balance, meditation

Oolong is a partially withered tea, mildly caffeinated with a soothing flavor somewhere between green and black tea. It represents the marriage of black and green tea, making its magickal action that of love.

The ritual of brewing oolong leaves time for meditation and inner thought, making it appropriate for working magick for self-examination while brewing. The balance of green and black tea leaves also makes it perfect for finding balance in mind and heart.

Black Tea

Brewing: 1 tsp tea, 195°F water, steep 3-4 minutes.

Season: Winter

Magickal Correspondences: Banishing apathy, banishing sleepiness, overcoming directionlessness, bravery, freedom from boredom, adventure, expansive thought, prosperity

Black tea is made by fermenting green tea leaves in water for long periods. The longer the fermentation, the more caffeine. In the mountains of China where black tea was born, tea leaves would be picked, placed in a vat of water, and left in caves.

Black tea's higher caffeine content leads to feelings of bravery, freedom from boredom, and a sense of adventure. Like other stimulating substances (cinnamon, clove, cardamom), black tea can be beneficial for prosperity work.

Rooibos and Honeybush Tea

Brewing: 1½ tsp tea, 208°F water, steep 5-6 minutes. These do not get bitter if over-steeped.

Origin: South Africa (Rooibos = "red tea," Honeybush named for honey-like fragrance)

Magickal Correspondences: Health, motherly energy, fertility, prosperity, grounding, nurturing, divination (excellent base for tea leaf reading)

Rooibos (Aspalathus linearis) is left on the plant to ripen, fall, and oxidize in the sun. Green rooibos uses younger leaves not allowed to oxidize, retaining a sweeter flavor. Both plants are drought tolerant.

Honeybush (Cyclopia intermedia) was mostly unknown outside South Africa until 2001. These dark red-brown botanicals have a mild fruity flavor with earthy energies suitable for invoking motherly energy, fertility, prosperity, grounding, and nurturing.

See Also

  • Herbal Tea Magick
  • Tasseomancy Tea Leaf Reading

Making a Good Pot of Tea

Start with fresh, cold water and bring it to a full rolling boil in a tea kettle. While the water heats, warm your china or ceramic teapot by filling it with hot water and then pouring it out.

Add loose tea leaves directly into the warmed pot, or place them inside a tea ball. Pour the boiling water over the leaves and let them steep for 3 to 5 minutes.

Serving

Pour the tea through a strainer into your cup, or strain it into a fresh, warmed teapot for serving. Add milk, sweetener, or lemon to taste. Cover the teapot with a cozy to keep it warm between cups.

A Note on Dosage

⚠️
Limit yourself to 2 to 4 cups per day. Tea acts as a natural diuretic, and some herbs can be harmful in large amounts. For magickal teas brewed during spellwork, drink only 1 to 2 cups during the spell event itself.

Notes on Magickal Tea Recipes

When preparing herbal tea recipes that include spoken words:

  • Words listed alongside each ingredient should be spoken aloud as that herb is added to the pot.
  • Words listed after all the ingredients should be spoken before drinking the tea.

Charging Your Tea with Intent

To turn your cup of tea into a potion, you just add magick! Whether you're using loose-leaf teas or a tea bag, the intention has to be applied.

  1. Decide on a goal. Make sure it is appropriately worded in the positive.
  2. Center your purpose in your mind. For example: "I am going to pass my English final."
  3. Gather intent and power into the palms of your hands, and use the energy to charge the tea leaves.
  4. Pour your hot water over the leaves and allow the heat of the water to charge your brew.
  5. Remove the tea after the correct steep time, and add sugar and cream as you like.
  6. Enjoy, continuing to visualize your intended outcome.

Designing a Tea Spell

To create your own magickal tea, there are a few steps to consider. Once you have the idea, experiment. Keep making, keep blending those teas. The only way you master something is by doing it. Research is lovely (and necessary), but is no replacement for getting your hands in there.

💡
Tip: Many tea shops have 1- or 2-ounce containers of loose tea leaves. With these smaller containers, you can purchase several types and flavors of tea to experiment with.

Step 1: What is your goal?

Not every tea blend needs to be magickal. Sometimes the goal is just to get your family to drink something other than a canned soda. It can be as intricate as you wish. Remember, every material that goes into your potion is magickal; it is the intent that powers that spell.

Is your goal to bring harmony to your household? Is it to have the energy to finish a project on time? Is your aim to relax after a stressful day? Deciding on the intended outcome not only cements the magick in your mind, but it also helps inform the choices you make for the rest of the work.

  • If your goal is to de-stress after a stressful day at work, you might not pick a high caffeine base like Maté.
  • If you need quick cash, you might not pick only fruits associated with love.

Step 2: Grab a notebook!

When working out this process, write it out. It puts all of the options out there and makes it easy to recreate blends that are a) effective and b) tasty!

Write down all of the things you associate with your goal. This is the free-form, brainstorming portion of the exercise. Looking at your thoughts on paper can allow you to make connections you might otherwise have missed.

Example brainstorm for Money:

Almond, Basil, Bergamot, Cedar, Clary sage, Clove, Lemon, Orange, Patchouli, Strawberry, Tangerine

Step 3: Look at correspondences

Your brainstorm list will have things that maybe wouldn't taste great, or don't agree with you for reasons of preference or allergies. Listen to the preference as much as you would allergies.

⚠️
If you genuinely object to something and decide to push the issue and include it in your working: a) you won't want to drink it and will avoid the working because of it, and b) if you make yourself do it anyway, your magick is going to be blocked because you are rejecting an ingredient therein. It's much easier and psychically gentle to pick something else.

Example: Almond is associated with abundance, fortune, money, wisdom, and prosperity, each adds a different flavor to the magick. Almond is also associated with beauty, communication, consecration, peace, and joy. An almond-based prosperity tea would encourage spiritual growth, joy, and long-term budgeting. Adding a woody, stable element will root the prosperity in the long term.

Choosing a base: If your tea hopes to stimulate the situation, black tea is an excellent choice. If you are sensitive to caffeine, rooibos and honeybush produce a caffeine-free base with mellow flavor. In the case of a caffeine issue, add a stimulating plant to your rooibos base, like cinnamon paired with a plant associated with fertility, like dried apple.

Step 4: Smell a few combinations

Before starting to blend, smell a small amount of your intended materials together. Use small dishes like custard cups. If your pieces don't work well together, you can put them back into their containers without contamination. Nothing is wasted.

Use equal amounts for smelling, each canister has different amounts with different strength scents, where equal amounts are a better measure of how they will taste together.

Step 5: Write down your findings

The thoughts that go through your head while blending and sampling should be recorded so you can more easily recall the smells, combinations, and features of each for future creations. Just because strawberry and lemon work well together doesn't mean they are suited to your immediate need for a money spell; they might be more suited to attracting a faithful and loving partner in a later tea.

Step 6: Blend your tea!

Start with equal parts of each material in the initial blending so it is easier to figure out whether it needs more or less of a certain ingredient.

⏰
Note on woody materials: They need more heat over a longer period of time to release their highest potential. They will continue to release their flavor as long as they are in the teacup. Leaving something containing clove, for instance, can quickly overpower a more delicate brew if allowed to steep too long.

Step 7: Add water!

Once you think you have the perfect ratio, write it down—something like "Test batch #1." Remember to be as detailed as possible. If you like "x" ingredient, but "y" ingredient is too powerful a flavor, you should be able to try a lesser amount for a more ideal blend.

Blend a teaspoon to a teaspoon and a half of the experimental brew with water and see how it reacts. Try it without sweetener, then try it with. Try it with creamer or your favorite cream substitute.

Step 8: Evaluate

Think of what you liked and didn't like. Not every tea is going to be a winner. There will be things you adore and things that have their place. Not every person will like everything you create, even your favorite ones. That's okay. For now, just blend for you. You can take over the world tomorrow.

Step 9: Capture your tea

The choice between loose-leaf and tea bags is an old one:

  • Loose-leaf: You can see every glorious ingredient
  • Tea bags: Quick and convenient solution
  • Fillable tea bags (tea filters): A middle ground, they allow the tea to breathe and infuse properly
  • Tea infusers: Allow the tea to fully bloom and attain its best flavor (recommended)
  • Tea balls: Can fall open, leak leaves out of the large water holes, and can burn your fingers
🏷️
Above all, label your tea. Whether you make up a name for it or just put the ingredients on a label, label everything.

Storing Your Tea

Proper storage ensures you get the best life out of your ingredients. The three most important things to remember:

Block out light

UV rays destroy the integrity of the ingredients and break down volatile oils that give your cherished blends scent and magick. They rob the tea of its color and structure. Some companies make UV-blocking tea containers; they will specifically state this and cost a bit more.

Constant temperature

Steep fluctuations in temperature can greatly reduce shelf life. High temperatures can break down the volatile oils, and freezing temperatures can break down the plant matter anchoring those oils, making your tea crumble rather than unfurl.

Intercept oxygen

Oxygen robs you of the smell of your teas, as the volatility of materials is the rate at which their oils evaporate. Every molecule that evaporates is one less that adds to your taste, aroma, and experience. Airtight containers are the way to go.

Planetary Tea Blending

An enriching thought exercise in blending tea is to look up plants associated with astrological planets. The newer planets have fewer known associations, and many that are not potable or are poisonous. Pluto, for example, is a god of the underworld and rules over death, so the herbs associated with Him are poisonous.

Plants Associated with Venus

  • Apple
  • Apricot
  • Cardamom
  • Lavender
  • Peach
  • Strawberry
  • Vanilla
  • Honey (not a plant, but still carries Her association)

Example blends for Aphrodite:

  • Apples and apricot
  • Peaches and cloves
  • Vanilla and apple

Add honeybush or rooibos base for a warm flavor and to give the tea some body.

Tincture Guide

Tinctures are scented liquids created by soaking dried plant materials in alcohol, which captures the fragrance. They work just as effectively as oils in magickal practice, stimulating ritual consciousness through scent and adding their energies to spellwork. The process is quick, easy, and often more reliable than other methods for capturing certain plant scents.

The Alcohol Question

The alcohol used for magickal tincturing must be ethyl alcohol (also called ethanol or grain alcohol). This is a natural product distilled from grain, sugar, or grapes.

Do not use isopropyl (rubbing) alcohol. It is distilled from petroleum products and has a sharp odor that makes it unsuitable for capturing fragrances.

For best results, you need alcohol of at least 70 percent strength (140 proof). Higher concentrations like 96 percent (192 proof) also work well. Standard vodka at 90 proof (45 percent) is not strong enough to produce the best scent.

Alcohol TypeProofPercentSuitability
Everclear19296%Excellent
High-proof grain alcohol140+70%+Good
Vodka9045%Too weak
Isopropyl/RubbingN/AN/ADo not use

Check liquor stores, supermarkets, and pharmacies for sources of ethyl alcohol.

Creating Tinctures

Materials Needed:

  • Dried plant material (fresh herbs will not work due to water content)
  • Ethyl alcohol (70% or higher)
  • Mortar and pestle
  • Small bottle with tight-fitting lid
  • Small funnel
  • Coffee filter or cheesecloth
  • Castor oil or glycerine (for stabilizing)

Process:

  1. Grind the herbs. Reduce dried plant material to the finest possible powder using a mortar and pestle. This is especially important for woods like sandalwood. Consider buying woods pre-ground.
  2. Empower the herb. Focus on the magickal goal of the tincture you are creating.
  3. Combine herb and alcohol. Pour the powdered herb into a small bottle with a tight-fitting lid. Using a funnel, add just enough ethyl alcohol to wet and cover the herb. Cap tightly.
  4. Shake daily. Shake the bottle vigorously every day for one to two weeks. Each time you shake, visualize the tincture's magickal goal.
  5. Strain. Using a coffee filter or cheesecloth in a strainer, strain the alcohol. Work quickly since alcohol evaporates when exposed to air.
  6. Test the scent. If the scent is not strong enough (common with materials other than gums and resins), add more herb to the bottle and pour the strained alcohol back over it. Repeat the shaking and straining process.
  7. Final test. Apply a drop or two to your wrist. Wait until the alcohol evaporates, then smell. Many tinctures do not smell true while still in the bottle.
  8. Finish and store. When the plant scent has completely overpowered the alcohol odor, filter one last time, add a few drops of castor oil or glycerine to stabilize the fragrance, and bottle. Label and store in a cool place out of direct sunlight.

Dilution Option

If you want to stretch your alcohol supply or capture plant scents that are not fully soluble in pure alcohol, dilute the ethyl alcohol with distilled water. Some scents transfer better in a water-alcohol mixture.

Using Tinctures

Do not drink magickal tinctures. Many plant materials used in tincturing are harmful if swallowed, and high-proof alcohol is not safe for consumption.

Safe uses include:

  • Incense papers: Tinctures work well for scenting incense papers, especially gum and resin tinctures or any heavily fragranced variety.
  • Anointing skin: Some tinctures can be applied to the skin to bring the plant's power within you. The alcohol evaporates quickly, leaving the scent. Always test on a small area first. Some tinctures irritate skin, leave stains, or create gummy residues (especially frankincense and copal). Lavender, clove, and patchouli tinctures are generally fine for anointing, but all alcohol-based tinctures can dry sensitive skin.
  • Anointing tools: Apply to magickal tools, sachets, candles, and jewelry.
  • Bath water: Add to ritual baths.
  • Blending: Mix with oils or add to ointments.

Virtually all ritual uses for oils also apply to tinctures.

Recommended Tincturing Materials

Some plants transfer their scent to alcohol more readily than others. The following materials produce good results:

MaterialColorScentMagickal Uses
BenzoinDark brown, translucentClean, antisepticBusiness success, mental powers, purification. Add to oils and ointments as a preservative.
CamphorClearPenetrating, coolLessening desire, healing amulets, Full Moon baths. Use only real camphor.
CinnamonDeep red to brownish blackRich, gorgeousMoney sachets and baths, psychic powers, protection.
CloveTransparent, light brownIncredible, warm spiceProtection, exorcism, love. Anoint money before spending.
CopalLight yellow, translucentFrankincense and lemonProtection, spirituality. Feels tacky on skin.
DeerstongueLight greenWarm vanillaPsychic powers, attracting men.
FrankincenseGoldenFull resinous frankincenseSpirituality, exorcism, purification, luck, protection. Excellent for incense papers. Can be sticky.
GalangalLight yellowGinger and camphorLuck, money, protection, exorcism, psychic development.
LavenderLight greenFloral, cleanLove, sleep (anoint forehead and pillow), purification baths, chastity, peace.
MyrrhBittersweet brownAncient, resinousSpirituality, healing, protection. Excellent for incense papers. Evocative when mixed with frankincense.
NutmegTranslucent, reddish orangeWarm spicePsychic powers, money, health, luck amulets.
PatchouliGreenHeady, earthyMoney, love, fertility.
PeppermintMint greenCool mintMoney, purification, love, sleep pillows. Slow to tincture but worth it. Spearmint also works.
RosemaryYellowish greenRich, resinousNearly every goal: love, healing, protection, exorcism, sleep, lust.
SageGreenish brownCamphor with green noteHealing, purification, wisdom, protection, wish sachets. White sage recommended.
SandalwoodWarm amberSandalwood with cedary noteProtection, spirituality, healing, exorcism. Slowest to tincture. Use pre-ground wood.
Star AniseLight amberSassafras, spicyPsychic awareness, especially before divination with tarot or runes.
TonkaDeep amberRich vanilla with bitter noteMoney, love, courage, wish sachets. TOXIC: do not ingest.
VanillaAmberRich, warm, familiarLove, physical energy, mental processing.

Note: Do not sniff tinctures until after the alcohol has evaporated. Once applied to skin, the alcohol evaporates and the herb's true scent emerges.

Speed Notes:

  • Fast: Clove, Star Anise, spices
  • Medium: Gums and resins (frankincense, myrrh, benzoin, copal)
  • Slow: Peppermint, Sandalwood

Percolation Method

Percolation is an alternative to the standard soaking method that uses gravity to extract the soluble components of an herb. It is slightly more involved but produces results much faster.

Pack dried, powdered herbs into a cone-shaped container or closed funnel and moisten them with solvent until they reach a "wet sand" consistency. Cover the herbs with a mixture of alcohol and water and allow them to steep while controlling the flow of liquid through the material. Collect the percolation in a separate container below, and compost the spent herbs when the process is complete.

Blending Tinctures

Tinctures can be combined just like oils. Use equal parts unless your intuition suggests otherwise. All blends listed in the Recipe Grimoire that use oils can also be made with tinctures.

All herb tinctures are safe for skin anointing, though the alcohol content can be drying. Gum and resin tinctures may leave sticky residues.

As with all magickal herbal products, use tinctures with visualization and intention.

Caution

  • Always test tinctures on a small skin area before broader application
  • Some tinctures stain skin and fabric
  • Resin tinctures often leave sticky residues
  • Store away from heat and direct sunlight
  • Keep out of reach of children and pets

Recipe Grimoire

Infusion Guide

At its core, an infusion is about coaxing one substance to take on the energetic properties of another. Water and oil are the two most common receiving media, and if you have ever steeped a cup of loose-leaf tea, you already grasp the fundamental principle. Infusions are the gateway through which botanical power enters potions, ritual baths, floorwashes, magickal oils, and a wide range of other preparations.

Vinegar Infusions

Vinegar infusions use apple cider vinegar as the receiving medium. Pour one cup of apple cider vinegar over a quarter cup of your chosen herbs and allow them to steep for roughly a month, adjusting by a week or so depending on how much cellulose is in the plant material. Agitate the jar daily throughout the steeping cycle. When the cycle is complete, strain the liquid into a clean glass jar and compost the spent herbs.

Decoctions

Decoctions are necessary when working with the tougher, more rigid parts of a plant. Woody leaves, thick stems, dense roots, bark, and seeds all have a more resistant cell wall that a simple infusion cannot fully break down. To decoct, bring water to a boil, add the measured herbs, then reduce to a very low simmer and cover. Allow the mixture to gently release its properties over an extended period.

When preparing a magickal decoction, allow yourself to enter a meditative state and remain present with the herbs throughout the process. This has a practical benefit as well, since a heat source should never be left unattended. Once the decoction is finished, strain the plant material and compost it.

Water Infusions

The baseline ratio is one teaspoon of dried herb (or roughly one and a half teaspoons fresh) to each cup of boiling water. When blending several herbs together, scale each ingredient's portion individually rather than simply adding more total material.

Use a non-reactive vessel, glass rather than plastic. Pour boiling water directly over the botanicals and allow the mixture to steep for anywhere from five to fifteen minutes. Whether you strain out the solids or leave them in depends on the working. A floorwash performs better with the plant matter filtered away, while a potent ritual bath may gain strength from leaving it in, even though that makes cleanup considerably messier.

Concentrated Infusions

When you need something stronger, intended for baths or floorwashes rather than internal use, pack in a more generous amount of botanical material and pour just enough boiling water to submerge it. Let the brew cool to room temperature on its own, then strain or leave the solids depending on the application.

Cold Oil Infusions

A slower, no-heat alternative to the water bath method. Cover fresh or dried herbs in a carrier oil and store the jar in a dark, dry place such as a cupboard. Allow the herbs to soak for a minimum of two weeks and up to a month, then strain the oil through a cloth and transfer it to a dark, covered container.

Cold-infused oils retain the scent and some properties of the herb used. They can be used for culinary purposes when tonic herbs are chosen, and magickally to anoint candles, clear crystals, charge magickal tools, or consecrate a person by anointing pulse points.

Oil Infusions

Infusing oil takes a bit more effort than water, but nothing beyond a basic home kitchen setup. The working ratio is one ounce of fresh herb (or half an ounce dried) per cup of oil. Exceeding these proportions is not advisable unless a specific formula calls for it.

Place the plant material in a stainless steel bowl and cover it with oil. Warm gently over a water bath: a saucepan about a quarter full of simmering water, with the bowl sitting above the bottom rather than resting directly on it. A proper double boiler works too. Oil burns easily, so vigilance is non-negotiable. Keep the bowl covered, stir from time to time, and maintain a gentle simmer for around thirty minutes. If the oil starts smoking, bubbling hard, or scorching, the scent will go harsh and the infusion is lost.

After cooling, pour the oil through several layers of cheesecloth or a fine non-metallic strainer. Run it through a second time if needed. Getting every bit of plant matter out is critical, because any solids left behind will cause the oil to spoil. Essential oils or flower remedies called for in the recipe go in after straining, once the oil has cooled completely. Store the finished product in an airtight container.

A slow cooker offers a hands-off alternative to the water bath. Use the same proportions, set the temperature to low for about two hours, and strain exactly as described.

Solar-Charged Infusions

Steady warm, sunny weather opens the door to a method that produces unusually potent results, because the finished infusion carries the energy of the sun alongside the botanical properties. Pack the plant material into a jar with a snug lid, cover it completely with oil, and stir in one tablespoon of apple cider vinegar. Set the jar in direct sunlight during the day and move it to a warm cupboard at night (or, on warm evenings, under the moon). Maintain this cycle for a full two weeks, then strain as you would any oil infusion.

Flower Petal Infusions

Delicate petals respond best to a no-heat technique. Pull the petals apart and fill an airtight jar generously with clean, dry petals. Pour in an oil whose own scent is as neutral as possible, so the flower's fragrance comes through without competition. Let the petals soak for three days, giving the jar an occasional shake and keeping it in sunlight by day and a warm cupboard overnight.

After three days, strain the petals out through cheesecloth or a non-metal sieve, discard them, and keep the oil. Add a fresh batch of clean, dry petals to the same jar and pour the reserved oil back over them. Repeat the full three-day steeping and straining cycle. Each round deepens the fragrance. Three passes typically produces the intensity most practitioners want. After the final straining, make sure every last bit of petal is removed.

Preserving Infused Oils

Any sizable batch of infused oil that will not be used right away benefits from some form of natural preservation. A quarter teaspoon of simple tincture of benzoin (the plain variety, not the compound tincture sometimes labeled Friar's Balsam) per cup of oil is a reliable option. Benzoin comes from styrax gum, which carries its own traditional associations with purification and protection.

Vitamin E serves as another preservative, though much of what you find on the market is synthetically produced. Puncture a single capsule and squeeze the contents into each cup of oil. Jojoba, which is technically a liquid plant wax rather than a true oil, resists oxidation naturally and can be blended with other oils to extend their shelf life. Whenever you combine oils, keep the total oil-to-botanical ratio at the standard level.

Ink Guide

Ink has long served as a tool of magick, transforming symbols and images of our goals into visible form. These written or drawn images become focal points during ritual, helping to stir, program, and direct personal energy toward manifestation.

History

During the Middle Ages and Renaissance, many secret magickal textbooks contained sections on purifying and "exorcising" inks before use. Practitioners used these specially prepared inks to draw symbols thought to invoke or banish spiritual entities. The careful preparation was considered essential to the work's success.

Today, the magickal uses of ink have largely faded from practice. When a spell calls for inscribing symbols or images, many practitioners simply reach for a ballpoint pen and lined paper. In doing so, they miss the opportunity for deeper involvement in the ritual. Just as we create our own incenses and oils, we can also create our own inks.

The Charcoal Pen

The first "ink" was likely charcoal, and the first pen a charred stick. This primal method still works today.

  1. Burn a branch or stick until the end reduces to charcoal (not ash)
  2. Allow it to cool completely
  3. Use it as a natural charcoal pencil to trace images of your goal
  4. Create a new char-pen for each ritual
  5. Visualize your magickal need as you draw

This simple approach may be enough to spark your ability to move and direct personal power. For those who want more, creating your own magickal inks offers deeper engagement.

Tools for Ink Magick

All magickal inks work best with sharpened quills or dip pens. Dip pens are usually available at stationery and office supply stores. Practice using them before employing them in ritual work.

Making Lampblack

Lampblack is a key ingredient in several ink formulas. It is soot collected from a candle flame.

Candle Color Selection:

  • White candle for general magickal needs
  • Green candle for money inks
  • Pink candle for love inks
  • Match the candle color to your intention (see Color Correspondences)

Collection Process:

  1. Light a candle of the appropriate color
  2. Hold the back of a metal spoon's bowl in the flame, barely touching the wick
  3. After 30 to 45 seconds, the flame will coat the spoon with black soot
  4. Remove the spoon and hold it over a small bowl
  5. Carefully scrape the lampblack into the bowl using a piece of cardstock
  6. Work carefully. Lampblack is lighter than air and will scatter if disturbed
  7. Repeat 30 to 60 times (about 30 minutes to an hour of work)
  8. Visualize your magickal goal throughout the process

The longer you collect lampblack, the more ink you will be able to produce.

Simple Ingredient Inks

Several natural materials produce usable magickal inks with minimal preparation:

IngredientColorNotes
Saffron essenceGolden yellowExpensive but produces fine results
Pokeberries (crushed)PurpleSeeds are poisonous. Do not ingest.
Beet juiceReddishAdd gum arabic to thicken if needed
Blackberry juiceDark purpleNatural and accessible
Boysenberry juicePurple-redNatural and accessible
Grape juicePurpleNatural and accessible

For any ink that is too thin to write with, add a small amount of gum arabic to thicken.

Invisible Inks

Invisible inks are made from common household items such as milk or lemon juice. Write with a clean dip pen on white paper and allow to dry completely. The writing will be invisible until revealed.

To Reveal:

Hold the paper carefully over a candle flame (close enough for heat but not burning) until the writing appears.

Ritual Application:

  1. Write or draw an image of your magickal goal with invisible ink
  2. Visualize with power as you write
  3. When dry, stare at the blank paper. This represents your life without your need.
  4. Hold it near the candle flame
  5. As the image slowly appears, send energy into it, knowing the need will manifest in your life as well

Using Magickal Inks

  • Written Spells: Write or draw an image of your goal on appropriately colored paper. Visualize the letters glowing with energy as you write, or the picture shimmering with power.
  • Burning Rituals: Anoint the inscribed paper with oils matching your intention and burn it to ashes. As it burns, see the energy streaming out to manifest your need.
  • Scrying: At night, burn psychism-inducing incense. Add several drops of black ink to a small round bowl of water. When the water has darkened, turn off the lights and light a yellow or white candle. Gaze into the water, relaxing your conscious mind and opening yourself to receive information about possible future trends.

Caution

Some old spells call for ink to be taken internally, such as dissolving an inscribed paper in water and drinking it. Most commercially prepared inks are poisonous, as are many homemade formulations. Do not drink or eat ink. Always apply modern safety knowledge when working with historical rituals.

Spell Documentation Guide

Keeping careful records of your spellwork serves multiple purposes. It helps you track what works best for you, identify patterns in your practice, and refine your techniques over time. A well-maintained spell journal becomes an invaluable reference as you grow in your craft.

What to Record

For each spell or ritual you perform, consider documenting the following:

Basic Information

  • Spell name or type - What kind of working is this?
  • Date and time - When did you perform it?
  • Moon phase - What was the moon doing?
  • Weather conditions - What was happening outside?
  • Location - Where did you cast?

Personal State

  • Your physical health - How were you feeling physically?
  • Your emotional state - What was your mood?
  • Your energy level - Were you well-rested or depleted?

Spell Details

  • Purpose and intention - What were you trying to accomplish?
  • Tools and ingredients used - What materials did you work with?
  • Deities or spirits invoked - Did you call upon any entities?
  • Full text of incantations - What words did you speak?
  • Duration - How long did the working take?

Results

  • Immediate reactions - What did you feel during or right after?
  • Signs and synchronicities - What meaningful coincidences appeared?
  • Outcome - Did the spell manifest? How? When?
  • Lessons learned - What would you do differently?

Why Documentation Matters

Over time, your records reveal which correspondences resonate most strongly for you, which moon phases align with your energy, and which techniques consistently produce results. This personal data is far more valuable than any book's recommendations because it reflects your unique magickal signature.

Your spell journal also helps you avoid repeating mistakes and builds confidence as you see your successes accumulate. When a spell works beautifully, you can recreate those conditions. When something falls flat, you can analyze why and adjust your approach.

See Also

  • Anatomy of a Basic Spell
  • Journal Prompts
  • Dream Journaling

Ritual Grimoire

Ritual Types

The Ritual Database organizes workings by their physical form and method. Understanding these categories helps you choose the right approach for your intention and find similar workings across traditions.

Types of Magick (per Family Tradition)

Sympathetic Magick: "This IS That."

One object is treated as being another. Energy directed into the magickal object passes into the object it represents. Examples include poppets, sigils, and candle-burning spells.

Comparative Magick: "This REPRESENTS That."

A relationship is established between a magickal object and another object, typically using the word "as." Energy directed into the magickal object also enters the other. Examples include charms, connections, and growth spells.

Directive Magick: "This AFFECTS That."

The most common type. Magickal energy is raised, focused on a goal, directed into an object, and released for accomplishment. Examples include candle spells, herbal pouches, and stones and crystals.

Transference Magick: "This ENTERS That."

Negative energy is moved from an affected object into another. Common tools include onion or garlic braids, garlic cloves, and salt. In rare cases, deadly energy can be moved into a willing host, which may die as a result, such as a plant in a hospital room or a willing animal pet or familiar. Willingness is determined through intuitive communication.

Ritual Types and Techniques

Ancestor Work / Necromancy

What it is:

Magick specifically involving the dead. Communication with deceased ancestors, offerings, elevation work, graveyard rituals. Distinct from general spirit work.

When to use:

Seeking ancestral guidance, honoring the dead, requesting assistance from deceased family, elevation rituals for stuck spirits, graveyard work for specific intentions.

Examples:

Ancestor altar offerings, cemetery rituals, spirit elevation work, ancestral petitions, Samhain rituals.

Note:

Many graveyard and necromantic practices are closed by culture. Research before practicing.

Astral / Spiritual Journeying

What it is:

Intentional travel in non-physical realms for guidance, messages, problem-solving, or entity contact. Not the same as meditation.

When to use:

Seeking guidance from other realms, entity contact, problem-solving through spiritual travel, retrieving lost parts of self, exploring non-physical spaces.

Examples:

Hedge riding, shamanic journeying (closed in many cultures), trance-based movement between worlds, pathworking.

Note:

Requires specific techniques, tools, and safety guidelines. Practice with care.

Banishing

What it is:

Magick that removes something or someone from your life or space. Can target people, spirits, energies, or situations. Generally considered defensive rather than harmful. Focuses on removal, not harm.

When to use:

Toxic person leaves your life, unwanted spirit departs, negative energy clears from space, bad habit breaks, illness leaves the body.

Duration:

Immediate effect, but may require reinforcement.

Bath / Wash Magick

What it is:

Magickal baths, floor washes, cleansing washes, foot baths. Massive historical category across cultures.

When to use:

Road opening, spiritual cleansing, attracting luck, blessing a space, removing negativity, preparing for ritual work.

Examples:

Road opener baths, cleansing baths with herbs, Florida Water washes, floor washes, uncrossing baths.

Common methods:

Herbal infusions added to bath water, bathing with intention, pouring wash over threshold, wiping down surfaces with charged water.

Binding

What it is:

Magick that restricts or attaches. Can be defensive (restricting harmful actions) or positive (binding yourself to good things, binding willing participants together).

When to use:

Defensive: Stopping someone from causing harm, preventing gossip, neutralizing magickal attacks.

Positive: Securing prosperity, strengthening consensual relationships, binding yourself to success or healthy habits.

Duration:

Ongoing while the binding object remains intact or buried.

Ethics note:

Binding another person without consent removes free will, even if intended positively. Binding yourself to positive things or binding willing participants together is generally accepted.

Blessing

What it is:

Calling down positive energy, divine favor, or beneficial power onto a person, place, object, or situation. Can invoke deities, spirits, ancestors, or universal forces. Opposite of cursing.

When to use:

Welcoming new baby, blessing a home, consecrating ritual tools, sending good wishes, invoking protection and prosperity, marking life transitions, gratitude offerings.

Duration:

Can be momentary or lasting depending on intent and method.

Common methods:

Spoken prayers or invocations, anointing with oil or water, smoke cleansing, laying on of hands, sprinkling blessed water, marking with symbols.

Candle Magick

What it is:

Magick performed using candles as the primary tool. One of the largest categories in modern practice. May involve dressing with oils, carving, color correspondences, moving candles, flame reading, glass reading, or multi-candle arrangements.

When to use:

Nearly any intention. Candle magick is versatile, accessible, and foundational to many traditions.

Examples:

7-day candles, reversing candles, dual-color candles, moving candle spells, candle petitions, vigil lights.

Common methods:

Dressing candles with oils, carving names or symbols, color selection based on intent, burning in specific patterns, reading flame behavior and wax remains.

Amulet

What it is:

A protective object worn or carried to ward off evil, danger, or negative energy. Amulets are primarily defensive. They repel or shield rather than attract. Historically placed in tombs, carried into battle, and worn for safe travel.

The early Greeks called amulets amylon, meaning "food," suggesting people used food offerings to ask gods and goddesses for protection, perhaps eating or carrying a small bit as a token.

When to use:

Protection from harm, warding off evil spirits, shielding from negative energy, safe travel, guarding against illness or misfortune.

What can be used:

Many items found in the natural world have been made into amulets: plants, carved stones, metal objects. Amulets were often chosen for their shapes or where they were found:

  • Holey stones (any stone with a natural hole): European ancestors carried these to guard against malicious fairies, who would get trapped in the hole
  • Crystals found near sacred wells: Carried to protect the bearer's well-being
  • Amethyst: Long worn against drunkenness, as it increases self-control

Placement:

Amulets can be worn, placed with valuable items, affixed on pet collars, hung in windows, planted in gardens, or put anywhere you want protection. A horseshoe hung above a doorway is a familiar example.

Amulets from around the world:

AmuletOriginPurpose
Brass ring (right arm)LaplandKeep ghosts away
God figurines (buried near home)AssyriaProtect all within
Lapis lazuli eyes (in tombs)EgyptSafeguard soul's journey
Metal rattles (on children's clothing)Ancient RomeOverall protection
Miniature carved canoesIroquoisProtection from drowning
Monkey teethBorneoStrength and skill
Peach stoneChinaProtection against evil
Spruce needlesShoshoneKeep sickness at bay

Combining elements:

An amulet may be a single gem or contain several items, just make sure each relates to your intention and holds meaning for you. Going to a party? Amethyst earrings (self-control) plus amber perfume (protection against unwanted advances) creates layered protection.

See also: Creating an Amulet for the full ritual process.

Historical note:

Ancient Greek soldiers carried amulets into battle. Early Egyptians placed them in tombs of royalty to ensure safe passage into the afterlife

Charm

What it is:

Originally, charms were spoken spells: verbal incantations. The word comes from the Latin carmen, meaning "incantation" or "song." In a time when few could read or write, witches used verbal spells that rhymed or had distinct rhythm, making them easier to memorize.

Today, "charm" also refers to a portable object charged for a specific purpose: carried, worn, or placed in a location. Can be natural (stone, root, bone) or crafted (knotted cord, inscribed metal, assembled object).

When to use:

When you need magick that travels with you or protects a specific location. When the working requires sustained presence. When you want an object you can recharge over time. When speaking your intention aloud strengthens your focus.

Examples:

  • Verbal charms: Rhyming incantations, spoken spells, repeated affirmations
  • Physical charms: Protection stones carried in pocket, knotted cords, carved talismans, crystals programmed for intent

Creating verbal charms:

A charm is like a poem. Many rhyme or have distinct rhythm. The important thing is that it expresses your wish clearly and is easy to remember. Repeat it often to give it more energy and make the magick work faster.

Example:

Leaf of ash, I do thee pluck
To bring to me a day of luck.

You can add physical actions to spoken charms. As you speak "pluck," take a leaf from a tree whose properties match your intention, then carry it with you.

Affirmations vs. Incantations:

  • Affirmations are positive statements in present tense, as if the condition already exists. Keep them short, clear, and precise. Only include what you desire.
    • ✓ "I am healthy in body, mind, and spirit."
    • ✗ "I don't have any illnesses or injuries."
    • ✓ "I now have a job that's perfect for me."
    • ✗ "I want to get a better job."
  • Incantations follow the same rules but are written as rhymes. The catchy phrasing makes them easy to remember and gives them musical power.

Example love incantation:

As the day fades into night
I draw a love that's good and right.
As the night turns into day
We are blessed in every way.

Creative uses:

  • Write on a slip of paper and insert into a talisman or amulet
  • Place under your pillow at night
  • Repeat throughout the day: in the shower, driving to work, before sleep
  • Write on colored paper, decorate with meaningful images, post where you'll see it often

Talisman

What it is:

An object charged to attract specific energies or outcomes. Unlike amulets (which repel), talismans draw things toward you: love, wealth, success, health. Often inscribed with symbols, words, or sigils.

Many old stories say spirits lived in talismans, and whoever possessed the talisman could command the spirit to do specific tasks. Aladdin's lamp holding a genie who granted wishes is a mythological example of a talisman.

When to use:

Attracting love, drawing prosperity, manifesting success, invoking specific planetary or deity energies, enhancing personal power.

Examples:

  • Planetary seals, inscribed metals
  • Jade (Chinese tradition): worn for health, strength, and good fortune
  • Lockets with lover's hair: worn for centuries across cultures
  • Gemstones programmed for attraction
  • Written petitions sealed into objects

Timing:

Fashion talismans while the moon is waxing (between new and full). The waxing moon encourages increase and development.

Placement options:

  • Wear in a cloth or leather pouch
  • Place in a wooden box on your altar
  • If you know feng shui, place in the part of your home that relates to your intention

Creating a talisman:

Create essentially the same way as an amulet, with one or more ingredients that relate to your objective. Consider:

  • The purpose of the spell
  • Your own associations with the objects
  • If carrying: small, lightweight ingredients
  • If wearing: comfort, convenience, and beauty

Tokens as talismans:

Many simple talismans are ordinary objects infused with meaning by their owners. A pretty pebble found during a meaningful walk, touched fondly throughout the day, placed where you'll see it. This token now holds positive energy. The good feelings and thoughts associated with such objects give them their power. Objects from sacred sites are especially ideal.

Lifespan and maintenance:

Because talismans actively send out energy to attract what you desire, they burn out faster than amulets. If you don't get what you want in a reasonable time, you may need to "feed" your talisman to reinforce its strength. Dab a little essential oil on it. Choose an oil from a plant that relates to your talisman's purpose.

Historical note:

Aztec priests used gemstones as talismans to invoke deities and for prophesying. The tradition spans virtually every culture worldwide.

Key distinction:

  • Amulet = defensive, repels harm (passive until activated)
  • Talisman = attractive, draws desired outcomes (actively sends energy, burns out faster)
  • Charm = can be either, originally referred to spoken spells

Cleansing

What it is:

Removing stagnant, negative, or unwanted energy from places, objects, or bodies. One of the most-used categories in every magickal system.

When to use:

After illness or conflict, moving into new space, after unwanted visitors, clearing ritual tools, removing negativity, refreshing stagnant energy.

Examples:

Smoke cleansing (non-sacred herbs), sound cleansing, floor washes, salt bowls, egg cleansings (note: egg limpia is closed practice).

Common methods:

Burning herbs and passing objects through smoke, ringing bells or using sound, washing with salt water, placing salt in corners, sweeping with intention.

Consecration

What it is:

Making something sacred. Setting an object, space, or person apart for spiritual or magickal use. Purifies and charges simultaneously. Often involves blessing, anointing, and dedication to a specific purpose or deity.

When to use:

New ritual tools, altar setup, dedicating sacred space, preparing objects for magickal work, claiming items for spiritual use, temple or shrine creation.

Duration:

Generally permanent unless the item is deconsecrated or the energy needs refreshing.

Common methods:

Cleansing with salt, smoke, or water, then anointing with oil, speaking words of dedication, passing through elements (earth, air, fire, water), invoking deity or spiritual force, charging under moon or sun.

Cord Cutting

What it is:

Severing energetic connections between yourself and another person, situation, or energy. Uses physical cords, thread, or string as sympathetic representation. Cut, burn, or untie the cord to release the connection.

When to use:

Ending toxic relationships, releasing past trauma, breaking unhealthy attachments, moving on from situations that no longer serve you, cutting ties with harmful people.

Intent:

Release and freedom. Not necessarily harmful, often healing. Can be done with love and gratitude for what was while still choosing to move forward separately.

Common methods:

Two candles with cord between them (burn through cord), knotted cord cut with ritual knife, braided cord representing relationship unbraided and burned, visualization paired with cutting physical cord.

Crossing

What it is:

Deliberately blocking someone's path or luck. Laying a spiritual obstacle in their way. Can be done through physical items placed where they'll cross them (crossroads magick) or through ritual work.

When to use:

Blocking opportunities for someone causing harm, preventing someone's plans from succeeding, creating obstacles for toxic people.

Duration:

Until the crossing is removed or walked off.

Curses

What it is:

The most severe form of harmful magick. Intended to cause serious, lasting harm. May span years or even generations in some traditions. Requires significant energy and often has consequences for the caster.

When to use:

Extreme situations where other methods have failed. Many traditions consider curses taboo.

Duration:

Long-term to permanent unless specifically broken.

Warning:

Carries significant risk and ethical weight. Consider consequences carefully.

Decay / Weathering Magick

What it is:

Magick using rot, rust, mold, or decomposition as the spell engine. Niche but historically present.

When to use:

Banishing through decay, transformation through rot, breaking down old patterns, letting something waste away naturally.

Examples:

Leaving written names outside to rot and dissolve, burying biodegradable items to decompose, rust work for corrosion of harmful influences.

Common methods:

Writing names on biodegradable material left to weather, burying items to rot, using rust or decay as sympathetic magick.

Divination Ritual

What it is:

Rituals where cards, runes, scrying, pendulums, or bones are the core magickal act, not just tools for information. Fully functional spells, not just readings.

When to use:

Drawing a card to seal a spell's outcome, casting runes for manifestation, scrying to make contact with entities, using pendulum to direct energy.

Examples:

Drawing tarot card to determine spell method, runic casting for manifestation, scrying for entity contact, bone reading for decision-making magick.

Why it's distinct:

The divination method itself performs the magickal action, not just provides information.

Dream Work

What it is:

Casting spells to influence dreams, induce visions, receive messages, or travel astrally. Distinct from dream interpretation.

When to use:

Seeking guidance through dreams, inducing prophetic visions, lucid dreaming for magickal work, receiving messages from entities or ancestors, astral travel preparation.

Examples:

Sleep sachets under pillows, mugwort teas before bed, poppets or sigils under pillows, pre-sleep invocations, dream incubation rituals.

Common methods:

Herbal preparations (mugwort, lavender, chamomile), charged objects under pillow, spoken intentions before sleep, keeping dream journal as magickal record.

Elixir

What it is:

Liquid preparation meant for consumption or external application. May be charged through intention, moon water, crystal infusion, or spoken words. Must use non-toxic ingredients if consumed.

When to use:

When you want to take magick internally or apply it to skin. When water is the primary carrier for your intention. When you need something that can be shared or distributed.

Examples:

Moon water for various purposes, flower essence remedies, crystal-charged water, herbal infusions for specific intents (using safe herbs only).

Freezer Magick

What it is:

Placing a representation of a person or situation in water, then freezing it. Stops action, slows energy, creates distance, puts things on hold.

When to use:

Stopping gossip, slowing someone's harmful actions, putting distance between you and a person, pausing a situation until you're ready to deal with it, cooling hot tempers.

Common methods:

Name or photo in water in a jar or bag, frozen in back of freezer. Can add herbs, pepper, or vinegar. Leave frozen as long as needed. Thaw and dispose when ready to release.

Hex

What it is:

Magick intended to cause misfortune, bad luck, or general harm to a target. Less severe than a Curses but more aggressive than a Jinx. Often described as "crossing" someone.

When to use:

When someone is causing harm and other methods haven't worked. When consequences are needed but not devastation.

Duration:

Typically temporary unless sustained. Fades over time or when conditions are met.

Hot Foot

What it is:

Making someone leave a location or your life. Traditional Hoodoo technique using specific powders or oils. Forces someone to move, quit, leave town, or exit your sphere.

When to use:

Removing unwanted neighbor, making toxic coworker quit, forcing abuser to move away, getting rid of unwanted romantic attention.

Common methods:

Powders sprinkled where target will walk, oils on their shoes or doorstep, petition work with movement symbolism.

Jar

What it is:

Container magick using glass jars, bottles, or sealed vessels. Ingredients are layered or mixed inside, then sealed. Can be kept active indefinitely, buried, or disposed of when the work is done.

When to use:

When you want to contain, sweeten, sour, protect, or trap energy. When the magick benefits from ingredients combining and steeping over time. When you need a working that stays hidden or sealed.

Examples:

Honey jars for sweetening, vinegar jars for souring, protection jars with nails and herbs, witch bottles buried at property line, freezer jars for binding.

Jinx

What it is:

The mildest form of harmful magick. Causes minor inconvenience, irritation, or temporary bad luck. Often spontaneous or spoken ("jinxing" someone with words). Easiest to cast and easiest to break.

When to use:

Minor annoyances, temporary setbacks for someone who needs a small lesson.

Duration:

Short-term, often self-resolving.

Kitchen / Hearth Magick

What it is:

Magick performed through cooking, stirring, baking, or home tending. One of the most accessible and widely practiced forms of magick.

When to use:

Daily magick, feeding family with intention, blessing the home, creating abundance, protection through domestic work.

Examples:

Stirring clockwise for abundance, baking protective bread, simmer pots, enchanting meals, blessing ingredients.

Common methods:

Stirring direction (clockwise for increase, counterclockwise for decrease), speaking intentions while cooking, choosing ingredients by correspondence, sharing food to share blessings.

Knot Magick

What it is:

Tying knots in cord or string to trap, hold, or release intention. Each knot can hold a specific intention. Untying releases the magick.

When to use:

Storing spells for later release, binding intentions into physical form, creating portable magick, setting conditions for spell release, building power through multiple knottings.

Common methods:

Witch's ladder (9 knots with feathers or beads), speaking intention into each knot, carrying knotted cord as charm, untying one knot per day to release serial magick, sailors' wind knots.

Meditation / Energy Work

What it is:

Magick performed entirely through non-physical means. Includes visualization, breathwork, energy raising, grounding, centering.

When to use:

When physical tools aren't available or appropriate, personal energy work, preparing for ritual, cleansing your own energy, raising power.

Examples:

Chakra clearing, energy balls, aura cleansing, guided journey visualizations, breathwork for power raising, grounding and centering.

Common methods:

Visualization techniques, breath control, energy manipulation through intent, mental focus and direction.

Mirror Box

What it is:

A box lined with mirrors (or reflective material) facing inward, containing a representation of the target (photo, name, poppet, personal item). Reflects their negativity back to them. Traps and contains harmful energy.

When to use:

When someone is actively harming you and you want their actions to backfire. When returning energy to sender. When you need to trap and contain someone's influence.

Ethics note:

Reflects what someone sends out. If they're sending harm, they receive harm. If they stop, the reflection stops. Some consider this defensive rather than harmful.

Oil

What it is:

Blended oils for anointing, dressing candles, charging objects, or applying to body. Typically a carrier oil base with essential oils, herbs, resins, or other ingredients added. See also Recipe Grimoire for oil blending instructions.

When to use:

When you need to anoint candles, dress tools, apply to body, or consecrate objects. When scent is important to your working. When you want a working that can be reused for the same purpose.

Examples:

Protection oil for anointing doors, prosperity oil for money candles, love oil for relationship work, banishing oil for cleansing tools.

Petition / Manifestation Work

What it is:

Workings driven by written or spoken petitions, letters, written intentions, command phrases, or affirmations charged magickally. Appears across Hoodoo, folk magick, chaos magick, and modern witchcraft.

When to use:

When you need to state your intention clearly, when writing is your strongest form of focus, when petitioning spirits or deities, when working with specific phrasing or commands.

Examples:

Petition papers folded toward/away from you, burning petitions, placing petitions under candles, writing intentions on bay leaves, letter magick, spoken affirmations.

Common methods:

Writing full petition statements, folding toward you (attraction) or away (banishment), burning to release, placing under candles or in jars, speaking petitions aloud with power.

Poppet

What it is:

Doll or figure representing a person, animal, or spirit. Used for sympathetic magick: what you do to the poppet affects the target. Can be made from fabric, clay, wax, roots, or other materials.

When to use:

When you need to work magick on a specific person (with or without consent, depending on your ethics). When healing work requires directing energy to body parts. When binding or controlling someone's actions.

Examples:

Healing poppets with herbs in afflicted areas, binding poppets wrapped in cord, protection poppets for children, love poppets (ethically questionable), harmful poppets (use with extreme caution).

Related technique:

Taglocks (hair, nails, personal items) used to link poppet to specific person. Doll babies in Hoodoo are a specific closed practice unless culturally connected.

Potion

What it is:

Prepared mixtures for magickal purposes, broader than elixirs. Can be liquids, powders, pastes, or salves. May include ingredients not meant for consumption. Used externally, sprinkled, poured, or buried.

When to use:

When you need a prepared substance for a specific magickal purpose that isn't strictly an oil or consumable elixir. When combining multiple ingredients into a finished product.

Examples:

Magickal inks, ritual baths, floor washes, powders for sprinkling, salves for anointing.

Pouch

What it is:

Fabric bags filled with herbs, crystals, petition papers, and other materials. Typically tied or sewn shut. Can be carried, worn, placed on altar, hidden in location, or disposed of. Also called mojo bags, gris-gris, or medicine bags (note: some of these terms belong to specific closed traditions).

When to use:

When you want portable magick that holds multiple ingredients. When the contents need to be in contact with each other. When you need something more discreet than a jar but more durable than loose materials.

Examples:

Protection pouches carried in purse, prosperity bags kept in wallet, sleep sachets under pillow, healing pouches worn on body, banishing bags buried off property.

Protection

What it is:

Shielding, warding, blocking, reinforcing one's energy or space. Foundational magick distinct from banishing or binding.

When to use:

Daily shielding, protecting home or space, guarding against magickal attack, reinforcing personal boundaries, protecting loved ones or pets.

Examples:

Wards, protective sigils, barrier jars, iron nails, sound wards, mirror wards, personal shields.

Common methods:

Creating energetic shields, placing protective objects, using protective symbols, invoking protective entities, layering multiple protection methods.

Reversal

What it is:

Sending magick back to its source. Reversing a hex, curse, or negative energy back to whoever sent it. Can also reverse your own magick if you change your mind.

When to use:

When you're under magickal attack and want to return it. When you suspect someone hexed you. When you cast something and regret it.

Common methods:

Reversing candles (black on outside, red on inside), mirror work, reversal oils, speaking incantations backward, turning photos or names upside down or backward.

Ritual (Default)

What it is:

The catch-all category for general spellwork that doesn't fit into more specific types. Includes spoken invocations, ceremonial workings, symbolic actions, multi-step procedures that combine multiple methods.

When to use:

When the working doesn't fit neatly into another category. When combining multiple magickal methods. When following traditional ceremonial structures.

Examples:

Circle casting, invocations to deities, full moon rituals, sabbat celebrations, initiations, multi-step ceremonial work.

Sigil

What it is:

Symbol-based magick using drawn, painted, carved, or inscribed marks. The sigil itself holds and focuses the intention. Can be activated through various methods: burning, carrying, burying, charging with energy, or visual meditation.

When to use:

When you want a condensed, abstract representation of your intent. When you need portable magick that can be hidden or destroyed easily. When working with entities that respond to symbolic language.

Examples:

Created sigils from statement of intent, traditional magickal symbols, runes arranged in specific patterns, geometric designs charged with purpose.

Souring

What it is:

Magick that turns someone's attitude or situation bitter. Makes relationships go bad, ruins someone's mood, causes discord. Often uses vinegar or lemon as sympathetic materials.

When to use:

Making someone unpleasant to be around, turning a relationship sour, causing plans to fall apart through discord.

Duration:

Temporary to medium-term.

Sweetening

What it is:

Using honey, sugar, or sweet substances to make someone sweet toward you. Can be done to improve relationships, soften attitudes, win favor, or calm conflict.

When to use:

Improving relationship with boss, softening someone's attitude, court cases where you need favor, family conflict resolution, customer service situations.

Common methods:

Honey jar with target's name and herbs, petition paper folded toward you and placed in honey, sugar bowl workings, speaking sweetly while stirring honey clockwise.

Warding

What it is:

Constructing magickal barriers around home, body, objects, or pets. Architectural form of magick, distinct subset of protection.

When to use:

Setting up new home protections, creating long-term barriers, protecting thresholds and boundaries, guarding specific rooms or areas.

Examples:

Threshold protections, door sigils, iron nails in corners, energetic wards, boundary lines, protective circles around property.

Common methods:

Physical barrier placement (salt lines, iron nails), energetic barrier construction, sigil placement at entry points, invoking guardian spirits, layering protections at boundaries.

Weather Magick

What it is:

Workings that call, change, or influence weather: rain, storms, wind, fog. Ancient category recognized across multiple magickal traditions globally.

When to use:

Calling rain for crops, dispersing storms, raising wind, calling fog for concealment, working with weather spirits.

Examples:

Storm jars, wind knot magick, rain petitions, weather working with entities.

Note:

Weather magick affects entire areas and other people. Consider ethics and consequences carefully.

Choosing the Right Type

What form should the magick take?

  • Need portability? Charm or pouch
  • Need containment? Jar
  • Need simplicity? Sigil or candle
  • Need to direct energy at specific person? Poppet
  • Need something consumable? Elixir, kitchen magick
  • Need ongoing altar work? Keep as ritual
  • Need to work without physical tools? Meditation, energy work

How long should it last?

  • Immediate, one-time effect: Ritual, sigil (destroyed), petition (burned)
  • Ongoing protection or work: Jar, charm, pouch, wards (kept)
  • Long-term with maintenance: Altar objects, rechargeable charms, wards

What's the intent?

Work with what's available. Most intentions can be achieved through multiple formats.

Final Notes

The type you choose matters less than your clarity of intent and commitment to the working. A simple candle ritual with focused will outperforms an elaborate jar with scattered energy.

When in doubt, start simple. You can always repeat or escalate if needed.

Ritual Disposal Guide

After ritual work is complete, you're left with physical remains: candle wax, herb bundles, petition papers, jar contents, worn-out tools. What you do with these materials matters both magickally and practically.

The Five Primary Methods

Bury

When to use:

Grounding energy, long-term workings, growth intentions, binding that needs to stay hidden, anything you want to take root or remain stable.

How:

Dig at least 6 inches deep on your property, at a crossroads, or in a natural area where you have permission. Biodegradable materials only. Mark the spot mentally if you need to retrieve it later.

Magickal reasoning:

Earth absorbs, grounds, and transforms. Burial keeps energy localized and stable. Use for protection anchored to a location, prosperity that needs to grow, or bindings you want hidden and immobilized.

Examples:

Protection jars for the home, prosperity pouches, grounding work, binding someone's harmful behavior.

Burn

When to use:

Release, transformation, banishing, sending intentions skyward, destroying connections, purification.

How:

Use a fireproof container or outdoor fire pit. Never burn plastics, synthetic fabrics, toxic plants, or anything that produces dangerous fumes. Let it burn completely. Dispose of cool ash by scattering, burying, or flushing.

Magickal reasoning:

Fire transforms matter into smoke and ash, releasing energy upward and outward. Use for letting go, severing ties, sending petitions to spirits or deities, or destroying what no longer serves.

Examples:

Cord-cutting remains, banishing work, petition papers to deities, releasing past relationships, cleansing materials.

Keep on Altar or Person

When to use:

Ongoing work, talismans, charms, objects that need regular charging, workings that require sustained energy.

How:

Store on your altar, in a dedicated drawer, or carry with you. Refresh or recharge periodically. Cleanse if energy feels stagnant.

Magickal reasoning:

Keeping materials maintains the energetic link. Use for protection you wear daily, ongoing prosperity work, relationship charms, or any working that needs continuous presence.

Examples:

Protection charms, love talismans, prosperity pouches carried in wallet, altar jars that remain active.

Crossroads Disposal

When to use:

Banishing, removing unwanted energy from your life, sending work away from you, offerings to crossroads spirits, disposing of particularly heavy or dark materials.

How:

Take materials to a physical crossroads (intersection of two roads or paths). Leave them without looking back. Do not return to that crossroads for several days. Some traditions require you to walk away in silence.

Magickal reasoning:

Crossroads are liminal spaces where energy disperses in multiple directions. Use for banishing illness, bad luck, unwanted attachments, or anything you need completely removed from your sphere.

Examples:

Banishing work, illness transfers, bad luck removal, offerings to Hekate or Legba, cleansing materials from heavy work.

Running Water

When to use:

Carrying intentions away, cleansing, releasing emotions, sending work downstream, dissolving connections.

How:

Use biodegradable materials only. Natural bodies of water preferred (river, stream, ocean). Toss materials into moving water, ideally flowing away from you. Do not use for toxic materials or anything harmful to ecosystems.

Magickal reasoning:

Water flows and carries energy away. Use for releasing grief, washing away negativity, sending intentions to water spirits, or cleansing after difficult work.

Examples:

Grief release rituals, cleansing after baneful work, offerings to water spirits, dissolving emotional ties.

Special Cases

Non-Biodegradable Materials

The problem:

Many ritual materials can't be buried or released into nature: glitter, synthetic fabrics, plastic, metal hardware, glass jars with non-removable labels, electronic components.

Solutions:

  • Disassemble first. Separate biodegradable from non-biodegradable. Bury the herbs, dispose of the jar in trash.
  • Cleanse and reuse. Wash glass jars, metal containers, synthetic fabric pouches. Cleanse with smoke, salt, or sound. Reuse for future work.
  • Trash disposal with intention. If it must go in the trash, acknowledge that the work is complete. Say a closing statement: "This work is done. The energy is released." Then dispose normally.
  • Recycle when possible. Glass, metal, and clean paper can be recycled. The transformation into new material serves as symbolic release.

Wax Remains

Free-standing candles:

If the candle burned completely, bury or dispose of small wax remnants. If significant wax remains, it may indicate blockage or resistance. Read the wax shape for divination if you practice that. Then dispose based on the working type.

Container candles:

Clean out wax with hot water or freezing method. Bury the wax or dispose in trash. Cleanse and reuse the container.

Wax with herbs or petition papers:

If you can separate them, do so. Burn the paper and herbs separately. Dispose of wax in trash or bury if small amounts.

Jars You Want to Keep Active

Ongoing protection, prosperity, or relationship jars:

Leave sealed on your altar or hide in a relevant location (protection jar near front door, prosperity jar near cash box, relationship jar in bedroom). Refresh periodically by shaking, anointing with oil, or placing a candle on top.

When to dispose:

If the jar breaks, the working feels complete, or the intention no longer applies. Disassemble contents and dispose using appropriate methods for each material.

Poppets and Dolls

After healing or positive work:

Thank the poppet. Disassemble it respectfully. Burn natural fabrics and stuffing. Bury biodegradable elements. Dispose of synthetic materials in trash.

After baneful or binding work:

The disposal method depends on intent. Bury to keep the person bound and hidden. Burn to destroy their influence over you. Crossroads to remove them from your life entirely. Some practitioners keep binding poppets sealed in a box to maintain the binding.

Offerings Left for Spirits

Food and drink:

Leave for a set period (overnight, three days, a week). Then return the offering to nature by burying, composting, or leaving in a wild area. Some traditions allow you to consume offerings after the spirit has taken the essence. Know your tradition's rules.

Non-food offerings:

Some stay on the altar permanently. Others are buried at sacred sites. Follow the guidance of the specific entity or tradition.

Toxic or Dangerous Materials

Plants:

If you used toxic plants (belladonna, datura, oleander, hemlock), do not burn them. Do not compost them. Wear gloves. Seal in a bag and dispose in trash, or bury deep where animals and children cannot access.

Bodily fluids:

Blood, sexual fluids, urine, or other biological materials should be buried, burned (if dried and safe), or flushed. Never leave in public spaces.

Broken glass or sharp objects:

Wrap securely before disposal. If burying, mark the location so no one gets hurt later.

Environmental Responsibility

Never dispose in nature:

  • Plastics, synthetics, glitter, or non-biodegradable materials
  • Toxic substances, chemicals, or treated materials
  • Glass or sharp objects in unmarked locations
  • Anything that harms water, soil, or wildlife

Biodegradable does not mean instant:

Even natural materials take time to decompose. Paper takes months. Fabric takes years. If burying on public land or in a natural area, use minimal amounts and choose a discreet location.

Salt warning:

Salt is used in many rituals but is not environmentally neutral. It can kill plants and leach into groundwater. Dispose of salt in trash or down the drain, not in soil or natural areas.

When the Ritual Specifies Disposal

Some rituals include disposal instructions as part of the working. Follow those instructions. The disposal method is part of the magick.

If no disposal method is specified, use the chart below.

Quick Reference Chart

Intent → Disposal Method

  • Growth, stability, long-term → Bury
  • Release, transformation, sending upward → Burn
  • Ongoing work, daily use → Keep
  • Banishing, removal, sending away → Crossroads
  • Cleansing, releasing emotions → Running water
  • Binding (keep effect active) → Bury or hide
  • Binding (end effect) → Burn
  • Protection for home → Bury on property or keep inside
  • Offerings to spirits → Follow tradition, then nature
  • Toxic materials → Sealed trash or deep burial

Closing the Work

Before disposal, acknowledge completion:

  • "This work is done."
  • "The energy is released."
  • "I thank the materials and release them."

Then dispose without doubt or second-guessing. The work is complete when you say it is.

  • Caring for Your Magick Tools
  • Cleansing Objects and Ritual Tools
