Everyday Magick

Celebrating the sacred in each moment.

The practice of witchcraft is intensely personal. It comes with traditions, paths, and practices, but the way these speak to each practitioner and the way they are or are not integrated into daily life is deeply individual, perhaps even unique.

If you choose to join a firm tradition or practice, you will be following their dictums. But otherwise, you can and should feel free to forge your own path, integrating selected tools and practices into your own life rather than changing your ways to fit someone else's idea of "correct" practice. You can work with what speaks to you and set the silent bits aside. You can shape your own daily life into intentional, sacred space.

Where to Start

Begin by thinking about who you are and what aspects of the craft seem most meaningful to you. If you are new to witchcraft, what drew you to it? What jumped out and made noise to get your attention?

  • Are you fascinated by the ideas and intricacies of spellwork?
  • Is your heart in the kitchen, working magick with a tea kettle and wooden spoon?
  • Do you feel a strong magickal connection when you work in your garden or walk through the woods?
  • Are you drawn to creating a home space filled with magickal, liminal spaces?
  • Have you always had a knack for divination or prescience?

That which calls you to a certain path or place is where you should set your work in motion.

Three Rules for Everyday Practice

1. Keep It Simple

If you can find a tool in something you already own and something important to you, or if you can make your own, why spend money on a tool created elsewhere?

2. Be Aware of Need vs. Want

There is really very little we need to practice magick, and there is no need to crowd our practices with dozens of items we will never use. Ideally, every tool or item you acquire should have meaning and purpose.

3. Make It Fun (Or Meaningful)

If you are dealing with a challenging practice that really is not fun, at least make it meaningful. Do not do magick because of someone else's expectation or because the calendar says it is time. Do it because it means something to you. Do it because it enriches your magickal life.

Tools and Items to Begin With

Candles

Candles are a good place to start, as they are aesthetically pleasing and have multiple purposes. Use them in spellwork aligned with color and scent correspondences, gaze into the flame as a scrying tool, or simply allow a flickering candle to provide ambience.

You do not need fancy candles that cost thirty dollars each. A tealight might serve the purpose. Or make your own candles and carve runes, moon phases, or whatever speaks to you into each one, filling in the carvings with permanent marker.

Want to go rogue? Try LED candles. Who says witches cannot move into the modern age?

Wands

A wand's purpose is to direct energy, but you can do this equally well with your own arm, hand, and fingers. If you really want a wand, you could make your own by peeling bark off a branch, sanding it, and rubbing it with beeswax.

Or be creative:

  • A kitchen witch could use a wooden spoon as a wand, using a wood burner to engrave inscriptions
  • A witch who loves to write might use a prized pencil as a wand
  • A green witch might call upon a garden tool, like a dibbler

Athame

The athame (AH-thuh-may) is a small or medium-sized knife used to direct energy, create or manipulate ritual space, or for other purposes. An athame need not be fancy and can simply be a knife that you already know and love.

Herbalist Supplies

Think practical. Mason jars are great for herbal works, and a small, sharp knife for collecting herbs is as effective as a boline (the traditional sickle-shaped cutting tool).

Robes and Garb

If they speak to you and are appropriate, go for it. But are they necessary? Not unless a group requires them. Many practitioners prefer to work in everyday clothing, as it best represents their magickal selves.

An inexpensive option is to create a shawl from a piece of decorative fabric. Drawn around your shoulders or draped over your head while working, the shawl creates a feeling of magickal space.

Where Do I Practice?

Choose a location that aligns with your practices, one that means something and feels natural to you. This might be your kitchen, your backyard, the local woods, your altar space, or someplace else. Make your practice space intentional, not incidental.

Altars

Most witches invariably end up with one or more altar spaces. Depending on your focus, yours might be quite formal, complete with altar cloth, deity figures, candles, stones, and any number of magickal correspondences.

But an altar can also be informal: a corner of a bookshelf, space on a side table, or even a quiet spot in the garden. One or two items, placed intentionally in a significant location, become an altar.

Once it has been created, use your altar regularly, whether for spellwork and ritual or simply for contemplation, meditation, or a moment of quiet.

When Do I Practice?

Here is where the everyday witch is someone different. Rather than basing practice on the occasional ritual or holy day and otherwise remaining magickally inactive, everyday witchcraft sees every day as sacred in its own way and full of magickal potential, centering spiritual practice in a simple, grounded approach that embraces the magick in each moment.

Ideas for Celebrating the Sacred in the Everyday

  • Upon waking: Pause, take three deep breaths, and speak aloud words of gratitude
  • Morning greeting: Spend five minutes outdoors with a cup of coffee or tea, welcoming the new day and feeling its fresh magick
  • Morning cuppa: Make the brewing of your morning beverage into a simple ritual
  • Bathing: Dip under the water three times and imagine negative energy being washed away
  • Before eating: Wash your hands and face, then offer thanks for the gift of food
  • Seasons: Follow the seasons, tracking the equinoxes and solstices
  • Cooking: Stir deosil (clockwise/sunwise), in the direction of the sun, and envision the substance gathering vitality
  • Working magick: Prepare by washing hands and face and, if appropriate, donning fresh clothing. Make your magickal actions special and unique to you. Take your time.
  • Before bed: Reflect on the day and offer gratitude
  • Prayer: Offer prayers to your favorite deity, the universe, or whatever appeals. Pray or petition for help, understanding, or answers, or pray to offer thanks. Yes, witches can pray.
In creating your own witchery, make it thoughtful, make it meaningful, make it a regular part of your everyday life, and make it yours.

Candle Magick

Candle magick is one of the most accessible and versatile forms of spellwork. A single candle, chosen with intention, can serve as the entire foundation of a working. This guide covers the key decisions involved in planning a candle spell: selecting the right candle type and shape, dressing it with oil, inscribing planetary symbols, timing your burn to the correct planetary hour, and aligning with the appropriate moon phase.

Choosing a Candle Type

Different types of candles serve different purposes. The shape, size, and style of your candle should match the kind of work you are doing.

Spell Work

Votive Candle or Pillar Candle candles are the standard choice for most spellwork. They burn steadily and can be carved, dressed, and charged with intention.

Ritual

Taper Candle candles are traditional for formal ritual use. Their tall, elegant shape makes them ideal for altar work, invocations, and ceremonial settings.

Meditation and Divination

Votive Candle, Pillar Candle, or Taper Candle candles all work well for meditation and divination. Choose whichever feels most comfortable for the length of your session.

General Aura and Atmosphere

For setting the mood or creating ambient energy in a space, use a Votive Candle, Pillar Candle, or Glass Container Candle candle. Glass jars are especially practical for long, unattended burns.

Specified Spell Work

Some spells call for candles shaped to match the target or intention of the working. Options include Votive Candle, Pillar Candle, Figure Candle (man or woman), animal shapes (Cat Candle, Owl Candle, Dragon Candle, Snake Candle), and Skull Candle candles for workings focused on the mind.

Multi-Day Spells (5 to 7 Days)

For spells that unfold over several days, use a Knobby Candle candle, a tall Pillar Candle, or a Glass Container Candle candle. Burn one portion (one knob, or a measured section) each day until the spell is complete.

Dressing the Candle

Before burning, dress (anoint) your candle with a magickal oil that matches your intention. Refer to the Oil Grimoire for oils organized by correspondence. Apply the oil by rubbing it onto the candle from the center outward toward both ends, or from base to tip for drawing energy in, or tip to base for sending energy out.

Inscribing Planetary Symbols

Carve one or more planetary symbols into the candle wax to align your spell with planetary influence. You may use any combination that supports your goal.

Timing by Planetary Hour

Burn your candle for one hour during the planetary hour that matches your intention. Each day and night is divided into twelve planetary hours, and each hour is ruled by a different planet depending on the day of the week. Consult the Hours Correspondences by Day of the Week in the Timing Grimoire to find the right hour for your working.

Moon Phase Alignment

Align your candle spell with the correct moon phase to strengthen the working.

  • Waxing Crescent Moon/Waxing Gibbous Moon: For spells of increase, growth, attraction, and building. Use when drawing something toward you.
  • Full Moon: Peak power. Ideal for manifestation, divination, charging, and any working that needs maximum energy.
  • Waning Gibbous Moon/Waning Crescent Moon: For spells of decrease, release, banishing, and letting go. Use when sending something away.
  • Dark Moon or New Moon: For deep shadow work, binding, cursing, endings, and workings that require stillness or secrecy.

For specific moon phase dates and additional lunar timing, see the Timing Grimoire.

Candle Techniques

A symbol may be inscribed near the top of a candle so that as the symbol melts, the magick is released. A pin may be used to designate an accomplishment point: stick a pin into the candle near the top, stating that when the candle melts to that point the spell is sent into action, then chant, shake a rattle, meditate, or do whatever feels right while the candle burns down to the pin.

A goal may be written down and burned in the candle flame during spell casting, seeing the spell as sent on its way. Herbs may also be burned in the candle flame, stating the herb and its purpose while seeing the energy released to perform the task assigned.

Lychnomancy: Divination by Candle

Any candle lit for any purpose can simultaneously serve as a divination tool. Lychnomancy focuses on candle flames as the primary source of oracular information, but the wax, shadows, smoke, and ashes that a candle produces all carry interpretive value as well. Flame, wax, and smoke can each be read independently or coordinated together for a more layered reading. Those new to candle divination may find it easier to focus on one source at a time before working with all three.

Reading Candle Signs

Altar candles dedicated to a deity can serve as a direct oracular channel. The flame, wax, and smoke each carry interpretive meaning when working with an invoked spirit.

  • Flame shooting high and bright: The spirit you have invoked has arrived and is present.
  • Steady, calm flame: The working is proceeding without interference.
  • Flame guttering or going out: Resistance, interference, or the spirit's absence.
  • Smoke patterns: Observe the direction and shape of the smoke as it rises for additional signs.
  • Wax formations: As the wax melts and pools, shapes and patterns may form that carry oracular significance.

Working with Photos

A photo may be used in spellwork, but exercise great care so as not to violate the Rules of Conduct. It is wrong to try to force someone into an unwanted action. Photos may be used in healings and similar workings, and may be burned, torn, wrapped, or buried as the spell requires.

Pouches

Items may be combined into pouches to place somewhere or carry as ongoing spell vessels.

Putting It All Together

A complete candle magick working follows this sequence:

  1. Set your intention clearly.
  2. Choose a candle color that matches your goal (see the Material Grimoire for candle color entries).
  3. Select a candle shape that fits the type of working.
  4. Dress the candle with a corresponding oil.
  5. Inscribe planetary symbols that align with your intention.
  6. Burn for one hour during the appropriate planetary hour.
  7. Perform the working during the correct moon phase.

You may also use multiple candles of different colors, or candles with multiple colors, to layer intentions within a single working.

Each candle color carries specific applications in baneful and destructive magick. Black should be present alongside any other color used in these workings, as it is the all-purpose foundation for dark spellcraft. Magick in Your Darkest Hour

A guide to using magick during major life crises, when darkness grows slowly and you feel lost, without direction or purpose.

The Core Principle

Magick is not only for minor issues. It is here, it is now, it is powerful. It is here to be used in your darkest hour, even when your sky is so dark that there is no moonlight, not even a glimmer of the faintest star.

Yet many practitioners, when faced with a major crisis, forget to draw on their magickal beliefs. This guide is a reminder: your magick, your affirmations, and your prayers will help you in your darkest hour.

Professional Help First

⚠️
For magick and spirituality to work properly, you must first seek out and receive the proper professional help you need.

First get medical treatment, legal counsel, financial advice, or whatever help your situation requires. Then begin your magickal and spiritual healing work.

This approach lets you project your magickal power to enhance the situation. For example, during a health crisis, each ritual can ask the Divine to guide your doctor's healing hands. Request that treatments work effectively. Let your magick enhance and empower the forces already helping you in the physical realm.

Focus, Ground, Center

Do not start your magickal work right away. First, decide what needs to be done. This is especially important if you face more than one dark situation.

Prioritize your focus:

  • Health crisis: Focus first on the most urgent medical need
  • Legal troubles: Focus first on finding knowledgeable counsel
  • Grief: Focus first on drawing a caring therapist into your life, along with healing energies
  • Financial crisis: Focus first on finding qualified financial advice

Everyone's situation is different. There is no wrong or right way to approach magick for crisis situations. But you need to stay focused and grounded.

Keep It Simple

For crisis magick, simplicity is power.

Repeat often. Daily ritual is more effective than elaborate monthly ceremonies during a crisis. The consistent repetition builds momentum and keeps your intention focused.

Minimize setup. You do not need an elaborate altar or exotic ingredients. A spare room with morning light streaming through windows is enough. Use a few favorite ritual items if you wish, but avoid anything too time-consuming to set up or take down.

Why simplicity matters: When you are in crisis, your energy and focus are already strained. A simple ritual you can actually perform daily serves you better than an elaborate one you cannot sustain.

Structure for Crisis Ritual

1. Announce Your Intent

Decide if you wish to call upon a favorite deity, or simply direct your magick to the Divine, Spirit, or the Universe. Call upon positive energy to surround you.

2. Speak Your Words of Power

Write them down and read them aloud. After a while, you will be able to repeat them from memory. Make your request simple and to the point.

3. Expand Your Blessings

Ask the Divine to bless the people who have helped you through the ordeal: those who have given transportation, offered support, or assisted in any way.

4. Acknowledge Lessons

Tell the Divine what you have learned from this experience and that you are ready to be healed or helped.

5. Close with Gratitude

End by thanking any deity or spiritual energies you have called upon. Release any protective energies. The ritual is over.

Example: A Daily Healing Ritual

Performed every morning in a quiet room with natural light:

  1. Stand before the windows
  2. Announce to the Divine that you are about to send out a healing affirmation
  3. State your intent clearly (request that treatments work, that healing come)
  4. Ask the Divine to bless those who have helped you
  5. Acknowledge that you have learned from the experience and are ready to be healed
  6. Close the ritual

This takes only a few minutes but, performed daily, creates a sustained current of intention.

Flashes of Light in Darkness

Even in your darkest hour, dim flashes of light begin to appear. A neighbor who happens to know the way to the clinic. A helpful stranger. An unexpected resource. Watch for these signs. They are confirmations that your magick is working, that the universe responds.

Science and medicine do their work. But faith in your magick puts you on the right path to find that healing.

Ritual Grimoire

Magick for Low/No Vision

A guide to adapting magickal practice for practitioners who are blind, have low vision, or wish to explore non-visual approaches to ritual work.

Beyond the Visual

Much of modern magickal writing assumes practitioners can see. Candles are lit and the flame watched. Grimoires are read. Energy is visualized as light. But magick existed long before written language, and its power has never depended on sight.

For practitioners with low or no vision, or for anyone seeking deeper sensory engagement, every other sense offers equally valid pathways to power.

Hearing

Elemental Association: Air

Sound carries intention with remarkable precision. Consider:

  • Spoken incantations and chants
  • Singing bowls and bells for cleansing
  • Drumming for trance work
  • Recorded guided meditations
  • The crackle of fire, the rush of water, the whisper of wind
  • Verbal cues from ritual partners

Many traditions consider the spoken word more powerful than the written one. Your voice is a tool that requires no adaptation.

Touch

Elemental Association: Earth

The hands know what the eyes cannot. Consider:

  • Textured altar cloths to mark sacred space
  • Carved or raised symbols on tools
  • Braille labels for jars and bottles
  • Knotted cords for counting repetitions
  • Clay or wax for shaping intention
  • Temperature differences between elements
  • The weight and shape of stones and crystals

Runework adapts beautifully to touch. Carve runes deeply into wood or trace them in sand.

Smell

Elemental Association: Fire

Scent bypasses conscious thought and speaks directly to memory and emotion. Consider:

  • Incense for marking ritual phases
  • Essential oils for anointing
  • Fresh herbs crushed between fingers
  • Smoke cleansing
  • Seasonal scents to mark the Wheel of the Year

Build a personal scent vocabulary where specific smells signal specific intentions or deities.

Taste

Elemental Association: Water

Often overlooked even by sighted practitioners. Consider:

  • Cakes and ale rituals
  • Herbal teas aligned with intention
  • Honey for sweetening spells
  • Salt for protection and purification
  • Seasonal foods for sabbat celebrations

Adapting Common Practices

Candle Magick: Focus on the warmth radiating from the flame, the scent of the wax, the sound of the match striking. Carve symbols you can feel.

Visualization: Reframe as "sensing" or "knowing." Feel energy as temperature, pressure, or texture rather than color or light.

Divination: Tactile systems work beautifully. Runes carved in wood or clay. Ogham staves. Pendulums with textured chains. Even tarot with braille overlays or audio descriptions.

Circle Casting: Walk the boundary. Feel the shift in energy. Use scent markers at the quarters or textured items to mark directions.

Teaching Without Visual Language

If you teach or write about magick, examine your assumptions:

  • Replace "visualize" with "sense," "feel," or "imagine"
  • Describe energy in terms of temperature, weight, or texture
  • Offer audio alternatives to written materials
  • Include tactile components in group rituals
  • Ask practitioners what works for them

The Gift of Limitation

Every sense you cannot use sharpens the ones you can. Practitioners who work without sight often develop extraordinary sensitivity to energy, presence, and subtle shifts that sighted practitioners miss entirely.

There is no "correct" way to perceive magick. There is only your way.

Crafting Incantations

Why Incantations Work

A charm or incantation is what ties your will, faith, and imagination into a single, focused release. Spoken words give a working its shape and its trigger point.

Borrow Freely

Witches have always borrowed style and substance from wherever it resonates — folklore, religion, myth, herbal lore, whatever else carries emotional weight. Mixing traditions freely is normal practice; what matters is how strongly an image or phrase stirs your own deep mind, not where it originally came from.

Using Names and Words of Power

Names of deities, Cabalistic words, and other "words of power" work through the emotional charge they carry, not through doctrinal correctness. A name may carry slightly more force if you have some genuine connection to the tradition it comes from, but that's not a requirement — any name, sacred or entirely secular (a loved one, a public figure, even someone you strongly dislike), can work if it reliably provokes a strong reaction in you.

Rhyme and Rhythm

A beat helps. Many practitioners favor rhyming couplets because they're simple to construct and easy to repeat. The repetition and rhythm are what reach the deep mind — the polish of the verse matters far less than its pulse. Traditional charms that already carry an accumulated charge from repeated use are worth using as-is, but devising your own is the norm, and often more effective, since the incantation can be built entirely around what moves you personally.

What to Avoid

Lengthy, preachy invocations bogged down in dense theological language tend to lull the mind rather than awaken it. Favor short, rhythmic, emotionally direct language over exhaustive or ornate phrasing.

Manner of Dress

The Debate

Witches disagree over whether ritual work is best done nude or robed, and both camps consider their approach traditional.

The Case for Nudity

The usual argument is that clothing blocks the flow of witch power. That explanation doesn't hold up well, since power passes through walls and travels across distance without trouble, so a layer of fabric shouldn't stop it either. The real reason nudity helps is psychological: it supports release from tension, everyday concerns, and inhibition. If going without clothes puts you in the right headspace, that's reason enough to do it; just make sure you have privacy.

The Tabard Alternative

For colder climates or less enthusiastic practitioners, the tabard is the standard alternative: a long piece of heavy black fabric folded in half, with a head-hole cut poncho-style and the sides sewn up partway to leave arm openings, hanging to the ankles and belted with the Girdle Cord.

Many witches prefer more elaborate robes in colors like blue, violet, red, green, or white, sometimes with a hood or cowl for added anonymity during ritual. Sandals or bare feet are both acceptable.

Coven Uniformity

Covens often benefit from a shared dress code: many members keep one uniform robe for Sabbats and Esbats and a separate, more personal one for solo work. A witch name or personal signs can be embroidered on the hem or breast, though this is optional.

A Prop, Not a Requirement

Ultimately, the tabard (or nudity) works as a psychological aid rather than a magical necessity. Ordinary clothing serves fine for ritual as long as it doesn't pull your mind back to mundane concerns.

Circle

Circle Casting Notes

  1. Outdoor Adaptations — If outdoors, substitute "walls and floors" with "foliage, stones, and ground" or other appropriate description of the surroundings. Change "I" to "we" when others are participating. Use appropriate Altar and Circle decorations for the season: flowers, leaves, shells, stones, crystals, cord, or meaningful objects. Names for the Goddess and the God may be used with or instead of Lady and Lord.
  2. Anointing Sigils — The sigil used for anointing may be a Pentagram, Triple Moon, Solar Cross, Lunar Spiral, Solar Cross with Lunar Spiral over it, etc. as desired. Anointing may be added if desired when not part of the described Circle casting.
  3. Names in Ritual — Use Craft Name in rituals with others, or Secret/Working Name if alone.
  4. Directional Movement — Deosil (clockwise) is N-E-S-W-N and Widdershins (counterclockwise) is N-W-S-E-N unless otherwise noted, as when starting at the West or East, but the pattern follows the same from these starting points.
  5. Libation Disposal — If rinsing out libation bowl in sink, envision this as a journey to Earth waters.
  6. Circle Markers — The Circle area may be marked by a cord, by Elemental candles (votives in safe containers are easiest), by items relating to the ritual the Circle is being cast for, or by nothing at all save awareness of where it is from the energy sent to form it.
  7. Ritual Structure — Cast the Circle, insert rituals, spells, recitations, etc., where designated, then return to the Circle page for the Cakes & Wine and Circle Opening.
  8. Preparation — Decide in advance what will be done in Circle; place ribbons or paper slips in your Book of Shadows so each page used for the entire ritual can be easily turned to. A book holder or book stand makes it easier to turn to the desired pages. Do not feel rushed, but make the experience a meaningful one.
  9. Music — Music may accompany the Circle casting/opening and rituals; song, musical performance, and drumming may be added where it feels appropriate.

Another Method:
Preparation

Before casting your circle, gather everything you'll need for the ritual or spell you plan to perform. Once inside the circle, you won't want to break its boundary to retrieve forgotten items. Double-check your materials, tools, and any written words you might need.

Creating the Proper Ambiance

The atmosphere of your workspace affects the quality of your magick:

  • Lighting - Candles create ideal lighting, though a dimmer switch works if open flames aren't practical
  • Temperature - Keep the space comfortable, especially if skyclad (ritual nudity) is part of your practice
  • Sound - Silence electronics and minimize disruptions; soft instrumental music can enhance focus
  • Scent - Incense or essential oils can shift consciousness and support your intention
  • Privacy - Ensure you won't be interrupted; inform housemates or lock doors as needed

Your Magickal Workspace

You don't need a dedicated temple room. Any space can become sacred when properly prepared. Clear physical and energetic clutter, and arrange your altar or working surface to suit your needs. Some practitioners work indoors, others prefer the outdoors - what matters is your ability to focus.

The Four Elements Technique

Start facing East and place a feather, incense, or other air symbol on the floor around your workspace.

Use candles or another symbol to represent fire and place it on the floor at the South point.

Next, face West and use a glass of water on the floor.

Finally, turn to face North and place a cup of soil or another item to represent earth to complete the circle.

Face north and visualize an energetic white light coming up from the ground into your feet and entering your body.

You can use these words at the end: "The elements of Air, Fire, Water and Earth come together. I cast this circle of Protection and Power above, below, and within."

Basic Circle Casting & Opening

This is a complete step-by-step procedure for formal circle work.

Casting the Circle

1. Setup — Lay out Circle and at North set Altar items (may use fruit juice, water, or tea instead of wine). Ground and center.

2. Sweeping — Sweep the Circle area with a besom deosil (clockwise) NORTH, EAST, SOUTH, WEST, and return to Altar:

"As I sweep, may the Besom chase away all negativity from within this Circle that it may be cleared and ready for my work."

3. Lighting — Light incense and Altar candles (in selected colors); ring bell or clap hands 3 times:

"The Circle is about to be cast and I freely stand within to greet my Lady and my Lord."

4. Calling Light — Take center Altar candle deosil around the Circle, raising at each Quarter (and lighting Elemental candles if used), returning to Altar when done:

  • [N]: "I call upon Light and Earth at the North to illuminate and strengthen the Circle."
  • [E]: "I call upon Light and Air at the East to illuminate and enliven the Circle."
  • [S]: "I call upon Light and Fire at the South to illuminate and warm the Circle."
  • [W]: "I call upon Light and Water at the West to illuminate and cleanse the Circle."

5. Drawing the Circle — Raise athame in power hand in front of the Altar:

"I draw this Circle in the Presence of the Lady and the Lord that They may aid and bless me in my work."

6. Casting the Boundary — Lower athame at North; walk deosil around the Circle, envisioning a blue light shooting out from the point to form the Circle boundary:

"This is the boundary of the Circle, around me, through walls and floors, above me and below me as a sphere is the Circle cast and consecrated to the Lady and the Lord that They may work with and through Their child, [name]. This Circle is charged by the powers of the Ancient Ones! Only love shall enter and leave."

7. Blessing the Salt — Return to Altar; ring bell (or clap hands 3 times); touch point of athame in the salt:

"Salt is life and purifying. I bless this salt to be used in this sacred Circle by the Power of the Goddess and the God."

8. Creating Holy Water — Using tip of athame, drop 3 portions of salt into water; stir 3 times with blade:

"Let the blessed salt purify this water that it may be blessed to use in this sacred Circle. Through the Power of the Goddess and the God is this water cleansed."

9. Consecrating the Circle — Sprinkle blessed water deosil around the Circle:

"I consecrate this Circle by the Lady and the Lord. This Circle is conjured a Circle of Power that is purified and sealed. So Mote It Be!"

10. Censing — Put water bowl on Altar; take incense deosil around Circle to cense it:

"With the aroma of incense do I honor and make welcome my visitors and helpers, visible and invisible."

11. Self-Anointing — Dab anointing oil with fingertip on forehead in a sigil:

"I, [name], am consecrated in the Names of the Goddess and the God, in this Their Circle."

Admitting Others to the Circle

Cut doorway in circle for others to enter; close and seal with sigil. Challenge each as they approach the Circle, then anoint with oil and sigil of choice:

  • a. "What do you want?" — Answer: "To enter the Circle."
  • b. "What is the password?" — Answer: "In Perfect Love and Perfect Trust."
  • c. "Enter and Merry Meet! I bid you welcome."

12. Invoking the Elementals — With wand, invoke the Elementals at each Quarter starting at the North and moving deosil; raise and open arms to invoke, then close and lower arms, turning to the next Quarter until all are called:

  • [N]: "I call upon you, Elemental Earth, to attend this rite and guard this Circle, for as I have body and strength, we are kith and kin!" [visualize a powerful bull arriving]
  • [E]: "I call upon you, Elemental Air, to attend this rite and guard this Circle, for as I breathe and think, we are kith and kin!" [visualize a soaring eagle]
  • [S]: "I call upon you, Elemental Fire, to attend this rite and guard this Circle, for as I have energy and drive, and consume life to live, we are kith and kin!" [visualize a mighty lion]
  • [W]: "I call upon you, Elemental Water, to attend this rite and guard this Circle, for as I have emotions and my heart beats, we are kith and kin!" [visualize a leaping dolphin]

13. Cosmic Lemniscate — Draw Cosmic Lemniscate (∞) with wand over Altar.

14. Hailing the Powers — Set wand on Altar; raise athame in both hands straight overhead:

"Hail to the Elementals at the Four Quarters! Welcome Lady and Lord to this Circle! I stand between the worlds with Love and Power all around!"

15. Libation — Set down athame; pick up cup; pour some beverage into libation bowl, cauldron, or the ground to honor the Lady and the Lord, then take a sip; ring bell or clap 3 times.

At this point, proceed with your planned ritual work. When complete, return to the Circle Opening section below.

The Cord and Athame Method

A traditional way to lay out the triple circle using the consecrated cord and Athame together.

Preparation

Clear a space large enough for a nine-foot-diameter circle (eleven feet for coven work). Pin one end of the cord to roughly the center of the room, using a heavy object such as a chair or table leg, or have someone hold it in place if others are present.

Tracing the Circles

Stretch the cord out tightly and wrap it around the Athame's handle at the knot four feet six inches from the pinned end. Using the chair or anchor point as a pivot, trace a nine-foot-diameter circle lightly on the floor with the knife's point, keeping the cord taut throughout.

Move deosil (clockwise), starting and ending in the east; a small pocket compass can help you keep your bearings. As you trace, visualize blue witch fire streaming from the Athame's blade like a torch, leaving a line of flickering violet flame in its wake.

Shorten the cord to the next knot (four feet from the pinned end) and repeat the tracing to draw an eight-foot circle, then shorten it once more to the knot at three feet six inches for a seven-foot inner circle.

Purifying the Circle

Exorcise the ground within the finished triple circle by sprinkling it with charged water and censing it with charged incense at each of the four quarters, east, south, west, and north, moving deosil throughout. Once this is done, the circle is ritually purified and ready to focus the power raised within it.

Leaving the Circle

Sometimes you must leave a cast circle - perhaps you forgot an item or need to use the bathroom. Rather than breaking the entire circle, you can cut a temporary doorway:

  1. Using your athame, wand, or finger, trace a doorway shape in the circle's boundary
  2. Visualize the energy parting like a curtain
  3. Step through and complete your task quickly
  4. When returning, step back through the same spot
  5. Reseal the doorway by retracing it in reverse, visualizing the energy knitting back together

Try to minimize exits, as each opening temporarily weakens the circle's protective barrier.

Dismantling the Circle

When your work is complete, release the circle with respect. Move counterclockwise (widdershins), reversing the order in which you called the elements:

  1. Begin in the North - thank the element of Earth and bid it farewell
  2. Move to the West - thank Water and release it
  3. Continue to the South - thank Fire
  4. End in the East - thank Air

Visualize the circle's energy dissolving back into the ground or returning to the cosmos. Some practitioners say something like: "The circle is open but never broken. Merry meet, merry part, and merry meet again."

Ground yourself afterward by eating something, touching the earth, or simply sitting quietly for a moment.

Rune Grimoire

What is a Rune?

The word rune does not simply mean "letter." Across every ancient Germanic dialect, the term carries a primary meaning of "secret," "mystery," or sacred hidden knowledge. This concept parallels the use of arcana in the Tarot: each rune is first and foremost a holy idea that must be approached with reverence and worked with in concealment.

The modern reduction of runes to mere alphabetic characters strips away this foundational meaning. Understanding that a rune is a mysterium, not a letter, is the first step in genuine runic practice.

Etymology Across the Germanic Languages

The word rune is native to the Germanic language family and appears in every major ancient dialect:

DialectWordMeaning
Old NorserúnSecret, secret lore, wisdom, magickal signs, written characters
GothicrúnaSecret, mysterium (used by Wulfilas in his fourth-century Bible translation to render the Greek mysterion)
Old EnglishrúnMystery, secret council
Old SaxonrúnaMystery, secret
Old High GermanrúnaMystery, secret

The modern German cognate raunen means "to whisper." The word also appears in Old Irish (rún) and Middle Welsh (rhin), both carrying the same meaning of mysterium, likely borrowed from Germanic languages. The deepest root traces back to Proto-Indo-European \reu-*, meaning "to roar."

Letter Runes and Glyph Runes

Not all runes were used for writing. The runic tradition contains two distinct categories:

Letter runes received phonetic values and were organized into the Futhark system by the magickal guilds of the time. Their standardization followed specific numerological and conceptual criteria, not arbitrary convention.

Glyph runes remained in the purely ideographic realm. They carried meaning through symbol rather than sound, functioning as visual containers for magickal concepts.

Both categories are equally runic. The letter runes simply gained an additional function (phonetic representation) on top of their original ideographic and magickal nature. The symbol came first. The phonetic value came later. The sound never replaced the secret.

The Vitki

A vitki is a rune magickian. Where scholars see ancient writing symbols that bore religious or magickal significance, the vitki sees something deeper: complex hieroglyphs that encode processes of force and energy. Through investigation of both intellectual and magickal realms, the vitki recognizes runes as ideographs expressing the flow and state of power across self, planet, and multiverse.

The Threefold Nature of Runes

Every rune holds a threefold essence. These three aspects together constitute the full secret contained within each symbol:

  1. Form. The visual ideograph and its associated phonetic value. This is the rune as it appears when carved, drawn, or inscribed.
  2. Idea. The symbolic content the form represents. Each rune encodes a distinct world-concept, a specific pattern of meaning that exists independent of its physical shape.
  3. Number. The rune's position and dynamic relationship to other runes. This reveals how each rune interacts with and relates to the rest of the system.

Runes describe energy flows and states at every scale, from the personal to the planetary to the cosmic. Each one summarizes and graphically expresses a separate world-concept that can serve as a focal point for magickal and mystical operations, both individually and in combination.

The Origin of the Runic Forms

The mysteries encoded in the runes are timeless. They came into being alongside the emergence of the Nine Worlds from Ginnungagap, the magickally charged void. The runes are not products of creation but agents within it, preceding the arising of animate beings across the Worlds.

The physical shapes of the runes, however, can be placed in historical context. These forms originate from holy signs conceived by Bronze Age priests and magickians, and likely much earlier. They are abstract graphic expressions of the innermost content of religious and magickal teachings, found in abundance among the oldest rock carvings of Scandinavia. In this earliest period, these pre-runic signs functioned as pure ideographs, carrying meaning without representing sound.

From Ideograph to Phonetic Symbol

When Germanic peoples came into contact with Mediterranean cultures, the concept of representing language phonetically through symbols gradually entered the northern territories. Some scholars place this introduction in the second century BCE, when the Cimbri and Teutones invaded the Italian peninsula and encountered the North Etruscan and Latin alphabets. Others argue the runes were formulated by the Goths in the first and second centuries CE while they inhabited the Baltic coast.

When the Germanic peoples selected a cultic sign to represent a phonetic sound, they typically chose a shape that resembled the corresponding Etruscan, Latin, or Greek character. This resemblance played a significant role in the development of galdrar (number formulas) and their associations with specific runic forms.

Critically, the internal structure, ordering, naming, and symbolic content of the runes remain entirely unaffected by Mediterranean influence. A magickal deep-structure governs these elements. The priests and magickians of the Germanic cult knew this deep-structure intimately and transmitted the runic ideology across tribal boundaries through preexisting cultic channels. This ancient guild of runemasters maintained the system's internal integrity across countless tribal lines over several centuries. By the first century CE, Tacitus was already describing runes (which he called notae in Latin) being used in fully developed divinatory rites.

Odin and the Runic Initiation

Mythically, it is through Odin, the God of Magick, that gods and mortals receive rune wisdom. Odin was the first being to undergo full initiation into the runic mysteries, extracting the wisdom directly from its source and formulating it within his being so that it could be communicated to others. It is through the Odhinic force that the runes may be perceived most clearly.

This initiatory myth appears in the Elder (Poetic) Edda, in the song called the Hávamál ("the Sayings of the High One"). Stanzas 138 and 139 describe the ordeal:

I know, that I hung
on the windy tree
all of the nights nine,
wounded by spear
and given to Odin,
myself to myself,
on that tree,
which no man knows,
from what roots it rises.

They dealt me no bread
nor drinking horn,
I looked down,
I took up the runes,
I took them screaming,
I fell back from there.

This passage describes an initiatory process in which the initiate passes through the Nine Worlds of the World-Tree, descending to the realm of Hel (Death) and momentarily entering her sphere. In that instant, the entire body of rune wisdom is received and etched permanently into the initiate's being. The initiate then returns to Midgard with the knowledge encoded and ready for use and communication.

A Note on the Tarot and Runes

Some investigators have proposed that the runes are the origin of the Tarot's Major Arcana. Whether or not this is true, there may have been a point at which the two systems came into contact. The runes possess a documented past that reaches much further back than any existing documentation for the Tarot. Correspondences between the two systems do reveal interesting parallels, and each vitki is invited to explore these connections and draw their own conclusions.

Rune Grimoire

A Brief History of Runology

Runology, the systematic study of runes, originated with Johannes Bureus (1568-1652). As a member of the Swedish court, Bureus first proposed that runes served as vessels for ancient wisdom beyond their standard alphabetic function. Despite his Christian faith, he maintained that runes possessed mystical properties. While modern scholars often reject these esoteric associations, excluding them ignores a fundamental component of runic history.

Runic writing and speech declined by the late Middle Ages, yet the symbols retained their significance. By the mid-nineteenth century, runology emerged as a formal academic field. This multidisciplinary study incorporates linguistics, archaeology, anthropology, and philology to analyze runes as symbols, sounds, objects, and oracles.

Stages of Runic Development

The runic system may have been fully developed as early as 200 BCE. The magickal and religious practices of the ancient Germanic priesthood relied on many runic and pre-runic signs, still visible etched into stone across Scandinavia.

Rune development moved through three overlapping stages, all of which remain valid for modern practice:

  1. Ideographic. The earliest period, and the cradle of rune magick. Individual ideographs appeared in isolation, each one a self-contained symbol of sacred meaning.
  2. Sound-formulaic (galdrar). Magickal sound and number formulas began to be produced, combining runes into sequences intended to generate specific magickal effects.
  3. Phonetic. Runes were adapted to represent the common Germanic dialect in writing. This phonetic function arrived last, layered on top of the existing magickal system.

All three modes continued in use simultaneously. The runes were born from a magickal tradition, not a purely linguistic one, and that magickal association never left them. Runes have been found carved on wood, stone, metal, and bone. The vast majority of runic talismans were crafted in wood, which decayed quickly, meaning the surviving archaeological record represents only a fraction of what once existed.

The Rök Runestone

Sweden holds the majority of surviving runic inscriptions. The Rök Runestone, carved circa 800 C.E., represents a significant discovery in the field. Recent analysis interprets its text as the narrative of the Sun Goddess, whom a great wolf slew. Odin commands humanity to avenge her death. This myth links directly to the climate catastrophe following a massive volcanic eruption in 536 C.E. that obscured the sun for over a decade. The inscription describes a new Goddess rising to replace her mother, preserving the memory of this environmental disaster through ancient ciphers.

The Kylver Stone

The historical record includes over four hundred examples of the Futhark alphabet. The Kylver Stone in Gotland, Sweden, stands as a premier example. Dating to the fifth century, this carving displays the complete sequence of the Elder Rune Row.

Runic Artifacts and Trade Routes

Approximately 2,500 runestones are known, out of a total of nearly 5,000 runic artifacts. These stones were raised as sacred landmarks and memorials across Scandinavian countries, with controversial examples also found in the United States. Runic inscriptions have marked Nordic trade routes from Eastern Europe to Greenland and from the Arctic Circle to Greece and Constantinople.

Uses of Runes, Then and Now

Beyond historical records, ancients used runes for magick. Applications included weather influence, battle protection, crop harvesting, and love attraction. Runes blessed, honored, and protected people and places. These ancient purposes validate a modern runic tradition. The human condition remains largely unchanged. We still grapple with climate change, loss, and the need for protection. Runes remain valuable tools in these pursuits.

Ethics and Power

Modern practitioners must reconcile runic power with its potential for misuse. Some groups attempt to use runes as emblems of domination. This exclusion is particularly acute for witches, who historically faced scapegoating for societal maladies.

Domination of one group over another contradicts moral magickal practice. Closing oneself off from the collective culture denies wisdom. Practitioners must approach runes with awareness of the sacredness and validity of all beings. This inclusivity is key to successful divination.

The Younger Rune Row

Language complexity ironically led to runic simplification. Around the tenth century dawn of the Viking age, the Elder Rune Row (24 characters) evolved into the Younger Rune Row (16 characters). This system uses only four vowel sounds. Notably, the Elhaz rune appears inverted in this row.

Form and Variation

The Younger Futhark is also known as "long branch" (Danish term) or "staveless" runes. The system emphasizes economy. Each character uses a single vertical stave with curved or crossed offshoots, allowing for quick carving. Because the alphabet is concise, single characters represent multiple sounds.

Variations include "short twig" runes (Scandinavian term), which resemble script. Inscriptions with dotted characters suggest further sound differentiations.

Expansion and Evolution

Runic usage expanded beyond Scandinavia. Explorers carried writing systems across the seas to places like the Isle of Man. Syncretism took root as Latin phrases appeared in runic carvings and variations blended together.

The evolution of runes is counterintuitive. Instead of growing in complexity, the system became smaller and more simplified until falling out of common use. Note that terms like Younger Rune Row, Younger Futhark, and Norse runes are often used interchangeably.

Runes in Manuscripts

Few runic manuscripts survive, and fewer carry overt magickal intent, though they may reflect magickal practices. The rune poems found in Anglo-Saxon and Scandinavian traditions are of extreme importance for understanding each rune's symbolic meaning.

The oldest manuscript containing runic symbols is the Abecedarium Nordmannicum from the ninth century CE. The Codex Runicus, a fourteenth-century Danish manuscript written entirely in runes, contains the laws of the province of Sconia. During the Swedish phase of the Thirty Years War (1630-1635), the forces of Gustavus Adolphus used runes as a cipher to confuse Austrian intelligence.

Runes in Art and Architecture

Glyph runes frequently appear within runic inscriptions. The most common is the Thórshamarr (the hammer of Thor), also called the fylfot. This symbol represents the dynamic magickal force of the Æsir and the explosive power of the Thunderer. The sun wheel or cross is equally ancient, appearing from the Bronze Age onward. This common European symbol originally denoted holy places and was later adopted by Christians in their conversion efforts.

In the twentieth century, the Nazis revived certain runes as manipulative tools, adopting the Hakenkreuz (hook-cross) and a doubled S-rune as identifying marks. These appropriations are widely regarded as imbalanced misdirections of runic forces. The S-rune, for instance, is a rune of the sun, not of "victory."

Runic forms continue surfacing in modern life. The peace symbol popularized in the 1960s takes the form of the Ýr-rune of the Younger Futhark, an alternate form of Eihwaz and Elhaz from the Elder row. This shape became a symbol of "death" in early twentieth-century German runology and was used as such by anti-Nazi activists during the war. The bright blue Star of Life carried on ambulances echoes the Hagall rune in its later letter-rune form.

Germanic half-timbered architecture (Fachwerk) preserves runic shapes in its structural timbers. Originally, builders placed the timbers to form specific rune shapes, imparting that rune's power to the building and its inhabitants. The practice continued long after builders forgot the reason behind the configurations, surviving as simple tradition. The familiar Dutch hex signs also derive ultimately from a runic source.

The golden ritual drinking horns of Gallehus depict human figures in stances and postures that represent cultic signs and runes. These figures illustrate the ránastödhur (sometimes called "runic asanas"), bodily postures through which the vitki physically embodies runic forms. The Herrgott von Bentheim (Lord God of Bentheim) offers another example: a piece of statuary based on a wooden original brought from a nearby Thing-stead, its arms bent in the shape of an Anglo-Frisian rune. Though later given Christian significance, it is still used today as an object on which solemn oaths are sworn.

The Three Futhark Codifications

Three ancient codifications of the letter runes exist:

  1. The Elder Futhark (24 runes). The original system, in use from approximately 200 BCE to 800 CE.
  2. The Anglo-Saxon or Frisian Futhork (up to 33 runes). An expansion of the Elder system that survived the Christianization process until the tenth century CE.
  3. The Younger (Norse) Futhark (16 runes). A condensed system that began developing in the seventh century CE and was complete by approximately 800 CE.

Both the Anglo-Saxon and Younger systems are modifications of the Elder Futhark. The methodical manner in which the order and correspondences of the runes were maintained across all three systems strongly indicates that these modifications took place within a traditionally controlled cult. Across the various systems, individual rune shapes and names were sometimes altered, offering valuable clues and correspondences to their inner nature. All three systems remain magickally valid.

House Marks and Heraldry

After the Middle Ages, runes were driven underground in continental Germanic territory, finding expression through graphic arts attributed to the early nobility and farmers. House marks are symbolic or literal monograms formed from two or more runes, often stylistically modified. They served as property identification, inscribed into objects owned by lord and freeman alike. Unlike crests and coats-of-arms, a house mark could be drawn without color and by an unpracticed hand.

The history of house marks traces a three-stage degeneration:

  1. Cultic period (through the mid-fifteenth century). Marks were still formed and interpreted according to ancient runes and holy signs. Their value was highly symbolic and sacred.
  2. Phonetic period (mid-fifteenth to mid-eighteenth century). Runic letter forms spelling a surname or initials were welded together into a single composite shape. The deeper symbolic value had faded, and runes functioned only as phonetic symbols.
  3. Latin period (after the mid-eighteenth century). Runic forms were dropped entirely. Latin script replaced them, typically forming a person's initials.

Stonemasons' signs, merchants' signs, and masters' signs may in some cases be interpreted according to the same rules that govern house marks. This three-stage decline reveals how runic knowledge gradually eroded into modern times, but by retracing the path, the practitioner can recover some of what would otherwise have been lost.

Heraldic art also conceals runic forms in two ways: through the color pattern composing a coat-of-arms, or through symbolic figures that encode a rune's concept without reproducing its visible shape.

The Runic Revival

Many runic practices and much rune lore continued in various forms long after the arrival of Christianity, but the systematic transmission of sacred rune knowledge belonging to the ancient vitkar and eriloz slowly disappeared. By the nineteenth century, only scattered pockets of rune singers remained in the remotest areas of Scandinavia. Yet the runic mysteries are indigenous to the innermost selves of their people. This inner rune lore could never be eliminated entirely; it only retreated into the deepest shelters of human consciousness, waiting to be reborn.

As the Völuspá (stanza 59) describes the renewed world after Ragnarök:

Again the Æsir meet
on Idha-plain,
and speak of the mighty
Midgard-serpent,
and again remember
the mighty World-doom
and Fimbultýr's
elder runes.

The Armanen Movement

At the dawn of the twentieth century, the Pan-Germanic mystic Guido von List received a spontaneous runic initiation while recovering from a cataract operation. Lying in darkness with bandaged eyes for several months, the "secrets of the runes" were revealed to him. From 1902 until his death in 1919, List worked toward restoring what he called Armanentum. He founded the Guido-von-List-Gesellschaft to support his investigations and the Armanen Orden to carry out its esoteric functions.

List developed a magickal system of eighteen runes (the Armanen system) based solely on the textual authority of the Rune-Song in the Eddic Hávamál. He maintained this was the primal system, though no hard evidence beyond the Hávamál supports that claim. List's personal force and the influence of his Armanen Orden shaped the runic theories of German magickians from that time forward.

List's aims were often political, and his theories incorporated anti-Semitic ideas prevalent in his era. His runic teachings were later absorbed into the Germanen Orden, an esoteric precursor to the National Socialist movement.

Kummer, Marby, and Runic Yoga

List's ideas were further developed by two magickians, Siegfried Adolf Kummer and Friedrich Bernhard Marby, who created a system of "runic yoga" or runic gymnastics. Their publications and experiments laid foundations for a practical system, though they retained the Armanen rune row and reinforced its associated prejudices. Rudolf John Gorsleben produced an enormous compilation of rune lore based on the Armanen system as well. The early 1930s mark the twilight of this first esoteric runic movement.

The Nazi Period

In 1933, the Nazi regime began, and by 1935 the Ahnenerbe (Institute for Ancestral Heritage) was formed around the ideas of Professor Hermann Wirth, among others. During the Nazi regime, all things Germanic were mobilized toward politically manipulative ends. The runic forces themselves were used far less than some believe. The Ahnenerbe and Totenkopf Orden drew more heavily on Judeo-Christian and Manichean ideas in their magickal traditions and organizational principles.

The Nazis employed ancient Germanic symbolism (which was very popular at the time) and infused it with non-Germanic concepts for manipulative purposes, mirroring the very technique Christian evangelists had used centuries before: adopting old pagan symbols to convert the populace, then gradually replacing their original significance with contrary meanings. Runes and holy signs were abundant in Nazi symbolism, but the degree to which this perverted the tribal systems of the ancients into a totalitarian imperial scheme is evident at a glance.

The practical use of runes as a system of magick and personal development virtually died out or was driven underground during this period.

Spiesberger and the Post-War Reformation

After the war, the Armanen system was revived and reformed by the German magickian Karl Spiesberger, a widely qualified occultist who authored works in both the Hermetic and runic traditions. Spiesberger synthesized the work of all the German runic magickians who preceded him within a pansophical framework. He eliminated all the racist and volkisch elements while retaining the Armanen system of eighteen runes, which by the 1950s had become nearly traditional in German circles.

This eighteen-rune system forms a valid and working magickal system. However, it is not a traditional form, and to some extent it remains cut off from the innate powers slumbering in the ancient runes and their system. Whereas the Armanen tradition dates only from around 1904 CE, the oldest runic evidence extends roughly two thousand years earlier.

The Return to the Elder Tradition

Documents from the Viking and pre-Viking ages provide ample clues about how the runes were used, but the Armanen framework cannot fully accommodate this material because it is the product of a different organic system. The elder tradition is known to have worked, and to have worked for hundreds of years within well-developed cults. Unlocking those ancient runic treasure mounds, where the hoard of rune wisdom has been stored over millennia, is the most fruitful path forward. The psychic keys provided by the pioneering technical work of modern magickians in the Armanen tradition remain extremely helpful in this endeavor.

Traditional Rune Lore and Ásatrú

The traditional runic systems are rooted in the three ancient Futharks. The magickal system and cosmology of the Elder Futhark (twenty-four signs) draws its modern rebirth from a synthesis of comparative religion, anthropology, archaeology, and linguistics (collectively known as linguistic paleontology), combined with the methods of magick. This holistic view also incorporates the natural sciences.

The ancient eriloz still speak through their runestones and through the mind runes (ON hugrunir) they encode in consciousness. Their magickal system, however, was only part of a much larger cosmological pattern encompassing all the known and unknown worlds. For the ancient Germanic tribes, magick, religion, and law (including social organization) were expressions of the same basic divine force. For traditional magickal forms to be truly reborn, a vessel for this holistic conception first had to be nurtured.

That vessel arrived on May 16, 1973, when the Ásatrúarmenn ("those trusting in the Æsir") was founded in Iceland. Though precursors existed earlier in the decade, this event crystallized the movement now known as Ásatrú (the faith of the Æsir). Early major organizations included groups in Iceland, California, and England. Over time these larger bodies have evolved, disbanded, and reformed, with the movement shifting increasingly toward localized and regionalized tribal organizations rather than large international structures.

These groups maintain a healthy independence from one another, though this independence has at times devolved into polarized frictions. The organizations are primarily religious in orientation, and their remarkable breadth of expression and deliberate lack of dogmatism defies quick summary. The efficiency of any runic magickal system is strengthened by an understanding of the holistic principles of this faith, since this is the atmosphere in which rune lore was first practiced.

A runic order known as the Rune-Gild has existed since 1979 and now operates worldwide. As in ancient times when the runes brought people of various tribes and lineages together in the search for the mysteries, the problems of cultural polarization found elsewhere tend not to be an issue within this tradition.

Rune Grimoire

Foundations & Ethics

Runes combine archaeology, anthropology, linguistics, symbolism, and divination into a unified study. Rune casters share a secret yet common language that transcends cultures and locations.

Types of Rune Keepers

  1. Runologists (Scholars):
    • Academic keepers of archaeological, historical, and linguistic information.
    • Distinguish lexical runes (translatable) from non-lexical runes (decorative).
    • Study form, purpose, and meaning within archaeological context.
    • Example: Debunked the Mustang Mountain Cave runestone (Arizona, ~2012), revealing it as a 1990s creation using defunct Sudovian script.
  2. Runatics (Hobbyists):
    • Passionate rune hunters who delight in discovery.
    • Celebrate runes through secular festivities (e.g., Heavener, Oklahoma's annual runestone festival featuring feasting, ax throwing, fencing, blacksmithing).
    • Use runes as decor and seek validation from runologists.
  3. Runemal (Occultist Practice):
    • Magicko-religious rune casting taught orally by elders as sacred rite.
    • Associated with modern Heathenry.
    • Employs legomonism: direct channels of knowledge remain hidden.
  4. Rune-Masters (Occultist Teachers):
    • Highly skilled casters who train others.
    • Distinguished by their ability to teach, not just practice.

Key Terms

  • Heathenry: Modern revival of polytheistic pre-Christian religion focused on Germanic European traditions.
  • Ásatrú: American Heathenry drawing customs from Scandinavia.
  • Traditionalism: Adhering to established beliefs in opposition to modern/eclectic practices.

Misappropriation Warnings

Runes themselves are not problematic. What becomes problematic is when enthusiasts use them to deceive or pervert their meaning.

  • Political Co-option: Some groups incorporate racialist and nationalist ideas into rune practice. The Left-Hand Path refers to practices defined by the taboo absence of morals.
  • Sacred symbols can degrade into offensive emblems quickly. Engage with runes understanding how symbols can be corrupted through intention.
  • Commercial Use: Over 100 rune-bearing sites in North America are all relatively modern (18th century or later).

Ethics of Commercial Runes

  • Historically, runes were personal, often secret, and not commercial.
  • Modern commerce (selling rune sets, readings, games) is entirely contemporary.
  • No inherent wrong in buying runes or paying for readings, provided skill matches price.
  • Interact with runes and others honestly to avoid deviating into darkness.

Personal Boundaries

Runes Are Personal:

  • Do not lend your runes. They absorb vibrational energy of handlers.
  • Maintain this boundary as an exercise in autonomy, not isolation.

Avoid Self-Doubt:

  • Everyone has varying psychic ability that improves with practice.
  • Historical rune users were often barely literate.
  • As long as you use runes ethically without spreading misinformation, you are using them correctly.

What to Avoid:

  • Harassing the oracle with excessive consultations
  • Becoming overly dependent
  • Re-pulling due to dissatisfaction
  • The Temple of Delphi bore "Nothing in excess." Find the balance point.

Rune Media & Materials

Runes carry an air of permanence. They can be additive (painted onto surfaces) or subtractive (carved, removing material).

Natural Inorganic Materials

  • Stone, rock, minerals
  • Metal (silver, gold, iron)
  • Example: Gallehus drinking horns (gold, Old Norse inscription), discovered 17th-18th century, stolen 19th century for gold value.

Natural Organic Materials

  • Wood (staves, branch cross-sections)
  • Bone and antler (deer, sheep, buffalo)
  • Shell
  • Paper (cellulose plant material)

Modern Options

  • Semiprecious stones with metallic staves
  • Ceramic tiles
  • Gems and crystals (add energetic properties used in meditation, grounding, spellcraft)

Old Norse Terminology for Rune Media

The connection between runes and the materials they were carved upon runs deep in the language itself. Three Old Norse words illustrate this bond:

  • Stafr: Stave, letter, secret lore. The word for a piece of wood is inseparable from the word for the rune inscribed upon it.
  • Teinn: Twig, talismanic word for divination.
  • Hlutr: Lot for divination, talismanic object, on which runes were also carved.

Wood was the most common medium for magickal runic work. Stone talismans exist but are relatively few; the large runestones served cultic and funerary purposes. Metal was extremely popular for talismanic work, especially bracteates: thin metal disks inscribed with runes and various designs, representing an important tradition in magickal practice. Utilitarian metal objects (particularly swords) were also inscribed with runes to impart special power, enhancing their function or protecting the user. Bone objects, typically connected with magickal practices, are not uncommon. Runes were carved with knife points or special pointed instruments dedicated to the runic art.

Rune Work & Learning

Through a combination of the runes and the vitki's personal will and ability, all things are possible; but in order to gain this power the vitki must develop the skills basic to all ritual work: concentration, visualization, breath and posture control, and the art of incantation. The best course of action is one in which time is devoted to exercises designed to develop the basic skills necessary to the successful performance of runagaldr.

Runic power is often slow to develop in people (this may be due to centuries of widespread neglect), but when the force manifests itself in the vitki's life it is all-pervasive in its potency, unshakable in its strength, and overpowering in the stimulation it produces. A vitki of patience and perseverance will be well rewarded!

Preliminary Exercises

I. Find a rune that is particularly appealing to you. Fashion a meditation card from white poster board (about 3" x 5"). Paint the chosen stave in bright red. Sit comfortably with the card at eye level. Begin an even breath rhythm. Concentrate on the stave's form while silently chanting the name three times, pause, then three times again. Then close your eyes and imagine the shape in your hugauga ("mind's eye"). Practice until you can perform this smoothly for ten minutes.

II. Repeat Exercise I, except sing the name out loud while maintaining a breath pattern of ten seconds inhalation, two seconds hold in, ten seconds exhalation (while singing), and two seconds hold out. Experiment with other postures, sitting and standing. Once you can maintain this for ten minutes, progress further.

III. Perform in the I-rune stadha with hands overhead. Set up a ten-two-ten-two breathing rhythm while facing north. Visualize the F-rune in blazing red while intoning its name three times. Slowly turn with the sun in a circle, visualizing and vibrating each rune in turn. Once you can perform this instinctually with few breaks in concentration, rune work may be confidently undertaken.

The vitki should also design a course of intellectual and physical development. The serious study of Norse mythology and religion, the science of runology, and the Old Norse language will greatly improve understanding of runecraft. A healthy, strong body will reflect itself in more powerful magickal abilities.

Learning Runes

Commitment Required:

  • Study origin of your chosen system
  • Learn individual attributes
  • Master different spreads

Allow Acclimation:

  • Give readings time to settle into your psyche.
  • If a reading seems incorrect, wait before reconsulting.
  • Things may already be in motion that have not revealed themselves.

Stave, Symbol, and Sound

Learning Approach:

  • Focus on one rune per week.
  • Use physical runes, drawings in your grimoire, or index cards.
  • Prioritize: names, sounds, or meanings first.

Stave (Form):

  • A stave is simply a line bearing mystery, secret, or cipher.
  • Study linear vs. curved forms:
    • Cross: choice, decision, obstacle
    • Curve: transformation, the unexpected
    • Straight line: clear path, forward movement, or standstill

On Reversals:

  • Reversals are entirely modern additions.
  • Linguistically, they make no sense; an upside-down letter retains its phonetic value.
  • Some runes are symmetrical, making reversals impossible to detect.
  • Recommendation: Turn upside-down runes right side up to read them.

Tactile Learning:

  • Trace patterns with fingertips.
  • Write in runes.
  • This lessens dependence on others' interpretations.

Symbol (Meaning):

  • Symbols are doorways for intuitive information.
  • Example: Teiwaz resembles an arrow. Consider direction of movement and what that reveals.

Sound (Vibration):

  • Speaking runes aloud creates transformational vibration.
  • Begin by saying each rune's name as dialogue.
  • Progress to pronouncing phonetic sounds.
  • Create bindrunes through sound (start with your initials).

Runic Codes & Numerical Symbolism

Runic Codes and the Ættir System

One of the most compelling runic practices is the concealment of magickal formulas through intricately devised codes. These codes served a dual purpose: making the messages more secret (and therefore more magickally effective) and keeping them incomprehensible to the uninitiated.

The basis of all runic codes is the numerical value of each rune. Both the Elder and Younger Futharks are divided into three groups called ættir (families). Through this system, any rune can be identified by a twofold numerical formula indicating its ætt and its position within that group. For example, the formula 1:2 identifies the second rune of the first ætt.

These cryptic systems reached their highest development during the Younger Futhark period, but they were certainly known and used in the older period as well, since ancient representations of the Elder row are also clearly divided into ættir. Two particularly remarkable methods are:

  • Branch runes (ON kvistrunir): A single glyph can portray a single rune. Strokes to the left of a vertical line indicate the ætt, while strokes to the right reveal the runic position. A change of word in the formula is indicated by the upward or downward direction of the ætt stroke.
  • Tent runes (ON tjaldrunir): Read in a clockwise direction beginning on the left, each segment encodes an ætt and position number.

The ninth-century St. Gall MS 270 portrays several additional cryptographic systems of rune writing.

Numerical Symbolism

Numerical criteria play an important role in the loading and working of rune tines and are often critical in other types of rune magick. In the ancient inscriptions the vitki sometimes sacrificed linguistic clarity for numerical or ideographic potency by leaving out staves (especially vowels) or by adding and doubling them. Number is one of the three keys to each rune, and much of the interpretation of individual runes is drawn from numerical criteria. The H-rune (9) connects to the Nine Worlds of Yggdrasill, and the J-rune (12) to the twelve months of the solar year.

The numerical values of inscriptions, tines, and magickal formulas place the power of the runes in various spheres of working while drawing on the power inherent in that number. A general principle holds: the more levels of meaning packed into the least amount of space, and the more cryptic the form, the more effective the magick. This applies equally to the shaping and interpretation of talismans.

Runic number formulas are analyzed in two ways. The first is the rune count, the number of staves in the formula. The second is the runic total, the sum of the numerical values of each rune (similar to gematria). These numbers are then broken down into their multiples to further analyze their powers. The formula luwatuwa, found on ancient talismans, demonstrates both systems: a rune count of 8 (2 x 4) and a runic total of 66 (6 x 11), forming an incantation of great ideographic, phonetic, and numerological power.

For the rune count, the numbers 1 through 24 are all powerful and imbue the formula with the force of the rune of that number. Using any twenty-four runes in an inscription provides a broad base of power and invokes the force of the whole rune row. To a twenty-four-fold rune count, the number eight and its multiples (and indeed twenty-four and its multiples) may be added to maintain the whole harmony while intensifying force. The multiple of the rune count also modifies the runic potency in subtle ways. These are common patterns in ancient inscriptions.

On the level of the runic total, the sums 1 through 24 indicate the sphere where that particular rune is at work. Prime numbers are especially powerful and express a tremendous amount of will. Whatever the runic total might be, it is through its multiple factors that the root force of the number is revealed:

  • Multiples of 3 and 9 are powerful in operations dealing with magickal forces working on many levels at once, including the earthly realm
  • Multiples of 10 are especially forceful when the intent is to cause a change in the manifest world of Midhgardhr
  • Multiples of 12 are also potent in this regard but produce a more prolonged and enduring effect
  • 13 and its multiples are the most universal numbers of power. A vast number of runic inscriptions manifest this numerological pattern. The number is indicative of universal potency and contains the mystery of Eiwaz as the world-tree (9) and the three realms (3) in the ontological oneness of Ginnungagap (1). The number by which this master number is multiplied further modifies and directs the overall force of the formula according to its runic nature

All of these principles may be used when constructing rune tines and rituals, but they need not dominate the form of the operation. Intuition and natural inclination should be the guide, and vitkar may totally dispense with numerical considerations without diminishing results. The correct use of runic numerology is an art in itself, one that needs to be supplemented with a deep grounding in Nordic lore to be completely effective.

It should be noted that the old Germanic attitude toward number differed considerably from that of their southern neighbors. To the Pythagorean and Gnostic mystics, number came to be the rule of all things. To the vitkar, number was only one among three equal expressions of the same holy mystery embodied by a rune. Where the Gnostics and Pythagoreans tended to see number as a way of measuring and distinguishing one thing from another, the vitkar saw numbers as points of connection and interrelation in a cosmos forever in a state of ebb and flow.
