Candle Magick with Runes

Runes provide illumination. They allow us to examine aspects of our lives from many perspectives, revealing information about the past and what is coming into being. Because runes are tools of illumination, they adapt naturally to candle magick.

Applications:

  • Focus intentions
  • Enhance meditations
  • Add power to spellwork
  • Augment seasonal rituals and lunar observances

A matrix is a specific altar arrangement incorporating runes, candles, and sacred objects (crystals, gemstones) to create a visual focal point for meditation and creative expression.

Pillar Candle Carving Basics

Pillar candles are a staple of witchcraft, used for spells, charms, rituals, and ambience. Their large surface area makes them ideal for rune work:

  • Creating sequences
  • Recording and illuminating a rune cast
  • Empowering magickal practice

Carving as Magickal Act:

Carving forces the practitioner to plan and focus. There is no erasing. Everything must be done with intention. This itself is a potent exercise in developing psychic abilities.

The Scribe

Before considering what to carve, consider your tool.

Bolline vs. Athame:

  • Bolline: The "practical" blade or white-handled knife, used for candle carving
  • Athame: Double-edged blade (often black-handled), used for carving sacred space

The choice of implement impacts the spell. Each auspicious element chosen with clear intention amplifies the outcome, either hastening it or adding effectiveness.

Understanding Power

Power in witchcraft refers to the effectiveness of the work, not dominion over others. A powerful witch channels intention into manifestation. The most successful spells are those with the most intentional work invested.

Choosing Your Scribe

Think about the nature of your work in broad terms first:

  • Invoking
  • Banishing
  • Changing

Then get more specific. You would choose a different tool for an uncrossing candle than for a hearth blessing.

Making a Scribe

A scribe can be a dedicated magickal tool or an ordinary household item:

  • Sharpened chopstick
  • Hefty toothpick or skewer
  • Pin or tack

DIY Method:

  1. Find a slender twig (diameter of your pinkie, length from palm base to fingertip)
  2. Sharpen with a pencil sharpener, or cut diagonally with scissors

Wood Correspondences for Scribes

WoodUse For
UntitledFavorable casts, memorable or revealing readings, increases power
UntitledUntitled or relationship queries
UntitledAssuaging grief
UntitledMemorializing a person, honoring the Untitled

Special Scribes

Breaking Point Scribe:

For radical change, find a fallen tree and examine where nature and gravity toppled it. If you need to tear down paradigms or break free of old patterns, the breaking point reveals your scribe.

Root Scribe:

For ancestral work or honoring the dead, trim a sturdy root from an uprooted tree. Roots symbolize ties to family and land. Consider using to honor indigenous spirits of the land you occupy.

Railroad Spikes:

Protection

The Template Method

For evenly spacing runes around a pillar candle.

Materials:

  • Paper, ruler, scissors
  • Calculator, pencil, pin
  • Your scribe

Steps

1. Calculate Circumference:

  • Measure candle diameter (edge to edge)
  • Multiply by 3.14 = circumference
  • Example: 3" diameter × 3.14 = 9.42" circumference

2. Create Template:

  • Cut paper strip ~1" wide × circumference length
  • Divide length by number of runes in your cast
  • Example: 9.42" ÷ 5 runes = 1.88" spacing
  • Draw vertical lines at each interval

3. Draw Runes:

  • Write runes from your cast right to left between the lines

4. Position for Timing:

PlacementManifestation Speed
TopFast, timing is of the essence
CenterModerate, balanced timing
BottomSlow, celebrations, things you want to last

5. Transfer Pattern:

  • Tape template around candle at chosen height
  • Use pin to prick through points along each rune
  • Remove paper
  • Connect the dots with your scribe

6. Scribe with Intention:

  • Focus on the prophecy revealed in your cast
  • Think about what you want to accelerate, prolong, celebrate, or change
  • Go over staves multiple times for consistency and depth

Dressing the Candle

Content coming next.

Creating a Rune Candle Matrix

A matrix is a specific altar arrangement incorporating runes, candles, and sacred objects (crystals, gemstones) to create a visual focal point for meditation and creative expression.

Building Your Matrix

1. Center Candle:

Start in the center of your altar and place one candle there.

2. Select Five Runes:

Arrange them around the outside perimeter of the candle so they are evenly spaced. Choose runes based on your intention. Consult the lists of meanings to make your choice. You may focus on a single influence or many. For example, select a combination of runes you would want to see in your ideal cast.

3. Outer Candles:

Place another candle at the other end of each rune stick or tile, creating a five-pointed arrangement radiating from the center.

4. Add Crystals:

Place tumbled stones or crystals in the negative spaces between the rune sticks and candles. When choosing stones, consider their metaphysical properties. You can consult resources on gem and mineral associations, or choose on instinct based on what you find visually or energetically appealing.

Lines, Crosses, and Curves

As you become more adept at matrix work, you may wish to create more complex patterns. Patterns occur in nature and are imbued with natural magick, the divine order of the universe follows numerous patterns observable in all life forms, from plants to sea creatures to celestial bodies. Developing skill at creating matrices aligns your practice with both terrestrial and celestial energies.

A matrix is a creative outlet, a place of focus, and something that beautifies your surroundings.

Lines

Beginning from a central point and adding lines that radiate outward is a symbolic way to manifest. You make it symbolically real on the earthly plane by infusing it with light, earth magick, and rune magick from the astral plane until it becomes actual reality.

  • A single line represents your present path
  • Repeating lines amplify intention so energy moves in all directions
  • Five runes around a center candle/crystal honor the sacred number five. Every fruit comes from a five-petaled flower; cut an apple and see five seeds arranged the same way

Five Aspects of Worldly Desire:

  1. Health
  2. Abundance
  3. Comfort
  4. Love
  5. Peace

Crosses

Incorporate intersecting lines, exploring the places where two lines meet:

  • Crossroads: Helps in decision-making
  • Celebration: Signifies points of change in the Wheel of the Year
  • Star motif: Adding vertical, diagonal, and horizontal crosses creates a star like those in the Witch runes
Etymology Note: The word "witch" may connect to "wicce," believed by many to have etymological ties to Wicca, meaning "to bend" or "to change."

Curves

Add curved lines to:

  • Accept the winds of change when they blow through your life
  • Imitate spirals found in nature
  • Remind yourself to smile

Realities in Magick

Whether your practice is secular or spiritual, learning variations in matrix work leads to deeper understanding of how magick works: how every color, pattern, shape, intention, and action shapes reality.

Accepted realities in magick include:

  • Nature and the observable world
  • Human-made creations and manipulation of the natural world
  • Entities and experiences unseen but deeply felt (including communication with oracles and spirits)
  • Personal gnosis: Spiritual knowledge gained by an individual practitioner without external validation

Subtle changes in the environment, both observable and intuitively felt, during a magickal working are accepted as affirmation that the work has power.

One theme that solidly recurs in all forms of magick is change.

Icelandic Stave Symbols

Overview

Early Icelandic grimoires, the magickal handbooks full of spells and occult lore, are filled with long lists of curious, angular signs known as staves. Each was drawn for a specific purpose, and their roots reach back to the ancient rune system, with a measure of later medieval and Renaissance magick woven in. Popularly called Magickal Staves, or galdrastafir, some are bind runes built from several runic signs merged into a single figure, while others stand entirely on their own.

A Book of Household Magick

The intentions behind the staves are wonderfully varied, with one for almost every occasion. They read like a magickal book of household management and tell the story of daily life down the years: the importance of a good catch for fishermen, protection against thieves and ghosts, ways to frighten off enemies, and even charms to keep butter wholesome, to break locks, and to raise the dead.

Notable Staves

Two of the best known staves have their own entries in the Rune Grimoire:

  • Helm of Awe (Aegishjalmur): an eight-armed sign, like a snowflake, meant to instil fear in enemies and to guard the wearer against the misuse of their own power. It became a cornerstone symbol of the Asatru faith.
  • Hulinhjalmur: a stave said to grant invisibility, recorded in the old texts with an infamous and grisly recipe and no counter stave to undo its effect.

A Word of Caution

The old stave recipes belong to their time and are preserved here as historical lore, not as instructions. Some, like Hulinhjalmur, call for ingredients that should never be sought or recreated. Study the staves for their history and symbolism rather than as literal workings.

Protection, Valkyrjur, and the Splayed Hand

This rune is historically perhaps the most complex of all from a symbological perspective. The Proto-Germanic form algiz means "protection," and its stave form is perhaps derived from the basic sign of defense and protection: the splayed hand.

The concept of the valkyrjur has been connected to this stave through the interpretation of the name as "swan." The valkyrjur are protective, life-giving beings who often fly by means of magickal cloaks made of swan feathers. They are protectors, power givers, and a mode by which Odin communicates with chosen heroes. The sign is often found carved into spears for protection and victory.

The Cosmic Harts and the Yew

Elhaz, meaning "elk," refers to the four cosmic harts that constantly bite at the needles of the World-Tree. The yew again enters the symbol complex through the Old Norse word ihwar, which occurs only in runic inscriptions. This term means either "yew tree" or "yew bow" and is later rendered by the word yr.

The Gothic word alhs (sanctuary) has also been related to this rune: a protected grove or enclosure dedicated to the gods. The Z-rune contains an aspect of the protective power of the divine twins. Alcis, the name of the twins reported by Tacitus, may indeed be related to the rune name. In their aggressive, warlike aspect, the twins are visualized as harts, while in other aspects they are represented as horses.

Bifröst and the Connection Between Gods and Humanity

Elhaz is the power of human life and spirit striving toward the world of the Aesir. It is the rune of the connection between gods and humanity, the force that draws the consciousness of mortals toward the realm of the gods.

The Z-rune is the three-colored bridge of shimmering light, Bifröst, the "Rainbow Bridge" of Norse mythology. This bridge connects Asgardhr, Midhgardhr, and Hel. It is another mode for the consciousness to traverse the worlds, the curved path of the branches and roots rather than the straight path of the trunk, a symbol of the magickal power of the hamingja.

The Z-rune is the force used by Heimdallr in his aspect as guardian of Asgardhr. Elhaz is a rune of consciousness and awareness (a hugrunin). It is over Bifröst that the rime-giants and fire-giants destroy the worlds of mortals and gods.

The stadha postures of the Z-rune are the traditional postures in which the Germanic peoples communicate with the gods. This shape was later employed as the M-rune in the Younger Futhark.

Rune Character

This rune is used for protection. It is also used in consecration and the banishing of negative energies. Excellent for the operator to wear when performing dangerous rituals as it protects against negative energies.

Ansuz connects to the divine and Loki, the trickster. As a messenger rune, it signals unexpected texts or intuitive hits. Ansuz advises alertness and careful attention to all forms of communication.

Cosmological Lore

Ansuz is the mysterium tremendum of the rune row. The A-rune is instrumental in the creation of humankind. It describes two of the spiritual gifts given to Askr and Embla (the primal man and woman) by the threefold aspect of Odin (appearing as Odin, Hoenir, and Lodhurr). These gifts were ond or anda (breath, spirit, the animating life principle) and odhr (inspired mental activity, inspiration). This is the stave of Odin as the numinous god of magick and ecstasy.

The Ecology of Spiritual Power

Ansuz is the receiver, container, transformer, and expresser of spiritual power and numinous knowledge. This force is received from the Æsir and transformed within humanity to be re-expressed toward the multiverse in magickal and religious acts. This ecology of power works in tandem with Odin reception of rune wisdom and subsequent expression of that wisdom to mortals.

The A-rune encompasses the medium through which numinous knowledge is received, the container of that power, and the force itself, which manifests as the ecstatic state. This container-contained equation is common for symbols of inspired or ecstatic states. In Norse mythology, the poetic mead of inspiration and the vessel in which it is held are both known by the name Othroerir ("the exciter of inspiration"). This is the ecstasy that leads to the formation of a body of lore and wisdom.

Word, Song, and Galdr

Ansuz is the rune of the word, song, poetry, and magickal incantation (galdr) as both a container and expresser of magickal force.

Ancestral Power and the Death Mysteries

Ansuz is a magickal ancestral power handed down from generation to generation along genetic lines. The ancient Germanic peoples understood themselves to be descended from their gods, as the genealogies of their kings, heroes, and clan chieftains attest. The power link between gods and mortals was, for them, unbroken, and it remains so. Through this rune, the realization of the bond between the ancestral gods and their people may be regained. This is an ecstatic concept that complements the more stable, institutional force of Othala.

The A-rune embodies the death mysteries of the Æsir.

Rune Character

Rune of the power of speech that destroys tyranny: "Your spiritual force sets you free." Order, the opposite of chaos. Creative inspiration, magickal oratory ability, and the power to persuade others and audiences through speech. Opens channels of self-expression and overcomes obstacles of every kind. Used in removing bindings. Assists in enhancing one's psychic and magickal abilities. Also used for work in invocations.

Symbol Grimoire

Introduction to Numerology

What Numerology Is

Numerology assigns meaning to the symbolic vibration of the digits 1 through 9, suggesting traits, strengths, and weaknesses for every day of the year. It rests on the idea that the universe is mathematically constructed and that the vibrational energy of people, places, and things can be expressed through numbers. Reducing birth dates and names to numbers allows a person's personality and destiny to be discerned.

Origins

Numerology likely originated in ancient Babylonia and among the early Hebrews, and many different systems developed across different parts of the world. The most familiar lineage traces back to the fifth-century BC Greek mathematician and philosopher Pythagoras. Pythagoras taught that mathematical connections linked the gods, mortals, and numbers, and that recurring number patterns could be codified to predict fate. He held numbers as the source of energy in the world, with 1 through 9 representing the nine stages of life, and said that the world is built upon the power of numbers.

How the System Works

Every number in numerology reduces to a value between 1 and 9, and each digit also corresponds to a letter of the alphabet. Any number larger than 9 is reduced by adding its digits together. For example, 123 becomes 1 + 2 + 3 = 6, so the qualities of 123 align with the symbolic number 6. Using single digits as the guide, the patterns of different dates and a person's name can be analyzed to describe character and forecast events.

The Nine Core Numbers

Each number carries a primary current and a shadow. The shadow names the challenge associated with that number. When the challenge is faced and integrated, it becomes a source of strength.

  • 1: Independent, creative, ambitious, extrovert. Shadow: selfish with tunnel vision.
  • 2: Sensitive, domestic, imaginative, musical. Shadow: timid and gullible.
  • 3: Scientific, powerful, knowledgeable, multi-talented. Shadow: superficial and hedonistic.
  • 4: Practical, stable, honest, trustworthy. Shadow: stubborn and overly serious.
  • 5: Energetic, sensual, daring, flirtatious. Shadow: difficulty committing.
  • 6: Perfectionist, creative, artistic, compassionate. Shadow: supersensitive and overemotional.
  • 7: Intellectual, philosophical, imaginative, intuitive. Shadow: impractical and secretive.
  • 8: Practical, just, trustworthy, powerful. Shadow: opinionated, impatient, intolerant.
  • 9: Spiritual, humanitarian, visionary, healer. Shadow: self-serving, possessive, volatile.

Numerology Alongside Astrology

Where astrology works through stars and Sun signs, numerology works through numbers. Both are symbolic systems and tools for understanding the self and life purpose. No sign is better than another in astrology, and no number is better than another in numerology. Every number carries both potential and shadow, and the shadow is simply the challenge the number invites you to face.

Your Birth Date Number

The date of birth carries a permanent influence on the life. Names may change over time, but the birth date number stays constant. To find it, add the digits of the month and day and reduce to a single digit. Someone born on April 17 has a birth date number of 1 + 7 = 8.

Numbers as Universal Symbols

On the surface, numbers are practical tools for counting. Beneath that plain function lies a deep tradition of philosophy and symbolism that recurs across nearly every culture and belief system in strikingly similar forms. The idea that numbers express not only quantity but also the inherent qualities, laws, and powers of the universe is extremely old. It runs through the mystery traditions, including those of the Pythagoreans, Babylonians, and Hindus, and through the Kabbalah. A number's form, its conceptual nature, and its symbolic meanings were all held to carry sacred significance, a hidden code that could reveal how the universe is constructed and where humanity stands within it.

Numbers demand precision and full understanding to be wielded accurately, and what they accomplish as mathematical instruments is inseparable from their symbolic meaning. Whether the universe is truly governed by numbers, and whether they were discovered rather than invented, the cosmos would carry on regardless. The Sun would still rise and set, the seasons would still turn, and the Moon would still wax and wane without our measurements. What numbers give us is a way to make sense of the cosmos and to locate ourselves within a far larger whole. Time illustrates this neatly. Sixty seconds make a minute, sixty minutes make an hour, and twenty-four hours make a day. The Sumerians devised this sexagesimal system roughly four thousand years ago, and it remains in use today as a neatly integrated framework, however much of a construct it may have been at the start.

Who Invented Numbers?

Unlike letters, which many myths describe as gifts from the gods, numbers are generally credited to human invention alone, despite their mystical importance. There is debate over whether numbers first arose in India or China, but it is clear that they came before letters. At some point a person recognized that a group of animals could be matched to the fingers of the hands, and counting began from there. It likely started in fertile, agrarian regions, where surplus produce had to be tallied so it could be traded or guarded against theft, since the worth of livestock or grain depends on knowing how much there is.

Children learn numbers the same way, counting fingers and then toes before moving on to tokens that extend the range. The Greeks and Romans did likewise, using small pebbles called calculi, from a word that originally meant limestone. This tally method gave rise to a system still in use. Roman numerals grew out of an earlier Etruscan practice of drawing lines to represent fingers, thought to descend from Italian shepherds notching wood to count sheep. One line stood for 1, two for 2, three for 3, and four for 4, followed by V for 5, which could be traced on the hand by running a line down the thumb to the wrist and back up to the little finger. Two V shapes joined end to end formed the X for 10.

Because this is a Base 10 system, every tenth V or X received an extra stroke. C, from centum meaning hundred, marked 100 and survives in the modern word cent. At this stage there was no symbol for zero, though the Romans named the concept nulla, meaning nothing. The absence of a zero symbol seriously hampered Roman numeral notation, which is why the Hindu and Arabic system, believed to date back as early as 400 BC, eventually became the most widely used way of writing numbers in the world.

The Esoteric Standing of Numbers

Numbers have long been described as a universal language given to humanity as a confirmation of truth. Numerology is the belief in a mystical, esoteric relationship between numbers and living things, physical objects, ideas, and concepts. It ranks among the oldest of the symbolic sciences, and Plato regarded it as the highest level of knowledge. The Greeks, Romans, Indians, Chinese, and Kabbalists all treated numerology as essential to understanding how the universe is constructed. Among the Fulani of Africa, numbers were held to carry such power that quantities tied closely to a person, such as their age in years or the size of their herds, were never spoken aloud, since naming them was thought to drain a little of that power.

Numerology is easy for modern skeptics to dismiss alongside fortune telling, yet it should not be set aside so quickly. Many Hindu families will not name a child until the numerology of the chosen name sits in harmony with the numerology of the birth date. Pythagoras declared that numbers rule all things, echoing an ancient Chinese conviction that numerology holds a key to the harmony between spirit and matter, humanity and the divine, microcosm and macrocosm. The I Ching points toward the same correspondence. Pythagoras went further, proposing that mathematics, music, architecture, and color all resonate together in a balance that numbers can help define. In this view, numerology does not strip numbers of their practical, mathematical role, it raises them to the standing of arbiters of a deeper truth.

Many of the ancient meanings attached to numbers reach back as far as the Chaldeans. The early Christian Church did not accept them, regarding the art with the same suspicion it directed at astrology and other forms of magick, and judging it ungodly. Over time the Church worked to undermine the concepts of numerology, and much of its mystery was lost, though a portion of the secret language of numbers has since been pieced back together.

A Key to the First Eleven Numbers

Although several systems of numerology exist, there is broad agreement on the meanings of certain numbers. The brief key below covers the first eleven numbers, including zero, the mysterious no number whose discovery ranks among the most important in human history.

  • 0: Nothingness, and yet also everything.
  • 1: The oneness of all, and the individual.
  • 2: Duality, balance, and separation.
  • 3: Spirit, communication, and wisdom.
  • 4: Earth, solidity, understanding, and order.
  • 5: Harmony, justice, protection, and love.
  • 6: Marriage, the union of male and female, and the balance of opposites.
  • 7: Spirituality, the occult, and intelligence.
  • 8: Eternity, infinity, and justice.
  • 9: The limited and the limitless, experience and virtue, completion.
  • 10: Death and rebirth, perfection.

Numerology & Colors

Life Path Numbers & Personal Colors

In numerology, your Life Path number reveals your soul's purpose in this incarnation. This number, derived from your birth date, corresponds to a specific color that carries significance throughout your lifetime. Unlike colors you choose based on circumstance or need, your Life Path color is an unchangeable signature of your spiritual journey.

Prosperity Stones by Life Path Number

Beyond the general prosperity stones that anyone can carry, each Life Path number has a specific crystal that attracts wealth and abundance aligned with that path's unique energy signature. These stones have been traditionally associated with financial success for their corresponding numbers.

  • Life Path 1: Ruby
  • Life Path 2: Carnelian
  • Life Path 3: Yellow Citrine
  • Life Path 4: Emerald
  • Life Path 5: Sodalite
  • Life Path 6: Azurite
  • Life Path 7: Amethyst
  • Life Path 8: Rose Quartz
  • Life Path 9: Tiger's Eye
  • Life Path 11: Hematite
  • Life Path 22: Gold Topaz

Working With Your Prosperity Stone

Carry your prosperity stone close to your skin, in your pocket, or wear it as jewelry. Allow it to receive plenty of sunlight to charge its energy. Place it on your altar during wealth workings to amplify your intentions.

Daily Affirmation Practice:

Hold your prosperity stone in your hand at least once a day while speaking positive affirmations aloud. Affirmations are phrases repeated in the present tense, as if you already possess the quality you seek. This instills the thought pattern in your mind and programs the stone with your intention.

Create affirmations that resonate with your specific goals and circumstances. Here are a few examples to get you started:

  • I create wealth and abundance.
  • I gratefully accept my share from an abundant universe.
  • Prosperity flows to me all the time.
  • All the money I spend returns to me multiplied.

Your prosperity stone works in harmony with your soul's purpose to draw prosperity that supports your life's mission. Through regular contact, sunlight charging, and affirmation work, you attune the crystal to your unique energetic signature and financial goals.

Calculating Your Life Path Number

Add together your birth month, day, and year, then reduce to a single digit. Exception: Stop reducing when you reach 11 or 22, these are Master Numbers with special significance.

Calculation Method

To preserve Master Numbers, calculate in stages rather than adding all digits in a straight line:

  1. Month (as single or double digit)
  2. Day (as single or double digit)
  3. Year (add all four digits together, reduce if needed)
  4. Add these three sums together
  5. Reduce to single digit (unless 11 or 22)

Example 1: July 12, 1973

  • Month: 7
  • Day: 12
  • Year: 1 + 9 + 7 + 3 = 20, then 2 + 0 = 2
  • Total: 7 + 12 + 2 = 21, then 2 + 1 = 3

Life Path: 3 (Yellow)

Example 2: February 29, 1944

  • Month: 2
  • Day: 29
  • Year: 1 + 9 + 4 + 4 = 18, then 1 + 8 = 9
  • Total: 2 + 29 + 9 = 40, then 4 + 0 = 4

Wait, let's recalculate using the sum method to check for Master Numbers:

  • 2 + 29 + 1944 = 1975
  • 1 + 9 + 7 + 5 = 22

Life Path: 22 (Gold), Master Number preserved

Why this method matters: If you add straight across (2 + 2 + 9 + 1 + 9 + 4 + 4 = 31, then 3 + 1 = 4), you lose the Master Number 22 hidden in the calculation. The staged method reveals Master Numbers that would otherwise disappear.

Life Path Colors & Soul Purposes

Life Path 1, Red

Purpose: Learning independence and self-reliance. Once you master standing on your own, you become a natural pioneer and leader who blazes trails for others.

Life Path 2, Orange

Purpose: Developing cooperation and harmony with others. You're caring, intuitive, and deeply sensitive to the emotional currents around you.

Life Path 3, Yellow

Purpose: Self-expression through creative outlets, singing, dancing, writing, speaking. Your gift is embodying and communicating life's joy with enthusiasm and optimism.

Life Path 4, Green

Purpose: Understanding the value of structure, organization, and steady effort. You're grounded, practical, and excel when you have clear systems and expectations.

Life Path 5, Blue

Purpose: Making constructive use of personal freedom. Versatile and adaptable, you thrive on change and variety. Once you discover your true field, progress comes rapidly.

Life Path 6, Indigo

Purpose: Learning to carry responsibility with grace. Naturally caring and service-oriented, you're drawn to helping professions. You possess refined taste and creative talents.

Life Path 7, Violet

Purpose: Pursuing wisdom and spiritual understanding. Intuitive and contemplative, you need solitude for meditation, study, and inner development.

Life Path 8, Pink

Purpose: Mastering the material realm without losing your humanity. Ambitious and practical, you pursue worldly success but must learn to balance power, status, and wealth with compassion.

Life Path 9, Bronze

Purpose: Learning to give selflessly and serve humanity. Tolerant, idealistic, and humanitarian, you express generosity in countless ways. Like 3 and 6, you carry strong creative potential.

Master Numbers

Master Numbers (11 and 22) indicate souls capable of extraordinary achievement, but this potential often takes decades to activate. The heightened nervous energy associated with these numbers can create obstacles in early life. Many require multiple incarnations to fully embody their Master Number gifts.

Life Path 11, Silver

Purpose: Accessing heightened awareness and spiritual perception unavailable to most. You're an intuitive visionary who generates brilliant ideas and plans. Your challenge is translating inspiration into manifestation rather than remaining in the dreamer realm.

Life Path 22, Gold

Purpose: Building something of lasting significance for humanity. You combine vision with practical mastery, making the impossible tangible. Your challenge is learning to focus and direct your immense power toward collective benefit rather than personal gain.

Your Unchangeable Personal Colors

Life Path Color: Fixed by your birth date, this color reflects your soul's purpose. You may love it or resist it, but it remains your spiritual signature throughout this incarnation.

Birth Day Color: The day of the month you were born (reduced to a single digit, unless you were born on the 11th, 22nd, or 29th) also corresponds to a personal color. This secondary color adds another layer to your numerological profile.

These colors can be incorporated into your wardrobe, altar decorations, candle magick, and visualization practices to align more deeply with your soul path.

Expression Number, Your Natural Talents

While your Life Path reveals your soul's purpose, your Expression Number illuminates your innate abilities and natural talents. This number is calculated from your full birth name and shows the gifts you brought into this incarnation.

Letter-to-Number Conversion Chart

Each letter corresponds to a number from 1-9:

123456789
ABCDEFGHI
JKLMNOPQR
STUVWXYZ

Calculation Method

  1. Convert each letter in your full birth name to its corresponding number
  2. Add the values for each name separately (first, middle, last)
  3. Reduce each name total to a single digit (or Master Number 11/22)
  4. Add those reduced values together
  5. Reduce final sum to single digit (or Master Number)

Example: Bradley Sebastian Smith

First Name, Bradley:

  • B(2) + R(9) + A(1) + D(4) + L(3) + E(5) + Y(7) = 31
  • 3 + 1 = 4

Middle Name, Sebastian:

  • S(1) + E(5) + B(2) + A(1) + S(1) + T(2) + I(9) + A(1) + N(5) = 27
  • 2 + 7 = 9

Last Name, Smith:

  • S(1) + M(4) + I(9) + T(2) + H(8) = 24
  • 2 + 4 = 6

Final Calculation:

  • 4 + 9 + 6 = 19
  • 1 + 9 = 10
  • 1 + 0 = 1

Expression Number: 1 (Red)

Bradley's Expression Number of 1 indicates natural independence, enthusiasm, and ambition. Red, the color of Life Path 1, reinforces these pioneering qualities throughout his life.

Expression Number Meanings

Your Expression Number shares the same color correspondences as Life Path numbers:

  • 1 (Red): Natural leaders with pioneering spirit and independent drive
  • 2 (Orange): Gifted diplomats who excel at cooperation and partnership
  • 3 (Yellow): Natural performers and communicators with creative flair
  • 4 (Green): Builders and organizers who create lasting structures
  • 5 (Blue): Versatile adventurers who adapt and explore
  • 6 (Indigo): Natural caregivers drawn to service and harmony
  • 7 (Violet): Seekers of wisdom with deep analytical minds
  • 8 (Pink): Natural executives who understand material mastery
  • 9 (Bronze): Humanitarians with gifts for compassion and teaching
  • 11 (Silver): Visionaries with intuitive and spiritual perception
  • 22 (Gold): Master builders who manifest large-scale visions

Your Expression color may match your Life Path color, or differ, creating a layered color profile that influences your magickal work and self-understanding.

Soul Urge Number, Your Inner Desires

While Life Path reveals your purpose and Expression shows your talents, your Soul Urge Number exposes your deepest motivations and heart's true desires. This number is calculated from the vowels in your full birth name, revealing what drives you at the soul level.

Identifying Vowels: The Y Rule

Standard vowels are A, E, I, O, U. The letter Y requires special consideration:

  • Count Y as a vowel when: It's silent or creates a vowel sound (Bradley, Carolyn, Yvette)
  • Do NOT count Y as a vowel when: It's pronounced as a consonant at the beginning of a name (Yolande, Yusuf, Yasmin)
  • Names with multiple Y's: Some surnames contain two Y's, one vowel, one consonant (Yancey, Yockney). Evaluate each Y individually.

Calculation Method

  1. Identify all vowels in your full birth name (including Y when appropriate)
  2. Convert each vowel to its number using the chart above
  3. Add vowel values for each name separately (first, middle, last)
  4. Reduce each name total to a single digit (or Master Number 11/22)
  5. Add those reduced values together
  6. Reduce final sum to single digit (or Master Number)

Example: Bradley Sebastian Smith

First Name, Bradley:

  • A(1) + E(5) + Y(7) = 13
  • 1 + 3 = 4

(The Y is silent/forms vowel sound, so it counts)

Middle Name, Sebastian:

  • E(5) + A(1) + I(9) + A(1) = 16
  • 1 + 6 = 7

Last Name, Smith:

  • I(9) = 9

Final Calculation:

  • 4 + 7 + 9 = 20
  • 2 + 0 = 2

Soul Urge Number: 2 (Orange)

Bradley's Soul Urge of 2 reveals a deep desire for connection, harmony, and diplomatic relationships. He finds fulfillment through cooperation and bringing people together. Orange, the color of peaceful interaction, reflects his soul's true yearning.

Soul Urge Number Meanings

Your Soul Urge Number shares the same color correspondences as Life Path and Expression:

  • 1 (Red): Craves independence, leadership, and pioneering achievements
  • 2 (Orange): Desires harmony, partnership, and peaceful cooperation
  • 3 (Yellow): Longs for creative expression, joy, and communication
  • 4 (Green): Seeks stability, order, and tangible results
  • 5 (Blue): Yearns for freedom, adventure, and varied experiences
  • 6 (Indigo): Desires to nurture, serve, and create beauty
  • 7 (Violet): Craves wisdom, solitude, and spiritual understanding
  • 8 (Pink): Desires material success, recognition, and influence
  • 9 (Bronze): Longs to serve humanity and give selflessly
  • 11 (Silver): Seeks spiritual enlightenment and visionary experiences
  • 22 (Gold): Desires to build lasting legacies that transform the world

Your Personal Color Signature

Between Life Path, Expression, and Soul Urge, you now have up to three personal colors that form your numerological signature:

Life Path = Your soul's purpose and journey

Expression = Your natural talents and outer gifts

Soul Urge = Your inner desires and motivations

These colors may be identical (creating a unified, focused energy) or different (creating a multi-layered color palette for your magickal work). When all three numbers share the same color, that hue becomes exceptionally significant in your life. When they differ, you're working with complementary energies that add depth and nuance to your spiritual practice.

Incorporate these colors into candle work, altar cloths, visualization practices, wardrobe choices, and crystal selections to align with your numerological blueprint.

Day of Birth Number

Your Day of Birth number adds a fourth personal color to your numerological profile. Simply reduce the day you were born to a single digit (unless it's 11, 22, or 29).

Complete Example: Bradley Sebastian Smith

Born August 4, 1975:

  • Life Path: 7 (Violet), soul purpose
  • Expression: 1 (Red), natural talents
  • Soul Urge: 2 (Orange), inner desires
  • Day of Birth: 4 (Green), additional personal influence

Working With Your Four Colors

Each of your personal colors serves a specific function:

  • Life Path color (Violet): Use when working on something that plays a major role in your life purpose
  • Expression color (Red): Use when you want to excel at something or develop your talents
  • Soul Urge color (Orange): Use when you want to make something more enjoyable or fulfill your desires
  • Day of Birth color (Green): Use anytime, this is a supportive, always-available energy

All four colors are part of your energetic makeup. Each will prove stimulating and invigorating when you work with them consciously.

Name Variations & Shifting Colors

Few people are known by their full birth name in every context. Nicknames, shortened forms, and signature variations create different Expression and Soul Urge numbers, which changes your active color palette.

How Name Changes Affect Colors

Bradley Sebastian Smith (full birth name):

  • Expression: 1 (Red)
  • Soul Urge: 2 (Orange)

Brad Smith (nickname):

  • Expression: 4 (Green)
  • Soul Urge: 1 (Red)
  • Effect: More green reflected, orange eliminated from active palette

Bradley S. Smith (signature form):

  • Expression: 2 (Orange)
  • Soul Urge: 1 (Red)
  • Effect: All four original colors maintained, an excellent everyday name

The Permanence of Birth Name Colors

In numerology, it's believed that each soul chooses their birth name to receive specific experiences needed for growth in this incarnation. The colors from your birth name never entirely disappear, regardless of name changes. Your birth name colors form your foundational palette, while name variations temporarily emphasize different aspects of that foundation.

Missing Numbers & Colors

The individual letters in your full birth name reveal an even more detailed color portrait. By analyzing which numbers (1-9) appear in your name, you discover which colors are present and which are missing.

Analysis Method

  1. Convert every letter in your full birth name to its number
  2. Note which numbers from 1-9 appear in your name
  3. Identify which numbers are absent
  4. Those missing numbers indicate colors you need to consciously incorporate

Example: Bradley Sebastian Smith

Letter breakdown:

  • B(2), R(9), A(1), D(4), L(3), E(5), Y(7)
  • S(1), E(5), B(2), A(1), S(1), T(2), I(9), A(1), N(5)
  • S(1), M(4), I(9), T(2), H(8)

Numbers present: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9

Missing: 6 (Indigo)

Bradley would benefit from consciously adding indigo to his life, wearing indigo clothing, visualizing indigo, or working with indigo crystals. This would help him feel more whole and complete at a subconscious level.

Example: Wendy Fox

Letter breakdown:

  • W(5), E(5), N(5), D(4), Y(7)
  • F(6), O(6), X(6)

Numbers present: 4, 5, 6, 7

Missing: 1 (Red), 2 (Orange), 3 (Yellow), 8 (Pink), 9 (Bronze)

However, Wendy's Expression number is 8 and her Soul Urge is 9, which means pink and bronze aren't entirely missing. She would benefit most from consciously absorbing red, orange, and yellow, the three colors completely absent from both her name letters and core numbers.

Color Balance Analysis

Beyond simply identifying missing colors, you can assess whether each color is balanced, deficient, or excessive in your birth name. This reveals patterns in how you express (or struggle with) each color's qualities.

Ideal Balance Guidelines

For an 18-letter name, the ideal distribution is:

  • Red (1): 3 occurrences
  • Orange (2): 2 occurrences
  • Yellow (3): 2 occurrences
  • Green (4): 2 occurrences
  • Blue (5): 2 occurrences
  • Indigo (6): 2 occurrences
  • Violet (7): 1 occurrence
  • Pink (8): 2 occurrences
  • Bronze (9): 2 occurrences

For names with different lengths, scale these proportions accordingly. A color is considered low if it appears less than expected, balanced if near the ideal, and high if it appears significantly more than expected.

Interpreting Color Balance

Red (1), Independence & Initiative

Balanced: Confident, self-assured, able to initiate projects and rely on yourself

Low/Absent: Lack confidence and struggle to start new ventures; difficulty with independence

High: Aggressive, forcing your needs and desires onto others

Orange (2), Cooperation & Sensitivity

Balanced: Work well with others; cooperative, diplomatic, open, honest, and self-assured

Low/Absent: Oversensitive; struggle to cooperate easily with others

High: Highly emotional and overly reliant on others for validation

Yellow (3), Expression & Communication

Balanced: Outgoing, sociable, expressive; desire to communicate creatively

Low/Absent: Struggle to express yourself; retiring or shy nature; anxious and lacking enthusiasm

High: Frivolous, boastful, superficial; invariably put pleasure ahead of work

Green (4), Structure & Diligence

Balanced: Able to work hard when necessary; pay attention to details

Low/Absent: Avoid hard work; indecisive and careless with details

High: So immersed in minutiae that you fail to see the overall picture

Blue (5), Freedom & Adaptability

Balanced: Enjoy change and variety; generous, easy to get along with; use personal freedom responsibly

Low/Absent: Struggle to accept change; lacking in trust and ambition

High: Inclined to overindulge; make changes for no apparent reason

Indigo (6), Responsibility & Service

Balanced: Accept and handle responsibility well; gain pleasure from helping others

Low/Absent: Struggle to accept responsibility but expect perfection from others; difficulty trusting

High: Involved in family and domestic matters to the exclusion of virtually everything else

Violet (7), Wisdom & Spirituality

Balanced: Understanding, compassionate, analytical; interested in spirituality

Low/Absent: Impatient; little interest in organized religion; likely to build your own spiritual path

High: Constantly search for wisdom, knowledge, and truth (rare, few people have high violet)

Pink (8), Material Mastery & Self-Worth

Balanced: Engaged with the material world while maintaining proportion; healthy self-esteem; able to manifest ideas

Low/Absent: Struggle to appreciate true value beyond materialism; strive excessively for possessions and status; low self-esteem

High: Motivated solely by power, money, and worldly success; feel superior to those with less material achievement

Bronze (9), Humanitarianism & Compassion

Balanced: Concerned for humanity in general; compassionate toward collective needs

Low/Absent: Lacking compassion for humanity (rare, few people are deficient in bronze)

High: Rigid, stubborn, determined to do things your way; detached concern for humanity

Life Lessons Through Color

Color imbalances in your name represent lessons your soul chose to learn in this incarnation. People often repeat the same patterns until they finally integrate the lesson a color is teaching them.

By consciously working with your missing or imbalanced colors, wearing them, visualizing them, surrounding yourself with them, you accelerate your growth and feel more whole. This is not about fixing defects but about honoring the full spectrum of your being.

Color of the Day

You can apply the Life Path calculation method to any specific date to discover that day's color. This practice offers a dynamic way to experiment with color energy and observe how different hues influence your mood, energy, and behavior.

How to Calculate

Use the same method as Life Path calculation:

  1. Add the month + day + year of any date
  2. Reduce to a single digit (or Master Number 11/22)
  3. Note the corresponding color

Monthly Experiment

Try wearing or carrying the color of each day for a month. Observe how different colors affect you:

  • Extroverts might notice themselves becoming quieter and more contemplative on violet (7) days
  • Introverts might find themselves more outgoing and bold on red (1) days
  • Everyone will notice subtle shifts in energy, mood, and self-expression

This experiment teaches you firsthand how each color feels in your system, which colors energize you, which calm you, and which challenge you.

Intentional Color Use

After experimenting with daily colors, you can make conscious wardrobe and decor choices to support who you're becoming:

If you're shy or retiring: Add red or orange to boost confidence and assertiveness

If your work demands mental focus: Incorporate yellow to enhance intellect and clarity

If you need to collaborate: Wear orange to improve diplomacy and cooperation

If you're seeking wisdom: Choose violet for introspection and spiritual connection

This isn't artifice, it's alchemy. You're not pretending to be someone you're not. You're using color as a tool to amplify qualities you want to develop and embody qualities that serve your highest expression.

Beyond Personal Colors

While your Life Path, Expression, Soul Urge, and Day of Birth colors reveal core aspects of your being, they don't tell the complete story. All nine colors (plus Master Number colors) exist within your energetic field. Your personal colors are simply the most prominent frequencies in your natal blueprint.

Working with color of the day allows you to consciously explore the full spectrum, developing relationship with each hue and discovering how they support different facets of your life and work.

Color Healing

Color healing, also known as chromotherapy, operates on the principle that specific colors can stimulate energy in different parts of the body, enabling healing to occur. This ancient practice has been used for thousands of years across cultures and is experiencing a modern revival as science confirms many traditional beliefs.

Historical Foundation

Ancient Egypt

Archaeologists have discovered special rooms in ancient Egyptian temples designed to break up sunlight into rainbows. Patients would sit in rooms corresponding to the specific color they needed, demonstrating that color healing principles have been known for millennia.

India & Ayurveda

Color healing has been practiced in India for thousands of years through work on the aura and chakras. The Kurma Purana, a sacred Hindu text, refers to the creator as "Grandfather," visualized as millions of colored rays reaching every part of the universe, providing light and life.

Chinese Medicine

Traditional Chinese medicine has used color to promote healing for thousands of years, integrating chromotherapy into their holistic approach to health.

Ancient Greece

Greek physicians studied color healing extensively. The principles formulated by Pythagoras and Hippocrates remained unchallenged in the West until the Middle Ages.

Medieval & Renaissance Period

Avicenna (980–c.1037), an Arab physician, wrote Canon of Medicine describing his color therapy system. He prescribed:

  • Red flower potions for blood disorders
  • Yellow flower potions for bile duct problems

Paracelsus (1493–1541), the Swiss-German physician also known as Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim, used light and color extensively in his medical practice during the Renaissance.

Modern Revival

By the nineteenth century, Western medicine had shifted to treating only the physical body, ignoring mental and spiritual aspects. Color healing declined until three pivotal books appeared in America during the 1870s:

The Foundational Texts

1876: *Blue and Sun-lights* by Augustus Pleasanton

  • Claimed to heal animals and people through blue light exposure
  • Popular with the public but ignored by medical establishment

1877: *Blue and Red Lights* by Dr. Seth Pancoast

  • Written by an eminent physician
  • Endorsed color healing principles, lending medical credibility

1878: *The Principles of Light and Color* by Edwin S. Babbitt

  • Monumental work that became hugely successful
  • Considered Babbitt a miracle worker
  • Established different schools of color therapy still active today

Edwin Babbitt's Contributions

Babbitt is arguably the father of modern color healing. He identified red, blue, and yellow as the main healing colors, each with a complementary color that could restore balance. For example, green (complementary to red) would calm hostile or aggressive patients, as it counters red's negative traits.

20th Century Developments

Colonel Dinshah P. Ghadiali, a Hindu scientist, published Spectro-Chrome Metry Encyclopedia in 1933. He discovered that every organ could be either stimulated or inhibited by a specific color, enabling targeted healing when you know the affected organ and its corresponding color.

Contemporary Practice

Today, organizations like the International Association of Colour ensure practitioners receive proper training. Research continues, and color healing is regaining recognition as a valuable means of healing body, mind, and spirit.

Scientific Validation: Dr. Robert Gerard, a Los Angeles psychologist, confirmed that blood pressure, respiration rate, eye blinks, and brain wave patterns increase with red exposure but decrease with blue exposure.

Symbol Grimoire

The Nature of Symbols

Symbols exist everywhere. They live and breathe as part of the landscape of human understanding, present in religions and belief systems across the world, from the lavish iconography of the Catholic Church to the elaborate meanings behind the seemingly simple mudras of the East. They appear chiseled into rock, woven into coded alphabets said to contain secrets given by angels or demons, and hidden within arcane scripts of languages long forgotten.

Etymology

Secret comes from the Latin secretus, meaning "separate" or "set apart."

Sacred also derives from Latin, sacrere, meaning "holy" or "consecrated."

Symbol comes from the Greek verb symballein, meaning to "throw together," literally a "coincidence." As an object, the symballon (meaning "mark" or "token") appeared on ancient Egyptian artifacts used as signs of identification, like a ticket. As a verb, symballein was used by the Greeks to describe a gathering that was occluded or veiled, understood only by the initiate and camouflaged to the casual observer.

In this sense, all symbols are, by their very nature, secrets of one sort or another.

The Symbolate

Any object that also carries symbolic meaning is called a symbolate. A wine glass might be a handy vessel for drinking, but as the chalice or goblet it becomes a significant and universal symbol of the feminine, used as such in ritual. As the Holy Grail, it transforms further into a symbol of the deepest spiritual quest, the search for the Goddess within, the marriage of opposites, and one of the ultimate aims of alchemy.

Mercia Eliade defined the sacred as that which manifests itself as a reality different from "normal" realities. The sacred is present in everything. When a particular tree, mountain, or stone is recognized as sacred, that object becomes greater than the mere sum of its parts. If something miraculous occurs at a certain place, that place becomes sacred, and the person associated with the event may be venerated as a saint or equivalent.

Hidden Languages

Throughout history, there have been occasions when keeping certain information hidden was essential. Knowledge can be dangerous, yet recognizing other members of a secret cult or society could be a matter of survival.

In the early days of Christianity, when allegiance to the faith could result in death, followers used a simple symbol of a fish as a secret code of recognition. Gypsies, Romanies, and other traveling people developed an extensive symbolic language to keep track of one another, communicating which farmers were friendly, where companions were headed, and which towns might best be avoided. Groups like the Cathars and the Knights Templar left visual clues along the course of their wanderings, the true meaning of which we are still trying to unravel centuries later.

Native American trackers and hunters used signs and symbols invisible to anyone not attuned to them, yet carrying vital information to those who understood.

Symbolic Literacy

Symbolism concerns humanity's very knowledge of itself. Understanding symbols provides an elemental way of explaining the Universe, a method of interpreting reality that transcends time, race, culture, and everyday concerns.

J.C. Cooper expressed it this way: "The symbol goes beyond the individual to the Universal and is innate in the life of the spirit. It is the external expression of the higher truth which is symbolized."

Pictorial symbols override literacy. The messages they carry have nothing to do with the ability to read or write. The alphabetical symbols we juggle so readily are themselves among the most potent and magickal symbols ever devised, yet pictorial signs predate them all.

At the heart of symbolic study are constantly repeating themes that go to the core of human concerns: fertility, protection from the elements and the evil eye, communication with spirits and the Gods, good health and good luck, and a fine time in the Afterlife.

The Paradox of Analysis

If mystique is inherent to a symbol's nature, does explaining it strip something away? How can words describe something designed to transcend words in the first place?

To understand a symbol properly requires pinning it down for a moment, examining it from all angles, climbing into the heads of its creators and understanding their time, their beliefs, their daily concerns. Yet there is a danger in this process. Like a butterfly killed with chloroform, the outward appearance may be preserved while the essential nature is destroyed.

The Moon illustrates the counterargument. Along with the Sun, she is arguably one of humanity's most important symbols, visible to everyone, universally acknowledged. Her constantly changing face mirrors the menstrual cycle, allegedly governs tides and growth patterns, and has inspired myths, legends, and romances across every culture. The term "lunatic" derives from Luna, whose swollen fullness was believed to draw out underlying madness. When humans physically walked on her surface, fears arose that the act would somehow anger the Moon Goddess or render her symbolic meaning obsolete.

It did not. The Moon is no more a simple lump of rock than a mother is merely a member of the species with functioning reproductive organs. Instead, the "giant leap" yielded a new perspective. For the first time, humans saw their home planet from above: tiny, jewel-like, and frighteningly alone. Earth itself became a symbol, and the sorcery of a full Moon remained intact. A different perspective increased understanding without diminishing mystery.

The Mutable Nature of Symbols

A simple symbol in a film, a book, or an advertisement says far more than any wordy explanation could, acting as a visual shortcut to the part of our minds that understands them. The eye as the "mirror of the soul," the butterfly's metamorphosis as a sign of transformation, the number of the Beast, all function as compressed meaning that bypasses literacy entirely.

The meanings of symbols can change, just as a caterpillar changes into a butterfly. The number 666, personified in some cultures as the number of the Beast, sends a frisson of terror through the soul. Yet scholarship has suggested the original number may have been 665 or even 616, the subject of a scribal error thousands of years ago. It does not matter. The symbol 666, imprinted on collective consciousness after centuries of association with evil, is what carries the weight. The symbol itself has become the reality.

No Beginning, No End

Rodin said, "Man never invented anything new, only discovered things." While some symbols have been constructed for specific purposes, everything is inspired in some way by the natural world. Sometimes the revelation is immediate. Other discoveries are the result of years of painstaking observation.

The pentagram is one such discovery. The shape made in the sky by the planet Venus as she orbits the Sun describes a definite five-pointed star over the course of eight years and one day. The ancient Akkadians first charted this design and realized that the Morning Star and the Evening Star, previously considered separate celestial bodies, were one and the same. The Greeks called the morning star Eosphoros, "bringer of the dawn" (later known as Lucifer, the brightest angel cast out of the Heavens). As the Evening Star, it was Hesperos, "star of the evening," giving us the name of evening prayers, vespers.

The Goddess known to the Akkadians as Ishtar/Inanna presided over this planet, divinity of both love and war. Venus remains the only major planet aside from Earth designated a feminine spirit. The Mayans determined their calendrical system from her movements and chose propitious positions to time their wars. The five-pointed star still used as a military symbol, stenciled onto tanks and woven into insignia, derives from the stately movement of this great astral Goddess.

The apple given by Eve to Adam contained a hidden symbol within it: the pentagram created by the pattern of the seeds. Eve offered not only knowledge of the divine feminine but a symbol of the true marriage of opposites, the feminine number two wedding to the masculine number three. Eve personifies Ishtar, Venus, Aphrodite as the Goddess of sensual love, and the word "venereal" derives from Venus herself. Ishtar was later demonized as the Whore of Babylon.

A seemingly simple shape made in the sky by a planet's path, full of complexities and contradictions, clarifying some aspects while posing further questions. The quest to understand a symbol's meaning is as much a personal voyage of discovery as a collective one.

In Nature's temple, living pillars rise
Speaking sometimes in words of abstruse sense;
Man walks through woods of symbols, dark and dense,
Which gaze at him with fond familiar eyes.
Like distant echoes blent in the beyond
In unity, in a deep darksome way,
Vast as black night and vast as splendent day,
Perfumes and sounds and colors correspond
Charles Baudelaire, "Correspondences"

The Secret Language of Letters and Signs

The most versatile secret symbols we will ever meet are the letters of the alphabet. Even as your eyes move across a page, you are instantly translating these curious squiggles, marks that between them hold all the secrets of the Universe. The symbols bear no real relationship to sound, yet we still "hear" the sounds they stand for and grasp their complex ideas thousands of times a minute. What follows looks at how signs, sounds, and ideas converge, and at how other signs have been used to keep information hidden.

Sound

Everything in the Universe has its own frequency, its own vibration. The human ear cannot catch some of these frequencies, but they exist all the same. The dog whistle is a simple example, heard by dogs yet seldom by their owners. Some frequencies are powerful enough to destroy physical objects, as when a soprano's note is so pure that it shatters glass. In the biblical account, the walls of Jericho fell not to physical force but to the power of sound. Certain very low frequencies can break matter apart by scrambling its molecules, and sound can even trigger avalanches. In one memorable film scene, travelers searching for a lost city are halted at an impassable ravine, until their helpless laughter sets off an avalanche that bridges the gap and lets them continue.

Every place has its own frequency, as does the Earth itself. The natural harmonic of our planet is said to be F sharp, a note recognized by ancient peoples including the Egyptians, whose Great Pyramid is said to "play" it, and the Chinese, who called it Hu. Native Americans, by the same account, tune their flutes to this note.

Does this mean our most secret and sacred symbols are inspired by something that can be heard but never seen? Sounds can only be set down by us as written squiggles, and like the wind we gauge them only by their effect on something else. Arguably the most important symbol in the world is one that can be neither touched nor seen.

This hidden power has long been tied to sacred architecture. At the Romanesque-Byzantine abbey at Souillac, built by Eleanor of Aquitaine, a carved capital on the eighth pillar shows doves dipping their beaks into an owl's ear. The owl is Athena's, a sign of access to knowledge, and the carving is said to mark a spot where the building's acoustics produce a startling second harmonic, audible only from that exact place, opening what the ancients called the "third ear." Ancient megalithic structures such as Newgrange in Ireland and Wayland's Smithy in England seem to have been raised to exploit such effects. Mogul palaces in India were designed so that guards could clap at set points, the loud echoes serving as an intruder alarm. The Whispering Gallery at St. Paul's Cathedral in London is built so that a whisper can be heard clearly on the far side, directly opposite the speaker.

Words

Many faiths agree on at least one point: that the primal resonance of a word, or sound, gave birth to the Universe, and that the source of this first sound was divine. The Bible puts it this way:

In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. (John 1:1)

The Quran speaks of it too:

Words of Truth that have the power to express the Truth are like flourishing trees whose roots, or direct meanings, are established deep in the earth of the heart, and whose branches, or subtle meanings, reach high into the sky of mystical knowledge.

So great is the power of a word that it is held to be the very seed of creation. The old line "sticks and stones may break my bones, but words can never hurt me" takes no account of the potency of a curse; whether that power rests in superstition or not, its consequences are real enough. In the same way, a blessing carries wishes that are a strong force for good.

For the Greeks, logos, meaning "word," was not only the spoken word or phrase but was bound up with the intellect and with ideas themselves. The gift of eloquence belonged to the gods, or lent godlike standing to those who mastered it; a leader without the art of oratory will never truly hold power. Among the Druids, whose oral tradition outlasted the coming of writing, there were charms and rituals said to confer eloquence, such as placing a cinquefoil leaf under the tongue. Learning by repetition was thought the purest way to take in knowledge, since passing words from one mouth to the next kept their intention undiluted by the "middle man" of writing.

Letters and Writing

The journey from primal sound to deliberate word to written symbol is a mysterious one. Just as children learn to draw before they can write, early humanity's first "writing" was symbolic, a pictorial way of setting down ideas. The history of writing is well documented elsewhere, but the sacred weight of the alphabet shows in how widely cultures credit its invention to the divine: Thoth for the Ancient Egyptians, Hermes or Mercury in the Greco-Roman world, Odin in Norse myth, and Ogma in the Celtic pantheon. In Hinduism, Sarasvati is not only the Goddess of Speech but is also called Lipidevi, the Goddess of the Alphabet. Letters, along with numbers, are the most potent of all secret signs and sacred symbols, their meanings so ingrained in us that we take them for granted.

The letters of any alphabet carry great power; they are not merely letters but calendars, calculators, symbols, and ideas of divinity. It is worth remembering that, not so long ago, reading and writing were arts reserved for the powerful and priestly castes, for with them came the power of knowledge, even the power to transcribe the very Word of God. The first printed texts were religious. Once ordinary people could read and write, and so choose for themselves which ideas to favor, the grip of both secular and religious authorities was much loosened.

The Hebrew language is said to hold secrets known only to God, secrets dangerous enough to work miracles, even the raising of the dead. The Torah likens the vowels of the alphabet to the living soul of a person and the consonants to the world of matter. Fittingly, the vowel signs are rounded in shape while the consonants are angular: the vowels are seen as spiritual, perhaps because they are formed freely, without the tongue or teeth needing to meet, while the constructed consonants stand for the material world. It is also said that God gave Adam 32 letters, of which some 10 were lost, leaving the 22-letter alphabet we have today.

For all its power, writing in some ways "kills" ideas by fixing them in permanent form. Ideas change, and revolutionary theories harden into everyday fact. As with every sign and symbol gathered here, it is worth keeping that in mind when exploring the hidden meanings of the alphabets themselves.

Sacred Geometry in Sacred Places

Sacred geometry is the study of proportion and form as an expression of divine order. The word geometry comes from the Greek for "measurement of the Earth." People have always needed ways to define and order space, and geometry answers that need. Geometry becomes sacred when its proportions are shaped to please the gods, when a structure is built with the conscious aim of resonating in harmony with the natural, divinely created world. The same reasoning that frames the solid material plane also lets us measure the movement of the stars and planets, and so understand our own place in the cosmos.

Sacred geometry was never the property of a single culture. The intricate patterns of Islamic architecture grew from the belief that certain measurements belong to a divine plan, and Gothic and Renaissance builders followed the same principles. Its influence runs from the Pyramids to modern landmarks both secular and sacred. Contemporary engineering lets fluid, organic shapes enter large structures, as in Gaudí's Sagrada Família in Barcelona, Jørn Utzon's Sydney Opera House, and Norman Foster's 30 St. Mary Axe in London, popularly called the Gherkin.

What sets these proportions apart from ordinary measurement is harmony. Spatial proportion is only one part of the picture. The same principles underpin the harmonics and frequencies of music and color as well as the patterns of natural forms. Numbers, like letters, were treated as sacred symbols in their own right, and our ancestors saw the two as deeply connected. Phi is one such symbol, known also as the golden mean, the golden section, the golden ratio, and the divine proportion.

Golden Section

Of all the sacred signs, the golden section may be the most surprising, since it surfaces throughout the natural world in the most unexpected places. Clench your hand, tuck the index finger into the base of the thumb, and wrap the thumb in tight, and you trace its form. The spirals of shells and ammonite fossils, the seed heads of sunflowers, and the stylized unfurling fern fronds of Māori art all obey its rules. The Fibonacci sequence (see the Numbers section) serves as a kind of instruction manual for building this never-ending spiral.

Technically, the golden section is any point that divides a line so that the smaller part relates to the larger part exactly as the larger part relates to the whole. This divine proportion runs through every line of the Pentagram, which helps explain why the five-pointed star feels so satisfying and intriguing a symbol.

Platonic Solids

Though named for the Greek philosopher and mathematician Plato, these shapes were known long before him, and the first three were identified by Pythagoras. Plato set out his account around 360 BC. Because each solid corresponds to an element, the group was said to encompass everything within the known universe.

The Platonic solids are the only five regular polyhedrons. Each is a multi-sided, three-dimensional figure whose corners all touch the surface of a single orb. Irregular polyhedrons number in the millions, but only five regular ones exist, and each is matched to an element:

  • Earth: the cube, or hexahedron, a fitting emblem for the solidity of the planet.
  • Fire: the tetrahedron, its pyramid form suitably flame-like.
  • Air: the octahedron.
  • Water: the icosahedron.
  • Ether, or aether: the dodecahedron. Aristotle named the fifth element, though he did not tie it to this solid, while Plato held that God used the dodecahedron to arrange the constellations across the heavens.

The five solids also shaped the model proposed by Johannes Kepler, a German astronomer of the early seventeenth century. With five planets then known, Kepler tried to fit their orbits to the shapes of the solids. He abandoned the idea, but his experiments led him to discover that planetary orbits are not circular.

At first glance the Platonic solids may not look secret or sacred. Their discovery, though, reshaped our understanding of how the universe is ordered, and the beauty of their regular forms remains a profound influence on sacred geometry and architecture. All five can be drawn out from Metatron's Cube, which is itself built from the Flower of Life.

Places of Pilgrimage

The structures that most clearly follow sacred geometry tend to be places of worship or tombs, though not always, as the hogan and the yurt show. Sometimes a natural feature of the landscape becomes part of the building itself, as with the church that once crowned Glastonbury Tor. Siting a temple on a high place adds value to the work of human hands, making it prominent in the landscape and drawing on the shared symbolism of the altar, the holy building, and the mountain, all of which express the human reach toward the divine.

The places gathered under this theme range from the famous to the obscure, the grand to the humble, including some that few would think to call a pilgrimage site at all. What unites them is that each was built with the conscious use of sacred geometry, an attempt to please God by shaping a small piece of Heaven on Earth. That single intention is what renders them holy. The outward form of this celestial reflection may change, but its meaning holds steady, and like every symbolic discipline sacred geometry keeps growing and evolving, much like the spiral traced by the golden mean. Some whole cities are revered as earthly images of the heavenly archetype, among them Varanasi, Jerusalem, and Mecca.

Temples, Cathedrals & Shrines

Symbol Grimoire

The Body as a Sacred Map

In trying to grasp the deeper mysteries of the Universe, our ancestors understandably began with the most accessible and easily defined thing they knew: themselves. The human body, with its head in the stars and its feet on the ground, is the most universal of all sacred symbols. Ancient peoples believed that the body held every secret of the Universe within it, both inside and out.

The opening book of the Bible offers a short statement that captures an idea which has fascinated humankind for thousands of years:

So God created man in His own image. (Genesis 1:27)

Philosophers, theologians, poets, artists, and mystics have all tried to explain this idea in their own ways. In the thirteenth century, the philosopher Albertus Magnus held that humankind was not only the image of God, the imago dei, but also the image of the Universe, the imago mundi. The Theosophist Helena Blavatsky echoed this in the early twentieth century when she described a person as a little world, a microcosm set inside a great Universe.

In what may be the most profound act of mutual adoration ever witnessed, humans in turn created their gods in their own image. Ancient peoples believed that deities ruled over each part of the body, so that every part was charged with divine qualities and its own mythology. We see this in the All Seeing Eye of God, the Eye of Horus, the feet of the Buddha or Vishnu, and the phallus of Priapus. Pythagoras taught that to disfigure the body in any way was a sacrilege against the dwelling place of the Gods.

For the Pythagoreans, the magick resonating within numbers also helped define the nature of humankind. Five is widely accepted as the number of the human being, because it counts the body's most important extremities: the head, the two hands, and the two feet. The feet correspond to the elements of earth and water, the hands to air and fire, and the head to ether, the fifth element that governs all the others.

Our modern ideas about the body are not so different from these older beliefs. Like Pythagoras, we sanctify the body by calling it a temple, and we grant powers to certain parts that have nothing to do with their mechanical roles. These associations persist despite all our advances in biology and physiology. The heart is still the symbolic seat of the emotions, and of love above all. To be "gutsy" is to be brave and forthright. To vent one's spleen is to air an irritation. To say that the head rules the heart is to say that intellect prevails over emotion.

The practical ways we use our bodies have shaped how we make sense of the wider Universe. Our ten fingers govern how we count and give their name to the base-10, or digital, way of measuring. Because a warrior typically held a weapon in the right hand and defended with a shield on the left, the right side of the body became associated with attack and the left with defense. From this, the right side came to be seen as the masculine side, linked to the Sun, fire, and light, while the left belongs to the feminine, the Moon, water, and darkness.

The physical and spiritual aspects of a person are bound up with the greater Universe as well. The body houses the spirit for as long as it survives. In another sense, the body is the clothing of the spirit, and each part of it reflects the soul, the breath of life preserved within.

The Greeks pictured the Earth itself as a giant human figure curled into a ball, with Delphi as the Omphalos, the navel of the world. Early philosophers held that all things represented the body, if not in form then in essence. The natural world is full of these analogies: mountains become the nourishing breasts of the Mother Goddess, caves her womb, and certain trees and rocks become phallic symbols. In effect, the body is a measuring stick for the Universe.

Centuries after the Greeks, Leonardo da Vinci expressed the same idea in his famous drawing of the Vitruvian Man. Vitruvius was an influential Roman architect of the first century BC, and the idealized building proportions he set down inspired Leonardo, who worked from the belief that mathematics provided the foundation for everything. The sketch shows a figure set inside both a circle and a square, with the navel at the exact center. These same proportions appear in architecture, art, music, and harmony, and we seem to recognize this "divine proportion" instinctively wherever it is applied. The drawing is regarded as the ultimate rendering of the body, its measurements a symbol of divine intention.

The Kabbalistic Tree of Life is often laid over a human figure, its proportions aligning with the parts of the body that represent the esoteric principles of that arcane system. The idea of the body as a blueprint for the Universe appears in astrology as well, where each sign of the Zodiac rules a different body part. The first sign, Aries, governs the head, and the authority of the signs flows downward through the body to the last, Pisces, which rules the feet.
